metadata.title: These 3 Equipment Niches Pay $12,500 to $20,000 Per Deal
metadata.author: Equipment Finance Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Grab the full broker training and brokerage playbook at https://www.equipmentfinanceacademy.com

Most brokers chase small leases and wonder why the commissions stay small. The money in this business isn't in volume — it's in the asset class you choose to specialize in.

In this video, I break down the three equipment niches that routinely produce $12,500 to $20,000 commissions on a single transaction, why lenders love financing them, and exactly where to find the deals.

Niche #1 — Heavy Construction & Earthmoving Equipment
Units routinely run $250,000 to over $1 million. A $350,000 Caterpillar excavator package pays a broker $14,000 to $17,500 at a 4% to 5% spread. Lenders favor these because heavy machinery holds strong resale value — if a borrower defaults, there's a liquid secondary market at equipment auctions.

Niche #2 — Medical & Aesthetic Technology
Equipment typically priced $150,000 to $750,000. A $250,000 multi-platform laser system pays $12,500 to $15,000 at a 5% to 6% fee. Medical professionals bring strong personal credit, clean debt-to-income ratios, and predictable revenue — and practices upgrade their technology every 3 to 5 years.

Niche #3 — Specialized Vocational & Commercial Fleets
A single high-spec hydrovac truck costs $300,000 to $500,000. Two vocational units totaling $500,000 pays $20,000 at a conservative 4%. Vocational contractors usually have long-term municipal, utility, or commercial pipeline contracts attached to the machinery.

Where to source each one: independent machinery dealerships and regional auction reps for construction, medical device manufacturer sales reps for technology, and local public municipal contract awards and infrastructure bids for vocational fleets.

If you're building a brokerage or looking to move into bigger deals, subscribe to Equipment Finance Academy — new broker training every week.

https://www.equipmentfinanceacademy.com

Disclaimer: Results vary. Commissions described in this video are one broker's experience and Sam's own deal history, not a guarantee of income or results for anyone else.

segments.text: At the end of the video there is a free gift for you, it’s a quality business
plan template that will guide you through the whole process of starting a business
and ensures you start on the right foot. Starting a heavy equipment business can
be a lucrative venture, but it requires careful planning and execution due to the
substantial investment involved. Here's a step-by-step guide to help you get started:
1. Market Research: Begin by researching the heavy equipment industry in your area. Understand the
demand for various types of equipment, existing competitors, pricing, and potential customers.
2. Business Plan: Develop a comprehensive business plan outlining your business goals,
target market, services offered, marketing strategy,
financial projections, and operational plan. This will serve as a roadmap for your business.
3. Legal Structure and Registration: Choose a suitable legal structure for your business,
such as sole proprietorship, partnership, or LLC,
and register your business with the appropriate authorities. Obtain any necessary licenses and
permits required to operate a heavy equipment business in your locality.
4. Financing: Determine the amount of capital required to start and operate your business.
Explore financing options such as loans, investors, or personal savings. Consider
leasing or financing the equipment rather than purchasing outright to conserve capital.
5. Equipment Acquisition: Acquire the necessary heavy equipment for your business. Research
different manufacturers and suppliers to find reliable and high-quality equipment
at competitive prices. Consider factors such as warranty, maintenance support, and resale value.
6. Insurance: Obtain insurance coverage for your heavy equipment, business premises,
and liability protection. This may include general liability insurance,
equipment insurance, and workers' compensation insurance, depending on your specific needs.
7. Location: Depending on the size and scope of your business, you may need a physical location
for office space, equipment storage, and maintenance facilities. Choose a location
that is easily accessible to your target market and complies with zoning regulations.
8. Marketing and Branding: Develop a marketing strategy to promote your heavy equipment business.
This may include creating a professional website, attending industry trade shows, networking with
contractors and construction companies, and advertising through online and offline channels.
9. Staffing: Hire qualified employees to operate and maintain your heavy equipment, as
well as administrative staff to handle day-to-day operations, customer inquiries, and bookkeeping
tasks. Invest in training programs to ensure safety and proficiency among your workforce.
10. Compliance and Safety: Familiarize yourself with industry regulations and safety standards
governing the operation of heavy equipment. Implement strict safety protocols and provide
ongoing training to ensure compliance and minimize the risk of accidents or injuries.
11. Customer Service: Focus on providing exceptional customer service to build
long-term relationships with clients and generate repeat business. Promptly
address any issues or concerns raised by customers and strive to exceed their
expectations in terms of reliability, efficiency, and professionalism.
12. Continuous Improvement: Stay abreast of industry trends, technological advancements,
and customer preferences to remain competitive in the heavy equipment market. Continuously evaluate
and optimize your business processes to maximize efficiency and profitability.
Starting a heavy equipment business requires dedication, hard work,
and a willingness to overcome challenges along the way. With careful planning and execution,
you can build a successful and sustainable business in this thriving industry.
Thank you for watching. As we conclude the video go to the description below
this video to get your free business plan template gift. It will guide you through
the whole process of starting a business and ensures you start on the right foot.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Heavy Machinery Rental Business
metadata.author: A Finance Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
📌Have you ever wondered how much money it really takes to own a heavy machinery rental business? Renting excavators, bulldozers, cranes, loaders, and other powerful machines may look like a straightforward business, but behind every rental is a complex operation involving expensive equipment, maintenance, transportation, insurance, employees, and customer demand.

In this video, we explore the complete economics of owning a heavy machinery rental business from the ground up. How much does it cost to buy construction equipment? How much can a rental company charge per day or per month? Where does the money actually go? And how many rental days does a machine need to generate before it becomes profitable?

We break down the real business model behind heavy equipment rental companies, including machinery purchase costs, financing, depreciation, maintenance, repairs, fuel, transportation, storage yards, insurance, operator requirements, employee wages, construction contracts, rental pricing, utilization rates, operating expenses, revenue, profit margins, and the financial risks that can make or break the business.

If you enjoy business documentaries, economics, entrepreneurship, investing, construction, real estate, industrial businesses, and learning how major businesses actually make money, this channel is for you.


⚠️Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only. Financial figures are estimates and may vary depending on equipment type, location, utilization, financing, and market conditions.


#heavymachinery  #equipmentrental  #constructionbusiness  #MachineryRental #businesseconomics  #economicsexplained  #businessexplained  #entrepreneurship  #investing  #construction #finance

But used machinery comes with real risk. hidden hydraulic wear, engine hours nearing the end of their productive life, and none of the manufacturer warranty coverage that protects a new purchase. A genuinely functional starter fleet, something like 8 to 12 pieces of mixed equipment covering excavation, loading, and compaction work, typically requires an investment of 1 to$3 million before you've rented out a single machine for a single day. And here's the detail almost every firsttime buyer misses. You're not just buying machines. You're buying massive depreciating assets that lose value every single month, whether they're working or sitting parked. Which is exactly why banks scrutinize these loans so heavily and typically require 20 to 30% down in cash before they'll even discuss financing the rest. Now, here's where it gets interesting, because the purchase price is honestly the easy part to understand. a number you negotiate once and move past. The real financial commitment of owning a rental fleet is a recurring relentless set of costs that exist. Whether every machine in your yard is out working or every single one is sitting idle. And this is exactly where the passive income fantasy starts to fall apart. Financing costs are the first shock because most rental businesses finance the bulk of their fleet. And at commercial equipment lending rates, typically running 7 to 10%, a $2 million fleet can carry a monthly loan payment of 25 to $35,000 due every single month, regardless of how much of your equipment actually got rented that period. Insurance is the next major line item. And heavy equipment insurance runs dramatically higher than a standard commercial policy because you're insuring machines that operate on unpredictable job sites, get transported constantly, and carry genuine liability risk if something goes wrong while someone else is operating your property, typically running 3 to 6% of the equipment's value annually. Then there's maintenance. And this is where the real weight of this business sits. Because heavy machinery requires scheduled service at fixed hour intervals, regardless of your rental calendar, oil changes, hydraulic fluid replacement, undercarriage wear on tracked equipment, and a single major component failure, a blown hydraulic pump, or a failed transmission can run 8 to $25,000 to repair, arriving on its own schedule with zero regard for whether that machine is currently generating you any income at all. If you've subscribed already, thank you. And if you haven't yet, this is genuinely the moment because what comes next is the part that decides whether a rental yard becomes a genuinely profitable business or a very expensive parking lot full of machines slowly losing value. Let's talk about utilization rate because this is the single most important number in this entire industry and it's almost never explained honestly before someone buys their first fleet. Picture this. You've bought a beautiful $200,000 excavator. Confident it'll rent constantly given how busy the local construction market looks. The first month it rents for 18 out of 30 days. Feels great. Revenue is flowing. Then a slow season hits. A couple of big local projects wrap up and suddenly that same machine sits in the yard for three straight weeks. still accumulating its loan payment, still depreciating, still requiring insurance coverage, generating exactly 0 in rental income the entire time. Industry data on rental utilization shows that even well-run equipment rental businesses typically only achieve 50 to 65% utilization across their fleet on an annual basis. Meaning a significant portion of every single machine's calendar year is spent sitting completely idle. And that idle time isn't a minor inconvenience. It's baked directly into the economics of the business from day one. This is exactly why experienced rental operators price every single day of rental income, not against the days the machine is actually working, but against the entire year, including the idle stretches. Because a machine that needs to generate enough revenue to cover its own costs across 365 days, can only actually do that if the working days are priced to also cover the empty ones. This connects to something almost nobody explains to firsttime operators before they build out their fleet. The type of equipment you choose determines your entire risk exposure to local market swings. A yard heavily concentrated in equipment used almost exclusively for new residential construction will see utilization collapse the moment interest rates rise and housing starts slow down. While a yard with a more diversified mix, equipment used in road maintenance, utility work, and municipal contracts alongside private construction tends to weather those same downturns far more smoothly because government infrastructure spending doesn't pause the same way private construction does when the broader economy tightens. This is exactly why the operators who survive multiple economic cycles in this business obsess over diversifying both their equipment mix and their customer base. Because a yard that depends entirely on one type of client, say residential homebuilders, is one interest rate hike away from watching utilization across the entire fleet collapse simultaneously. Quick reminder if this is helping you see the numbers more clearly. Subscribing genuinely helps this channel keep making these breakdowns and there's a lot more coming on exactly this kind of decision. Now, let's put the entire picture together because this is where the busyard dream and the actual financial reality either line up or they don't. Take a midsize rental operation with a $2 million fleet financed with roughly 70% debt, generating an average of 55% utilization across the year at a blended daily rate of $350 per machine across 12 pieces of equipment. That works out to roughly $500,000 in annual rental revenue. Loan payments on the financed portion run approximately $300,000 a year. Insurance takes another $80,000. Maintenance and repairs, budgeted properly rather than reactively, run another 12 to 15% of revenue, roughly $70,000. Transportation costs, since heavy equipment needs to be delivered and picked up from job sites using specialized flatbed trucks and drivers with the right licensing, add another $40,000 annually. Yard rent, staff wages for equipment technicians and a dispatcher and general overhead add another 60,000. Add it all together and total annual expenses land somewhere around $550,000 against $500,000 in revenue. Meaning a business that looks genuinely impressive from the outside, a full yard, trucks constantly coming and going can actually be operating at a loss in a below average year. And the gap between a strong utilization year and a weak one can easily swing several hundred,000 in either direction on the exact same fleet. Here's the part that never shows up in the glossy equipment dealer brochure. And it's worth saying plainly before we close this out. The operators who actually build real lasting wealth in this business almost never do it by simply buying more machines and hoping utilization sorts itself out. They do it by becoming genuinely disciplined about fleet age. Selling equipment before major component failures become likely rather than after. Because a well-maintained used fleet sold at the right moment recovers real resale value that keeps the entire financial cycle sustainable. They do it by building relationships with repeat commercial and municipal clients who book equipment months in advance, smoothing out the unpredictable swings that destroy operators relying purely on walk-in rental demand. And they do it by understanding from the very first machine they buy that every single piece of equipment sitting in that yard is not a passive asset quietly earning money in the background. It's a depreciating expensive liability the moment it's not out working. And the businesses that survived decades in this industry are run by the people who never forgot that distinction, even when the yard looked completely full and business looked impossibly good. If this video helped you see what's actually happening behind that busy equipment yard, do yourself a favor and subscribe because we break down the real numbers behind the businesses people assume are simple. And this is exactly the kind of thing nobody tells you before you sign that fleet financing agreement.

metadata.title: How Construction Equipment Rental Companies Quietly Make $60 Billion a Year
metadata.author: The Markup
metadata.shortDescription:
Every time you drive past a construction site, you're looking at a $60 billion industry and almost nobody talks about it.
The excavators, scissor lifts, and concrete mixers you see aren't owned by the construction companies using them. They're rented. And the companies behind those rentals are printing money in one of the most overlooked business models in America.
In this video, we break down exactly how construction equipment rental companies make their money — from the core rental model to the hidden revenue streams most people never see coming.
🔔 Subscribe for more business breakdowns every week.

#business  #HowMoneyWorks #construction #entrepreneurship  #finance

When was the last time someone sold you an item of construction equipment?   Not when did you BUY a machine; but when someone SOLD you a machine that you didn't know you wanted or needed.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning an Excavator Rental Business
metadata.author: Millionaires Fast Track
metadata.shortDescription:
One excavator can cost more than a house. And the company that owns it does not sell the machine — it sells time with the machine. That is the whole business, and it is worth billions.

In this documentary, we follow the money through one machine: what it costs to buy, what it earns when it works, what it costs to keep working, and where the profit actually sits.

We start with real American list prices by size class, then the financing, the yard, and the used market — where hours matter more than age. We look at United Rentals, the largest equipment rental company in the world: $15.3 billion in revenue in 2024, 85% of it from renting equipment, and $1.5 billion from selling used rental machines — more than five times its new-equipment sales. We break down real rental rates, the utilisation number that decides everything, and the costs most owners underestimate: fuel, maintenance, transport and depreciation. Then we do the arithmetic — two clearly labelled illustrative examples, built from verified prices — and compare the thin margins of a one-machine owner with the scale of the big rental companies.

Every figure in this video is sourced. Where no price could be verified, we say so — including the fact that neither Caterpillar nor Komatsu publishes an American list price for a 20-tonne excavator.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Title
0:03 Hook
0:48 Introduction
1:33 Initial Investment
4:42 How the Business Works
7:43 Revenue Model
10:03 Operating Expenses
12:53 Profit Breakdown
16:35 Risks and Challenges
18:34 Final Conclusion

SOURCES (all figures verified in research, see RESEARCH/research.md)
- American Rental Association — US construction & general tool rental industry, 2024
- Kubota — published American list prices by size class, October 2026
- United Rentals, Inc. — FY2024 results (total revenue $15,345m; rental revenue $13,029m; fleet $21.43bn; net income $2,600m)
- Herc Holdings — FY2024 results and Q3 2026 dollar utilisation (43.5%)
- Ashtead Group / Sunbelt Rentals — FY2025 results (adjusted operating profit $2,687m)
- DOZR rental pricing guide — 1,193 real rental quotes, updated March 2026
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — median wage, heavy equipment operators, May 2025 ($28.78/hr)
- U.S. Energy Information Administration / AAA — US diesel prices 2025–2026
- City of Pocatello, Idaho — Caterpillar 304 lease, February 2026 (public record)

FOOTAGE
Real footage and photographs only — Pexels, Mixkit and Wikimedia Commons, each asset licence-checked and logged (FOOTAGE/asset_license_log.md). No AI visuals.
Attribution: excavator digging/loading footage by KEmel49, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

not sell the machine. It sells time with
the machine. That is the whole business,
and it is worth billions.
In the United States alone, the
construction and general tool rental
industry took in more than $80 billion
in a single year according to the
American Rental Association.
More than half of all construction
equipment in America is now rented
rather than owned.
So here is the question. If a 20 ton
excavator costs hundreds of thousands of
dollars, how does anyone make money by
renting it out by the day?
The answer is not the daily rate. It is
utilization, financing, fuel,
maintenance, and what the machine is
worth when it is finally sold.
This is the economics of owning an
excavator rental business. An excavator
is one of the most common machines on
any construction site.
It digs foundations, loads trucks, tears
down old buildings, and grades roads.
It is also one of the most expensive
tools a contractor will ever touch.
A small mini excavator can cost less
than a family car.
A full-size 20 ton machine can cost as
much as a house in many American cities.
Almost no contractor wants that much
money sitting in a machine they only
need for 3 weeks. So they rent.
And that simple decision created an
industry.
In this video, we will follow the money
through one machine,
what it costs to buy, what it earns when
it works,
what it costs to keep working,
and where the profit actually sits.
Because the answer is not where most
people expect it.
Let us start with the purchase because
everything else in this business is
measured against it.
Excavators are sold by weight class, and
the price rises fast with size.
A mini excavator under 1 ton lists from
around $28,000.
A 1 to 2 ton machine lists from around
A 3 to 4 ton machine, like the Kubota
U35, lists at $56,147.
A 5 to 6 machine lists from around
and an 8 to 10 ton machine at $138,273.
Those are published American list prices
from Kubota recorded in October 2026
excluding freight, tax, and attachments.
Then there is the yard, land, a fence, a
workshop, a truck and a trailer, and
insurance before the first machine ever
leaves the yard.
Add transport permits and the right
local zoning.
None of that is free and none of it
earns a dollar until a customer calls.
Now the 20 ton machine, the workhorse of
commercial construction.
Here is something unusual.
Neither Caterpillar nor Komatsu
publishes an American list price for a
20 ton excavator and a specialist dealer
states plainly that none exists.
So we will not invent one.
What we can verify is the used market.
In June 2025 a 2018 Caterpillar 320 sold
at auction for $137,500.
In December 2025 a 2023 machine with
only 89 hours sold for $167,200
in Oklahoma
and a 2021 machine with nearly 5,000
hours sold for $113,300
in Arizona.
Same model, wildly different prices
because in the used market hours matter
more than age.
Most owners do not pay cash. American
equipment finance typically runs from 6
to 14% a year over 2 to 7 years and a
lender will often finance 80 to 100% of
a new machine's value.
A used machine is harder, usually 80% at
most on shorter terms.
Caterpillar's finance arm also offers
low promotional rates on new compact
machines.
In one dealer offer from 2026 0% for 12
months for customers who qualify.
And here is a real lease on the public
record. The city of Pocatello, Idaho
leased a 2026 Caterpillar 304 mini
excavator in February 2026 at a sale
price of $69,808.
With five annual payments of $8,545
and a $40,000 balloon payment at the end
It was a government lease, not a small
business deal.
American tax law also offers a deduction
for equipment purchases. Section 179
allows up to $2.5 million in 2025,
but any owner should confirm it with an
accountant before counting on it.
So the purchase is only the beginning.
The real question is the monthly
payment. Here's how the machine actually
earns. A customer, a contractor, a
landscaper, a farmer, a homeowner
digging a pool books the machine for a
day, a week, or a month.
The rental company delivers it on a
truck, drops it on site, and picks it up
when the job is done.
Sometimes the customer operates it
themselves, sometimes they pay extra for
an operator.
When it comes back, it is washed,
inspected, and fueled. Then it goes out
again.
The speed of that cycle is the business.
The company we will keep coming back to
is United Rentals, the largest equipment
rental company in the world. In 2024, it
reported total revenue of $15.3 billion.
85% of that, $13 billion,
came from renting equipment, not selling
it, renting it.
It operates more than 1,600 locations,
employs nearly 28,000 people, and owns a
fleet worth $21.4 billion at original
cost, more than 1.1 million machines and
tools.
The model is the same at every size. Buy
the machine once, rent it hundreds of
times. The second half of the model is
what most people miss.
A rental company does not only earn
while the machine works, it earns again
when the machine is sold.
In 2024, United Rentals took in $1.5
billion from selling used rental
equipment and only $282 million
from selling brand new equipment.
Used sales were more than five times new
sales. The machine is bought, rented for
years, and then sold while it still has
value.
That second sale is part of the profit.
The third half of the model is the
extras, delivery, attachments, damage
waivers, and operator.
A hydraulic thumb rents for $50 to $100
a day. A breaker, $150 to $300.
A damage waiver is typically 10 to 15%
on top of the rental rate.
Delivery for a mid-size machine is $300
to $500 for the round trip.
Each of these is small. Together, they
change the economics of every rental.
And there is a fourth revenue stream
that only the big companies have, scale.
United Rentals and its rivals rent
everything, lifts, generators, pumps,
trench boxes, power systems.
An excavator customer often rents five
other things on the same job.
A one-machine owner cannot do that.
Keep that in mind because it matters
when we reach the profit.
The American Rental Association reported
that the rental business directly and
indirectly supported 666,000
jobs in 2024,
paid $47.4 billion in wages, and
contributed $115 billion to American
economic output.
The big operators measure success not by
one machine, but by fleet productivity,
a combined measure of rates,
utilization, and the mix of machines.
United Rentals reported fleet
productivity up 4.1% in 2024 and up 2.2%
again in 2025.
Now the rates, the actual money.
These are real American rental prices
from a pricing guide based on 1,193
real rental quotes across the United
States and Canada, updated in March
A mini excavator, 1 and 1/2 to 4 tons,
rents for $150 to $400 a day,
and $1,200 to $3,200 a month.
A small machine, 5 to 10 tons, rents for
400 to 700 a day.
A mid-size machine, 13 to 25 tons, the
class that does most commercial work,
rents for 700 to 1,500 a day.
2,100 to 4,500 a week and 5,500
to 12,000 a month.
A large machine, 30 to 50 tons, rents
for 1,500 to 3,000 a day and up to
25,000 a month.
Across all sizes, the average is 719 a
day, 2,021 a week, and 5,108
a month.
Notice the pattern. A week costs about 3
days. A month costs about 3 weeks. The
longer you rent, the cheaper each day
becomes and the more the rental company
depends on the machine staying out, not
coming back.
Because here is the number that decides
everything, utilization.
Utilization is the share of the time a
machine is actually out earning.
A machine sitting in the yard earns
nothing while the loan, the insurance,
and the depreciation keep running.
The big companies measure it in dollars,
annual rental revenue divided by the
cost of the fleet.
United Rentals runs at roughly 44 to 47%
on that measure.
Herc Holdings, another large American
rental company, reported 43.5%
in the third quarter of 2026.
Think about what that means.
Even the best operators in the world
earn rental revenue equal to less than
half their fleet's value in a year.
A small owner with one machine does not
have a fleet to average across.
One slow winter month can erase the
margin of three good ones.
So the revenue model is not the daily
rate. The daily rate is the price of the
ticket. Utilization is whether anyone is
buying tickets. Now the other side of
the ledger, what does it cost to keep an
excavator earning?
Start with fuel. A mini excavator burns
roughly 2 to 4 liters of diesel an hour.
A 20 ton machine burns roughly 10 to 17
liters an hour, depending on the work.
On the American diesel price of 2025,
$3.66 a gallon on average, that is
roughly $15 to $30 of fuel for a mini
excavator on an 8-hour day and roughly
for a 20 ton machine.
Fuel prices move. In 2026, American
diesel averaged $5.15 a gallon through
early November with a weekly peak above
Next, the operator. In most rentals, the
customer supplies the operator and the
rental company avoids this cost
entirely.
But an operated rental, machine plus
driver, adds $400 to $800 a day and the
driver's wage is the floor.
The American Bureau of Labor Statistics
reports the median wage for heavy
equipment operators at $28.78
an hour in May 2025 or just under
That is the wage the operator takes
home. The employer's loaded cost is
higher.
Then maintenance. Tracks wear out,
hydraulic hoses fail, filters, oil,
grease, pins, and bushings are constant.
A mid-size machine is estimated to cost
$5,000 to $15,000 a year in maintenance
according to the rental pricing guide. A
rule of thumb, not a verified fact, and
it does not include a major failure.
An undercarriage replacement, the tracks
and rollers a machine runs on, is one of
the largest single bills an owner will
ever face and no verified American price
for it could be found in our research.
Insurance comes next. The machine itself
must be insured against theft and
damage. The business needs liability
cover and the trucks that move the
machines need commercial policies.
The only verified figure is the
customer's side, a damage waiver of 10
to 15% on top of the rental rate.
Then transport. Every rental begins and
ends with a truck, a low boy trailer, a
driver, fuel, and permits. $300 to $500
for a round trip on a mid-sized machine,
and 500 to 1,000 or more for a large
one.
And finally, the cost most owners
underestimate, depreciation. A machine
loses value every hour it works. The
trade estimates 15 to 20% a year in the
early years.
The auction prices tell the real story.
A 2023 Caterpillar with 89 hours sold
A 2021 Caterpillar with nearly 5,000
hours sold for $113,000.
Same model, 4 years and 5,000 hours
apart, $54,000 apart. So, with all of
that, where is the profit?
Let us do the arithmetic, and let us be
clear about what is verified and what is
illustrative.
This is an example built from verified
prices and stated assumptions so you can
see how the numbers move.
Start with a mini excavator. A new
Kubota U35 lists at $56,147.
Assume 10% down and a 9% loan over 5
years.
The monthly payment is $1,049.
Now the income.
The monthly rental rate for a mini is
Take the middle, $2,800 for a full month
rented.
But no machine is rented every day.
Assume 50% utilization, a planning
assumption, not a verified figure.
That gives $1,400 a month.
Subtract the loan payment, and $351 is
left before fuel, maintenance,
insurance, transport, storage, and tax.
At 40% utilization, almost nothing is
left, $71.
The loan alone eats most of the rent.
The business lives or dies on
utilization.
Now the 20-ton machine, and here the
arithmetic gets uncomfortable.
No new American list price could be
verified, So this example uses a claimed
price of $325,000
flagged as unverified.
10% down, 9% five years, about $6,072
a month.
The mid-size monthly rental rate is
Take the middle, $8,750.
At 50% utilization, that is $4,375
a month,
less than the loan payment.
still less than the payment.
Only at 80% does the rent cover the loan
with $928
left before fuel, maintenance,
insurance, and everything else.
That is why real operators buy used, put
more down, take longer terms, or run the
machine on their own jobs as well as
renting it out.
Now compare that with the big companies.
United Rentals reported net income of
$2.6 billion in 2024 on revenue of 15.3
billion, about 17%.
But its adjusted earnings before
interest, tax, depreciation, and
amortization were $7.2 billion,
not profit, because that measure
excludes the cost of the fleet itself.
Herc Holdings reported net income of
$211 million in 2024 on revenue of 3.6
billion, a net margin of about 6%.
Herc runs 602 locations across North
America.
After buying H&E Equipment Services in
2025, its revenue rose to $4.4 billion,
although its reported net income fell to
just $1 million because of the
acquisition costs.
Ashtead, which owns Sunbelt Rentals,
reported an adjusted operating profit of
$2.7 billion on revenue of 10.8 billion
in its 2025 financial year,
about 25% before interest and tax.
Its North American business runs 781
general tool stores and 588 specialty
stores.
Same industry, three different margins.
The lesson is that scale, utilization,
and the used equipment sale are what
turn a thin rental margin into a real
business.
And that brings us to the risks because
this business is not a guaranteed
income.
First, the construction cycle.
When building slows, rental slows with
it.
The American Rental Association reported
8% growth in 2024, but forecast growth
slowing to about 5% in 2025 and about 4%
in 2026 and 2027, citing economic
uncertainty and high financing costs.
Rental helps in a downturn. Contractors
rent instead of buying,
and the rented share rose to 57% in
But a downturn still means fewer
machines out and lower rates.
Second, fuel.
Diesel averaged $3.66 a gallon in 2025.
In 2026, it averaged more than $5 with a
weekly peak above 6 and 1/2.
A machine that burns $100 of fuel a day
at one price burns 150 at another, and
the rental rate does not automatically
rise to match.
Third, financing. 6 to 14% a year is the
range we found, and a new operator with
weak credit pays the top end.
A higher rate turns a workable loan into
an unworkable one.
Fourth, the machine itself.
One major breakdown, a hydraulic pump,
an engine, an undercarriage can cost
more than months of rental income.
And a one-machine owner has no spare to
send the customer while theirs is in the
workshop.
United Rentals has a million machines. A
small owner has one.
One breakdown, one lost customer, or one
slow winter month can erase a year's
margin.
Finally, regulation and competition.
Emissions rules tighten, transport
permits get harder, and every rental
yard in a city is competing for the same
contractors.
The moat in this business is not the
machine. Anyone can buy a machine.
The moat is utilization, reputation, and
the ability to keep the machine earning
while others sit in the yard.
So, is owning an excavator rental
business a good way to make money? The
honest answer is it can be, but the
machine is not the business.
The business is keeping an expensive
asset working week after week, year
after year.
The money comes from three places.
First, the rent itself,
$719 a day on average across all sizes,
but only when the machine is out.
Second, the extras, delivery,
attachments, damage waivers, and
operated higher.
And third, the resale.
A used machine that has spent years
earning rent and still sells for six
figures.
The costs are the loan, the fuel, the
maintenance, the insurance, the
transport, and the depreciation that
never stops.
The big companies earn real money
because they do this at scale with high
utilization and with a million machines
to average across.
The small owner earns money when the
machine is working and bleeds money when
it is not.
Our illustrative example showed why.
A mini excavator at 50% utilization
leaves $351 a month after the loan
before any other cost.
A new 20 ton machine at the same
utilization does not even cover its
loan.
That is the reason to understand it
before buying the machine.
Follow the money, see the machine, and
never buy the steel before you have done
the sums.
If you want the next machine in this
series, subscribe because next we follow
the money behind the crane.

In 2024, it reported total revenue of $15.3 billion. 85% of that, $13 billion, came from renting equipment, not selling it, renting it. It operates more than 1,600 locations, employs nearly 28,000 people, and owns a fleet worth $21.4 billion at original cost, more than 1.1 million machines and tools. The model is the same at every size. Buy the machine once, rent it hundreds of times. The second half of the model is what most people miss. A rental company does not only earn while the machine works, it earns again when the machine is sold. In 2024, United Rentals took in $1.5 billion from selling used rental equipment and only $282 million from selling brand new equipment. Used sales were more than five times new sales. The machine is bought, rented for years, and then sold while it still has value. That second sale is part of the profit. The third half of the model is the extras, delivery, attachments, damage waivers, and operator. A hydraulic thumb rents for $50 to $100 a day. A breaker, $150 to $300. A damage waiver is typically 10 to 15% on top of the rental rate. Delivery for a mid-size machine is $300 to $500 for the round trip. Each of these is small. Together, they change the economics of every rental. And there is a fourth revenue stream that only the big companies have, scale. United Rentals and its rivals rent everything, lifts, generators, pumps, trench boxes, power systems. An excavator customer often rents five other things on the same job. A one-machine owner cannot do that. Keep that in mind because it matters when we reach the profit. The American Rental Association reported that the rental business directly and indirectly supported 666,000 jobs in 2024, paid $47.4 billion in wages, and contributed $115 billion to American economic output. The big operators measure success not by one machine, but by fleet productivity, a combined measure of rates, utilization, and the mix of machines. United Rentals reported fleet productivity up 4.1% in 2024 and up 2.2% again in 2025. Now the rates, the actual money. These are real American rental prices from a pricing guide based on 1,193 real rental quotes across the United States and Canada, updated in March 2026. A mini excavator, 1 and 1/2 to 4 tons, rents for $150 to $400 a day, $450 to $1,200 a week, and $1,200 to $3,200 a month. A small machine, 5 to 10 tons, rents for 400 to 700 a day. A mid-size machine, 13 to 25 tons, the class that does most commercial work, rents for 700 to 1,500 a day. 2,100 to 4,500 a week and 5,500 to 12,000 a month. A large machine, 30 to 50 tons, rents for 1,500 to 3,000 a day and up to 25,000 a month. Across all sizes, the average is 719 a day, 2,021 a week, and 5,108 a month. Notice the pattern. A week costs about 3 days. A month costs about 3 weeks. The longer you rent, the cheaper each day becomes and the more the rental company depends on the machine staying out, not coming back. Because here is the number that decides everything, utilization. Utilization is the share of the time a machine is actually out earning. A machine sitting in the yard earns nothing while the loan, the insurance, and the depreciation keep running. The big companies measure it in dollars, annual rental revenue divided by the cost of the fleet. United Rentals runs at roughly 44 to 47% on that measure. Herc Holdings, another large American rental company, reported 43.5% in the third quarter of 2026. Think about what that means. Even the best operators in the world earn rental revenue equal to less than half their fleet's value in a year. A small owner with one machine does not have a fleet to average across. One slow winter month can erase the margin of three good ones. So the revenue model is not the daily rate. The daily rate is the price of the ticket. Utilization is whether anyone is buying tickets. Now the other side of the ledger, what does it cost to keep an excavator earning? Start with fuel. A mini excavator burns roughly 2 to 4 liters of diesel an hour. A 20 ton machine burns roughly 10 to 17 liters an hour, depending on the work. On the American diesel price of 2025, $3.66 a gallon on average, that is roughly $15 to $30 of fuel for a mini excavator on an 8-hour day and roughly $77 to $131 for a 20 ton machine. Fuel prices move. In 2026, American diesel averaged $5.15 a gallon through early November with a weekly peak above $6.50. Next, the operator. In most rentals, the customer supplies the operator and the rental company avoids this cost entirely. But an operated rental, machine plus driver, adds $400 to $800 a day and the driver's wage is the floor. The American Bureau of Labor Statistics reports the median wage for heavy equipment operators at $28.78 an hour in May 2025 or just under $60,000 a year. That is the wage the operator takes home. The employer's loaded cost is higher. Then maintenance. Tracks wear out, hydraulic hoses fail, filters, oil, grease, pins, and bushings are constant. A mid-size machine is estimated to cost $5,000 to $15,000 a year in maintenance according to the rental pricing guide. A rule of thumb, not a verified fact, and it does not include a major failure. An undercarriage replacement, the tracks and rollers a machine runs on, is one of the largest single bills an owner will ever face and no verified American price for it could be found in our research. Insurance comes next. The machine itself must be insured against theft and damage. The business needs liability cover and the trucks that move the machines need commercial policies. The only verified figure is the customer's side, a damage waiver of 10 to 15% on top of the rental rate. Then transport. Every rental begins and ends with a truck, a low boy trailer, a driver, fuel, and permits. $300 to $500 for a round trip on a mid-sized machine, and 500 to 1,000 or more for a large one. And finally, the cost most owners underestimate, depreciation. A machine loses value every hour it works. The trade estimates 15 to 20% a year in the early years. The auction prices tell the real story. A 2023 Caterpillar with 89 hours sold for $167,000. A 2021 Caterpillar with nearly 5,000 hours sold for $113,000. Same model, 4 years and 5,000 hours apart, $54,000 apart. So, with all of that, where is the profit? Let us do the arithmetic, and let us be clear about what is verified and what is illustrative. This is an example built from verified prices and stated assumptions so you can see how the numbers move. Start with a mini excavator. A new Kubota U35 lists at $56,147. Assume 10% down and a 9% loan over 5 years. The monthly payment is $1,049. Now the income. The monthly rental rate for a mini is $1,200 to $3,200. Take the middle, $2,800 for a full month rented. But no machine is rented every day. Assume 50% utilization, a planning assumption, not a verified figure. That gives $1,400 a month. Subtract the loan payment, and $351 is left before fuel, maintenance, insurance, transport, storage, and tax. At 40% utilization, almost nothing is left, $71. At 80%, $1,191. The loan alone eats most of the rent. The business lives or dies on utilization. Now the 20-ton machine, and here the arithmetic gets uncomfortable. No new American list price could be verified, So this example uses a claimed price of $325,000 flagged as unverified. 10% down, 9% five years, about $6,072 a month. The mid-size monthly rental rate is $5,500 to $12,000. Take the middle, $8,750. At 50% utilization, that is $4,375 a month, less than the loan payment. At 65%, $5,688, still less than the payment. Only at 80% does the rent cover the loan with $928 left before fuel, maintenance, insurance, and everything else. That is why real operators buy used, put more down, take longer terms, or run the machine on their own jobs as well as renting it out. Now compare that with the big companies. United Rentals reported net income of $2.6 billion in 2024 on revenue of 15.3 billion, about 17%. But its adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization were $7.2 billion, not profit, because that measure excludes the cost of the fleet itself. Herc Holdings reported net income of $211 million in 2024 on revenue of 3.6 billion, a net margin of about 6%. Herc runs 602 locations across North America. After buying H&E Equipment Services in 2025, its revenue rose to $4.4 billion, although its reported net income fell to just $1 million because of the acquisition costs. Ashtead, which owns Sunbelt Rentals, reported an adjusted operating profit of $2.7 billion on revenue of 10.8 billion in its 2025 financial year, about 25% before interest and tax. Its North American business runs 781 general tool stores and 588 specialty stores. Same industry, three different margins. The lesson is that scale, utilization, and the used equipment sale are what turn a thin rental margin into a real business. And that brings us to the risks because this business is not a guaranteed income. First, the construction cycle. When building slows, rental slows with it. The American Rental Association reported 8% growth in 2024, but forecast growth slowing to about 5% in 2025 and about 4% in 2026 and 2027, citing economic uncertainty and high financing costs. Rental helps in a downturn. Contractors rent instead of buying, and the rented share rose to 57% in 2024. But a downturn still means fewer machines out and lower rates. Second, fuel. Diesel averaged $3.66 a gallon in 2025. In 2026, it averaged more than $5 with a weekly peak above 6 and 1/2. A machine that burns $100 of fuel a day at one price burns 150 at another, and the rental rate does not automatically rise to match. Third, financing. 6 to 14% a year is the range we found, and a new operator with weak credit pays the top end. A higher rate turns a workable loan into an unworkable one. Fourth, the machine itself. One major breakdown, a hydraulic pump, an engine, an undercarriage can cost more than months of rental income. And a one-machine owner has no spare to send the customer while theirs is in the workshop. United Rentals has a million machines. A small owner has one. One breakdown, one lost customer, or one slow winter month can erase a year's margin. Finally, regulation and competition. Emissions rules tighten, transport permits get harder, and every rental yard in a city is competing for the same contractors. The moat in this business is not the machine. Anyone can buy a machine. The moat is utilization, reputation, and the ability to keep the machine earning while others sit in the yard. So, is owning an excavator rental business a good way to make money? The honest answer is it can be, but the machine is not the business. The business is keeping an expensive asset working week after week, year after year. The money comes from three places. First, the rent itself, $719 a day on average across all sizes, but only when the machine is out. Second, the extras, delivery, attachments, damage waivers, and operated higher. And third, the resale. A used machine that has spent years earning rent and still sells for six figures. The costs are the loan, the fuel, the maintenance, the insurance, the transport, and the depreciation that never stops. The big companies earn real money because they do this at scale with high utilization and with a million machines to average across. The small owner earns money when the machine is working and bleeds money when it is not. Our illustrative example showed why. A mini excavator at 50% utilization leaves $351 a month after the loan before any other cost. A new 20 ton machine at the same utilization does not even cover its loan. That is the reason to understand it before buying the machine. Follow the money, see the machine, and never buy the steel before you have done the sums. If you want the next machine in this series, subscribe because next we follow the money behind the crane.

metadata.title: How Equipment Financing Brokers Actually Work (Banks Hate This)
metadata.author: Mehmi Financial Group
metadata.shortDescription:
The provided sources explore the equipment leasing and finance industry, an essential sector supporting business growth by making high-cost assets more affordable. These texts highlight that nearly half of all business equipment purchases are funded through loans or leases, covering diverse sectors from medical technology to heavy construction. While traditional banks are tightening their standards due to regulatory pressures, independent "story lenders" are increasingly filling the gap by offering flexible, relationship-based solutions for startups and non-investment grade companies. Furthermore, specialized brokers and manufacturers assist businesses in navigating these options to preserve cash flow, manage technology obsolescence, and simplify the acquisition process. Collectively, these documents serve as a comprehensive guide to the financial mechanisms, industry players, and strategic benefits driving modern equipment investment.

Equipment financing brokers play a major role in helping Canadian businesses secure funding for trucks, construction equipment, manufacturing machinery, and other business assets. Instead of working with just one lender like a traditional bank, equipment finance brokers connect businesses with multiple lenders across Canada to find competitive leasing and equipment loan options.

In this video, we explain how equipment financing brokers work in Canada, how equipment leasing companies structure deals, and why many small businesses in cities like Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, and Montreal use brokers to secure financing for commercial trucks, heavy equipment, and business machinery.

metadata.title: How Construction Equipment Rental Companies Make Money
metadata.author: Mr. Margins
metadata.shortDescription:
How Construction Equipment Rental Companies Make Money comes down to one thing: keeping expensive machines earning faster than they depreciate.
In this video, we break down how equipment rental companies generate revenue through rental rates, damage waivers, delivery fees, asset utilization, and used equipment resale.
Discover why financial utilization, fleet costs, maintenance, debt, and resale value determine whether a $100,000 machine becomes a profit generator or an expensive liability.
Subscribe for more breakdowns on how everyday businesses actually make money.

#EquipmentRental #ConstructionBusiness #HeavyEquipment #BusinessEconomics #HowBusinessesMakeMoney

segments.text: A $150,000 excavator arrives on a
commercial job site.
The contractor running the project
didn't buy it.
Instead, they are paying thousands of
dollars a month just to borrow it for
the season.
You see these massive yellow machines,
boom lifts, skid steers, and earth
movers on almost every major American
build.
At first glance, it seems like a
straightforward transaction. You need a
tool, you rent a tool.
But for the massive companies that own
these fleets, this isn't just about
handing over keys. This is a highly
leveraged financial operation where the
true profit relies on a race against
time, asset depreciation, and the
secondary resale market. So, how do
equipment rental companies actually make
money? The core customer for the US
heavy equipment rental industry is the
commercial payer. General contractors,
specialized trades like commercial
electricians, municipalities, and heavy
infrastructure builders. When these
operators need to move earth, lift
structural steel, or access a five-story
roof, they require massive, highly
specialized machinery.
However, buying that machinery outright
introduces a debilitating financial
burden.
What this business actually sells is the
avoidance of capital expenditure.
Instead of a construction firm dropping
massive sums of cash to purchase an
excavator that might sit idle in a
winter yard for four months out of the
year, they pay an equipment rental
branch for strictly time-based access to
that asset.
The visible product is the machine
itself, and payment is triggered by the
duration the customer needs it on their
site.
The payer is deliberately trading a
massive upfront fixed cost for a
predictable variable cost tied directly
to an active project.
By renting, the commercial contractor
successfully pushes the immense burden
of equipment debt servicing, complex
mechanical maintenance, off-season
storage, and relentless asset
depreciation entirely onto the rental
company.
Within the broader equipment economy, it
is the rental operator who must manage
these expensive assets and handle all
ongoing maintenance.
This dynamic creates a centralized
library of highly depreciating physical
assets.
The contractor gets the exact tool they
need for the precise duration of the
build,
and the rental company secures a
recurring stream of cash flow.
But by absorbing all of that capital
risk, the rental operator assumes the
massive underlying costs of ownership.
To survive and turn a profit, the
business relies heavily on asset
utilization, ensuring the expensive
asset is actively earning rather than
sitting idle.
Ultimately, the lifetime economics of
the business will also depend heavily on
the end of life resale value of these
machines. To understand where the money
actually comes from, we have to look at
the revenue stack, ranking the streams
by their true economic importance rather
than just what seems most obvious.
To make this tangible, let's model a
single unit transaction, a commercial
contractor needing a standard 40-ft boom
lift for a multi-month roofing project.
We will only include the revenue streams
that materially affect the model,
separating core income from attach rates
and capital recovery.
Time-based rental rates, core revenue.
This is the foundational cash flow.
Rental operators structure their pricing
on a sliding scale. Daily, weekly, and
monthly rates.
A daily rate is the most expensive per
24-hour period, economically punishing
the customer for short-term use.
A monthly rate offers a steep discount
on the per day math, but operators
heavily prefer it.
Why? Because a monthly contract
guarantees the machine is out of the
yard, actively generating recurring
revenue, and not consuming the branches
labor to process returns and yard
inspections.
If our contractor rents the boom lift
a month, that sets the baseline of the
stack.
The damage waiver, high-margin attached
revenue.
Here is where the margin begins to
expand. Equipment rental branches push a
product often called the rental
protection plan, RPP, or damage waiver.
This is a classic attach rate revenue
stream.
It is not technically insurance, it is
an agreement that the rental company
will waive the customer's financial
liability for accidental damage to the
machine.
Operators typically charge an additional
10% to 15% of the base rental rate for
this waiver.
On our $2,500
boom lift, that is an extra $250 to $375
a month. Because major damage incidents
are statistically low, this attached
revenue drops almost entirely to the
branches bottom line, serving as a
massive profit buffer.
Delivery and pickup fees ancillary
pass-through.
You cannot simply drive a 20,000-lb
piece of heavy machinery down the
highway.
Moving the equipment to and from the
commercial site requires specialized
flatbed transport, commercial drivers,
and expensive logistics.
The rental operator charges a distinct
delivery and pickup fee.
While this ancillary fee can add
hundreds of dollars to the invoice, it
is rarely a major profit center.
Instead, it functions as a pass-through
cost recovery mechanism, ensuring the
immense expense of logistics doesn't eat
into the core time-based rental margin.
Fuel and environmental surcharges fee
income. If a machine returns to the yard
missing diesel, or if the prep process
requires specific fluid disposal, the
operator tags on fuel and environmental
fees.
Like delivery, these are defensive
ancillary fee income streams designed to
protect the baseline rental profit from
variable operational bleeding.
Used equipment resale recovery value.
While it sits at the end of the
timeline, used equipment sales represent
a critical, massive influx of cash in
the broader revenue stack.
This business does not hold machines
forever.

channel at Hong new heavy industry. The
production process represents a fusion
of advanced technology and industrial
scale. It begins with steel making
utilizing 50 to 100 ton electric arc
furnaces, 150 ton ladle refining
furnaces, and vacuum pouring equipment
capable of casting ingots up to 450
tons. The refined steel is poured into
molds to produce large ingots or slabs.
These are then forged using a 12,000 ton
hydraulic open die press, one of the
most advanced and automated forging
systems in China, alongside a 450 ton
manipulator and 550 ton overhead crane.
Forged components undergo heat treatment
in one of 60 natural gas and electric
furnaces, including a 25 m long car
bottom furnace and a 30 m deep vertical
furnace. Precision machining follows
with over 320 heavyduty CNC machines,
including fiveaxis gantry mills,
vertical and horizontal lathes, and
boring mills capable of handling parts
weighing up to 300 tons and measuring up
to 28 m in length. This extensive
machining capability enables Tongyu to
produce highly accurate parts for wind
power, energy, marine, mining and
aerospace sectors.
Tong Yu has also developed advanced
materials such as ultra- lowcarbon 316L
stainless steel for AP-1000 nuclear
power main piping and produces Asia's
largest wind power main shafts and
ductile iron pipe molds through a fully
integrated production chain steel making
forging heat treatment and machining.
Tong Yu supplies critical components
such as rotors, pressure piping,
crankshafts, and castings to both
domestic and international markets. With
continual investment in innovation and
quality, Tong Yu has emerged as one of
Asia's leading heavy equipment
manufacturers, forming long-term
partnerships with major global firms and
contributing to key national projects in
nuclear and renewable energy.
The MCT 1000 machining center by
Birkhart Plus Weber is engineered for
multitasking operations, combining
milling, drilling, and turning
capabilities in one high power system.
Designed for high performance
applications, the MCT series features a
NC controlled tilting spindle providing
flexible and precise control over
various machining

metal sheets are transported to the
manufacturing facility ready for
processing. The metal sheets are then
cut into smaller uniform pieces
according to the desired dimensions for
the final product.
These smaller pieces are arranged
vertically in a frame, ensuring that the
gaps between them are evenly spaced,
creating the grid structure of the
grading.
Next, the metal pieces are welded and
automatically connected together using
advanced welding technology to form a
strong, durable grading with evenly
spaced gaps. This ensures that the
grading can withstand heavy loads and
harsh conditions.
After welding, the grading under goes a
protective coating process such as
galvanizing or painting to prevent
corrosion, especially when exposed to
outdoor elements or chemicals.
The grading is then thoroughly inspected
for quality, checking for any defects,
ensuring that the size and gap
dimensions are accurate, and confirming
its durability and strength. Finally,
the grading is cleaned, finished, and
packaged for delivery to customers.
This systematic process ensures that the
grading produced is of high quality,
durable and ready for installation in
various industrial and architectural
applications. The finished grading can
be customized for different
specifications, making it versatile for
a wide range of uses.

is a versatile tool designed for cutting
pipe openings, including saddle and fish
mouth joints. It can cut both GRP and

the pipe.

working on pipes that are already
installed, whether underground or above
ground. The ability to cut without the
need for large equipment makes this
machine an efficient and convenient
solution for on-site pipe cutting
applications, offering precision and
flexibility in various pipe materials.

cutting, offering a superior alternative
to traditional methods like wire, water
jet, and laser cutting.
The process begins with selecting
Dayron's micro grain carbide shank mills
and counter sinks designed for
high-speed machining at 15,000 to 60,000
RPM.
[Music]
These tools feature optimized edge
geometry for clean, smooth cuts on PU
foam, eliminating burrs and
post-processing needs.
The CNC machine such as the Neo or MX
Cube is set up with a high-speed spindle
and DRON Next software enabling
intuitive control via a touchscreen
interface. Foam sheets are secured on a
vacuum table for stability.

contours, bevels, and surface geometries
in a single operation, achieving micron
level precision. Datron's chip
management system ensures efficient chip
evacuation, maintaining clean cuts and
reducing downtime.

The process begins with selecting Dayron's micro grain carbide shank mills and counter sinks designed for high-speed machining at 15,000 to 60,000 RPM. [Music] These tools feature optimized edge geometry for clean, smooth cuts on PU foam, eliminating burrs and post-processing needs. The CNC machine such as the Neo or MX Cube is set up with a high-speed spindle and DRON Next software enabling intuitive control via a touchscreen interface. Foam sheets are secured on a vacuum table for stability. The milling process creates complex contours, bevels, and surface geometries in a single operation, achieving micron level precision. Datron's chip management system ensures efficient chip evacuation, maintaining clean cuts and reducing downtime. This method supports industries like aerospace, automotive and packaging, producing intricate foam parts with high quality finishes. By leveraging automation options such as tool assist with up to 143 tool stations, production efficiency is further enhanced, making it ideal for both prototyping and high volume runs.

Visit our website at https://www.coxmanufacturing.com/ or give us a call at 866-336-5916 for more information and to get started on your project today. 

In the last few years, Cox Manufacturing has continued to expand its campus with the acquisition of adjacent properties and continues to invest in people, technology, and facilities. In this video, you’ll get a tour of our facility and an inside look at what makes Cox Manufacturing such a trusted supplier for progressive manufacturers. 

We excel in manufacturing high precision, high production custom machined parts and products, producing and shipping over 1½ million made-to-order components per week. Our machine shop services include CNC turning, CNC milling, automatic bar machining, multi-spindle screw machining and more. 

There’s a lot happening at Cox Manufacturing. In total, we have nearly 100 primary production bar automatics, and we’re proud to say that throughout our 60+ years of operation, we’ve made a name for and brought back manufacturing to the USA. But even more than that, we are proud that the parts we make, not only serving essential industries around the world, but also provide a high quality of life for our employees, which allows us to be a positive influence for Christ.

Because when it comes to manufacturing, Cox Delivers.

We are hiring! Call us at 210-981-5349 if you are interested in our open job positions. 

If you are in need of high volume screw machined parts and production, Cox Manufacturing is a leading American screw machine company that has the latest technology to meet your specifications. Our machine shop is complete with Precision CNC lathes, Multi-spindle Cam Automatics, and an In-house Tooling Facility. We are equipped to serve you with JIT Delivery & Logistics Management, and an array of supply chain services.

metadata.title: Financing CNC Machine Tools as a Startup Business
metadata.author: Contend Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Ethan Leer started his business at the age of 20 while working for another local machine shop. 

Today, he celebrates the grand opening of his brand-new facility, running five CNC machines with two more incoming.

He shares his advice for those considering starting their own manufacturing business. 

He advises when the time is right to quit your day job, how to find a lender who will work with a startup business and how to get approved to finance your first CNC machine.

Using his equipment finance partner Contend Capital, Leer Custom Machine has been able to finance his CNC machines, while letting them pay for themselves each month.

For more on CNC machine financing - https://contendcapital.com/machine-tool-financing

Leer Custom Machine - https://www.leercustommachine.com/

metadata.title: The Money Behind a CNC Lathe Machine
metadata.author: Money Machines
metadata.shortDescription:
A single CNC lathe can manufacture thousands of precision components used in different industries. From metal shafts and bushings to threaded fittings and machine components, this technology plays an important role in modern manufacturing.

But the interesting part isn't just what the machine can produce. It's the range of products manufacturers can sell using CNC turning technology.

In this video, we explore the CNC lathe machine, also known as a CNC turning machine or CNC turning center, and how it transforms raw metal and plastic materials into finished components.

You'll discover how CNC turning works, how computer-controlled cutting tools shape rotating materials, and how operations such as facing, drilling, boring, grooving, and threading help produce different components.

We'll also explore the materials used, the types of products manufactured, and industries that depend on CNC-machined components.

The business opportunity: CNC turning creates opportunities for precision machining businesses, component manufacturers, and job shops supplying parts to other manufacturers. Potential products include shafts, bushings, pins, spacers, pulleys, threaded fittings and cylindrical machine components.

Customers can include automotive manufacturers, machinery companies, industrial equipment suppliers, electronics manufacturers and engineering businesses.

Rather than simply buying a machine, the real opportunity lies in identifying products that businesses already need, understanding their manufacturing requirements, and finding customers willing to pay for quality components.

EXPLORE MORE MONEY-MAKING MACHINES

Interested in discovering more machines and equipment that could create small-scale manufacturing and business opportunities?

My ebook, 101 Simple Money-Making Machines: The Garage Machine That Creates a Generational Money-Making Business, explores 101 machines and equipment worth researching for small-scale manufacturing and machine-based business opportunities.

Get your copy for $47 here:
https://bilson53.gumroad.com/l/idgynw

Subscribe for more videos exploring manufacturing machines, production processes, industrial equipment, small-scale manufacturing, and the businesses built around productive machines.

#CNCLathe #CNCMachining #ManufacturingBusiness

segments.text: A CNC lathe looks like an expensive box
that spins metal, but inside that box is
something much more interesting, a
production system capable of turning
ordinary metal stock into precision
components that other businesses are
willing to pay for.
And depending on the machine, we're
talking about an asset costing tens of
thousands of dollars. For example, Haas
currently lists its SD 10 CNC lathe from
around $65,000
in the United States.
Used examples can appear on the market
for roughly $27,000
to $30,000 depending on age, condition,
and equipment. But that raises a much
bigger question. What exactly are you
buying?
A CNC lathe holds a piece of material in
a chuck and rotates it while cutting
tools remove material according to a
computer-controlled program that allows
the machine to perform operations such
as turning, facing, boring, threading,
and grooving.
The result can be a shaft, bushing,
fitting, pin, coupling, housing, or
another precision component. And these
aren't products people usually buy
because they look attractive. They're
purchased because another machine,
vehicle, factory, or industrial system
needs them to work.
That's the first important business
lesson. You aren't really selling
machining. You're selling a component
that solves a customer's manufacturing
problem.
A company might send you an engineering
drawing and say, make 500 of these
parts, hold these dimensions, use this
material, and deliver them by this date.
Your CNC lathe becomes the productive
asset sitting between that drawing and
the finished component.
Modern machines can be surprisingly
capable. Take the Haas SD 10 as one
reference point. It has a 6,000 RPM
spindle, 15 horsepower of spindle power,
and a 12-station turret.
Another example, the DN Solutions Lynx
2100 series can reach 6,000 RPM and,
depending on configuration, handle
turning diameters around 300 mm and
turning lengths up
millimeters. So this isn't simply an
automated version of an old manual
lathe.
It's a programmable production system.
But here's where the business becomes
more interesting. A machine sitting idle
is not producing anything. The real
asset is machine time. And the people
who make money with CNC equipment are
usually not thinking only about buying
machines.
They're thinking about utilization. How
many hours can this machine actually
produce saleable parts? Who will buy
those parts? How quickly can jobs be
quoted? How efficiently can the machine
be set up? And how many orders can be
repeated? Real businesses demonstrate
this clearly.
For and manufacturing, for example,
operates a contract manufacturing
business serving industries including
aerospace, marine, medical,
telecommunications, and
microelectronics. Its lathe department
includes seven CNC turning centers and
multi-axis mill turn equipment and BIC.
Precision has used a collaborative robot
with a CNC turning center to automate
repetitive loading and unloading work
for parts produced in quantities of tens
of thousands per year. These examples
reveal something important. The machine
is only one component of a much larger
system.
Customers, programming, tooling,
inspection, material handling, and
delivery all matter. Now let's look at
the numbers.
Current 2026 industry pricing guides
commonly place conventional CNC turning
rates roughly around $50 to $100 per
machine hour in US
and Western markets, although actual
rates vary enormously by region, machine
complexity, utilization, and what the
quoted rate includes. Suppose, purely as
an illustration, a shop achieves an
average billable machine rate of $80 per
hour.
At 1,200 productive hours in a year,
that's $96,000 in machine time revenue.
But those numbers are revenue scenarios,
not profit. Material costs money.
Cutting tools wear out. Coolant needs
management. Operators need to be paid.
Programming and setup take time. There
is electricity, rent, inspection,
maintenance, transportation, software,
financing, and downtime.
And if a machine runs only a few hours a
week, its economics can change
dramatically. In fact, one of the most
revealing CNC case studies comes from a
small job shop using a CNC lathe.
The shop reported an $80 hourly rate and
used an automation system to add only
three extra production hours per night.
The supply calculated more than $60,000
of additional first-year profit from
those extra hours.
That's a supplier-published case, so it
should not be treated as a universal
result. But the underlying lesson is
powerful. Sometimes the opportunity
isn't buying another machine. It's
getting more productive hours from the
machine you already own. And that's also
where the hidden risk appears.
You can buy the machine. You can install
it. You can learn to operate it. But
none of that guarantees customers. A CNC
lathe without orders is an expensive
piece of industrial furniture. There is
also the skills problem.
Programming, setup, tooling selection,
work holding, and quality control all
affect whether the machine produces good
parts efficiently. The US
Bureau of Labor Statistics still
describes machinists as workers who set
up, monitor, and maintain CNC machine
tools while noting that automation is
increasing worker productivity, and the
physical operation isn't completely
risk-free either.
Metalworking fluids, flying chips, hot
parts, noise, and other hazards require
proper controls and safe working
practices. So, is a CNC lathe a good
business asset? Potentially. But the
best opportunity isn't simply buy a
machine and make money.
It's find a customer problem, understand
the part they need, calculate what it
costs to manufacture and then decide
whether a CNC lathe gives you a
competitive way to solve it. The machine
is the entry point. The real business is
everything around it. Raw material
becomes precision parts.
Precision parts become customer orders.
Customer orders become revenue. And only
after all the costs are paid does that
revenue become profit. That's the part
most machine videos leave out. The most
valuable thing in a CNC machine shop
isn't actually the machine.
It's having a machine that stays busy
producing something people are willing
to pay for.
Want to build wealth that lasts
generations using simple machines? Get
this eBook guide that helps you achieve
maximum profit from the simplest of
machines. Get yours for just $47 today.
Link in the bio.
Get it now.

It has a 6,000 RPM spindle, 15 horsepower of spindle power, and a 12-station turret. Another example, the DN Solutions Lynx 2100 series can reach 6,000 RPM and, depending on configuration, handle turning diameters around 300 mm and turning lengths up millimeters. So this isn't simply an automated version of an old manual lathe. It's a programmable production system. But here's where the business becomes more interesting. A machine sitting idle is not producing anything. The real asset is machine time. And the people who make money with CNC equipment are usually not thinking only about buying machines. They're thinking about utilization. How many hours can this machine actually produce saleable parts? Who will buy those parts? How quickly can jobs be quoted? How efficiently can the machine be set up? And how many orders can be repeated? Real businesses demonstrate this clearly. For and manufacturing, for example, operates a contract manufacturing business serving industries including aerospace, marine, medical, telecommunications, and microelectronics. Its lathe department includes seven CNC turning centers and multi-axis mill turn equipment and BIC. Precision has used a collaborative robot with a CNC turning center to automate repetitive loading and unloading work for parts produced in quantities of tens of thousands per year. These examples reveal something important. The machine is only one component of a much larger system. Customers, programming, tooling, inspection, material handling, and delivery all matter. Now let's look at the numbers. Current 2026 industry pricing guides commonly place conventional CNC turning rates roughly around $50 to $100 per machine hour in US and Western markets, although actual rates vary enormously by region, machine complexity, utilization, and what the quoted rate includes. Suppose, purely as an illustration, a shop achieves an average billable machine rate of $80 per hour. At 1,200 productive hours in a year, that's $96,000 in machine time revenue. At 1,600 hours, it's $128,000. At 2,000 it's $160,000. But those numbers are revenue scenarios, not profit. Material costs money. Cutting tools wear out. Coolant needs management. Operators need to be paid. Programming and setup take time. There is electricity, rent, inspection, maintenance, transportation, software, financing, and downtime. And if a machine runs only a few hours a week, its economics can change dramatically. In fact, one of the most revealing CNC case studies comes from a small job shop using a CNC lathe. The shop reported an $80 hourly rate and used an automation system to add only three extra production hours per night. The supply calculated more than $60,000 of additional first-year profit from those extra hours. That's a supplier-published case, so it should not be treated as a universal result. But the underlying lesson is powerful. Sometimes the opportunity isn't buying another machine. It's getting more productive hours from the machine you already own. And that's also where the hidden risk appears. You can buy the machine. You can install it. You can learn to operate it. But none of that guarantees customers. A CNC lathe without orders is an expensive piece of industrial furniture. There is also the skills problem. Programming, setup, tooling selection, work holding, and quality control all affect whether the machine produces good parts efficiently. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics still describes machinists as workers who set up, monitor, and maintain CNC machine tools while noting that automation is increasing worker productivity, and the physical operation isn't completely risk-free either. Metalworking fluids, flying chips, hot parts, noise, and other hazards require proper controls and safe working practices. So, is a CNC lathe a good business asset? Potentially. But the best opportunity isn't simply buy a machine and make money. It's find a customer problem, understand the part they need, calculate what it costs to manufacture and then decide whether a CNC lathe gives you a competitive way to solve it. The machine is the entry point. The real business is everything around it. Raw material becomes precision parts. Precision parts become customer orders. Customer orders become revenue. And only after all the costs are paid does that revenue become profit. That's the part most machine videos leave out. The most valuable thing in a CNC machine shop isn't actually the machine. It's having a machine that stays busy producing something people are willing to pay for. Want to build wealth that lasts generations using simple machines?
