metadata.title: Why CNC Machining Is So Cheap in China — But So Expensive in America
metadata.author: Subi Industries
metadata.shortDescription:
Why is CNC machining so cheap in China — while the same type of work can cost dramatically more in America?

In this video, **Subi Industries** explores the economics behind the global CNC machining industry. We look at how China built one of the world's largest manufacturing ecosystems, why thousands of machine shops are competing for orders, and how tariffs, supply chains, skilled labor, financing, and operating costs can create huge differences in manufacturing prices.

You'll discover:

⚙️ How China's CNC manufacturing ecosystem grew
🏭 Why intense competition can drive machining prices down
💰 How debt and fixed costs affect small machine shops
🌎 Why manufacturing is expanding into Vietnam, Mexico, and other markets
🇺🇸 Why CNC machining can cost significantly more in the United States
📈 How supply chains, labor, compliance, and demand influence manufacturing costs

The machines may look similar, but the economics behind them are completely different.

Subscribe to **Subi Industries** for more videos about manufacturing, factories, industrial technology, automation, and the business behind the machines.

#CNCMachining #Manufacturing #CNC #AmericanManufacturing #ChinaManufacturing #IndustrialTechnology #SubiIndustries

segments.text: Something strange is happening in the
global manufacturing industry. In parts
of China, CNC shops are competing so
aggressively for work that machining
rates have reportedly fallen to just a
few dollars per hour.
After labor, electricity, tooling,
maintenance, and other operating costs,
some shops may barely make a profit at
all. And even at those prices, winning
an order isn't guaranteed.
But travel to the United States, Europe,
or Japan, and the picture can look
completely different. Similar CNC work
can cost dramatically more.
Some manufacturers are dealing with long
lead times, while skilled machinists
remain difficult to find. That creates a
remarkable contradiction. The machines
can be similar. The materials can be
similar.
Even the CNC programs can be similar.
Yet on one side of the world, factories
are fighting for orders at extremely low
prices,
while on the other, manufacturers are
investing heavily just to keep up with
demand. So, what happened? Where did the
manufacturing orders that once poured
into China actually go?
To understand this, we have to go back
several decades.
Beginning in the late 1980s and
accelerating through the 1990s,
manufacturing investment began flowing
into places such as Dongguan, Shenzhen,
and Kunshan.
Cheap labor helped, but that wasn't the
whole story.
Low-cost industrial land, favorable
policies, tax incentives, and rapidly
developing supply chains created an
environment where manufacturers could
expand at extraordinary speed.
And foreign manufacturers brought
something even more valuable than
machines.
They brought customers, production
knowledge, and access to global orders.
That combination would eventually help
create one of the largest manufacturing
ecosystems the world had ever seen. But
that manufacturing ecosystem didn't
appear overnight.
In the early days, CNC machining in
China was a specialized business.
Customers weren't simply paying for
machine time. They were paying for
expertise. Knowing how to design a part,
program the machine, select the right
cutting tools, build fixtures, and
troubleshoot production problems
required skills that relatively few
people had.
And that technical knowledge was
valuable.
But, by the early 2000s, something began
to change.
Experienced machinists and programmers
who had learned inside established
factories started leaving to build
businesses of their own.
At the same time, used imported CNC
machines became easier to find, while
Chinese manufacturers began producing
increasingly capable domestic equipment.
Suddenly, opening a small machine shop
required far less capital than before.
A skilled machinist could rent a modest
workshop, buy a couple of used machines,
bring in a few relatives or former
co-workers, and start taking orders.
Then, those workers trained others. Some
of them eventually opened their own
shops,
and the cycle repeated.
Across manufacturing centers such as the
Pearl River Delta and Yangtze River
Delta, thousands of specialized
suppliers began clustering together.
In places like Dongguan and Ningbo, a
factory could often find raw materials,
specialized cutting tools, heat
treatment, plating, fixtures, and other
services within the same industrial
region.
This created an incredibly efficient
manufacturing network, but it also
changed the economics of CNC machining.
As technical knowledge became more
widespread and machines became easier to
acquire, customers stopped paying a
premium simply for knowing how to make
the part.
More shops could perform the same job
and when thousands of suppliers can
compete for the same order price becomes
the battlefield. That competition would
eventually push China's CNC industry
toward a problem few manufacturers
expected.
Too many machines chasing too few
profitable orders and that's when the
economics became brutal.
When dozens of shops can produce
essentially the same part, customers
stop paying a premium for technical
expertise.
Instead, every quote gets pushed closer
to the basic cost of keeping the machine
running.
But that creates an obvious question.
If Chinese factories are so efficient
and their machining costs are so low,
why would international customers move
production somewhere else?
At first, the numbers don't seem to make
sense.
Even after shipping and additional trade
costs, machining a component in China
can still appear far cheaper than
producing the same part in the United
States or Western Europe.
But after 2018, manufacturers had to
consider more than the hourly price of a
CNC machine.
Tariffs became a much bigger part of the
equation and instead of moving every
order back to expensive factories in the
United States or Europe, companies began
looking for alternatives. Vietnam,
Thailand, Mexico and other emerging
manufacturing hubs.
These countries didn't necessarily have
to beat China on pure machining cost.
They only had to make the total landed
cost competitive.
Once tariffs, shipping, supply chain
risk, lead times and import requirements
enter the calculation, the cheapest
factory isn't always the cheapest
supplier.
And there was another problem. Certain
industries were becoming increasingly
sensitive to export controls and
technology restrictions.
Components connected to semiconductors,
telecommunications, advanced automation
and other high-tech equipment could face
additional scrutiny.
For manufacturers, that meant sourcing
decisions were no longer based on price
alone.
Geopolitics had entered the factory
floor, and once that happened, the
global map of manufacturing began to
change. And that's exactly what
companies began to do.
Faced with tariffs, trade restrictions,
and growing political uncertainty, major
manufacturers started looking for ways
to reduce their dependence on a single
country.
For many global companies, the goal
wasn't necessarily to abandon China. It
was to build a backup, a second
supplier, a second factory,
sometimes an entirely separate
production network outside China.
That helped push more manufacturing
investment toward countries such as
Vietnam, Thailand, and Mexico.
But moving an order is much easier than
moving an industrial ecosystem.
And precision manufacturing makes that
difference painfully clear.
A CNC machine by itself isn't enough to
produce a sophisticated component.
Before machining even begins, a factory
may need specialized metals, cutting
tools, fixtures, engineering support,
and prototype development.
After machining, the part may still
require heat treatment, plating,
anodizing, surface finishing, or
precision inspection.
In established Chinese manufacturing
hubs, many of these suppliers can be
located within the same industrial
region.
A problem that might take days to solve
elsewhere can sometimes be handled
surprisingly quickly, simply because the
right supplier is nearby.
But when production moves to a newer
manufacturing hub, that network may not
exist at the same scale.
A factory can install modern CNC
machines. It can hire workers. It can
even offer competitive labor costs.
But if a specialized finishing process
requires sending parts hundreds of miles
away,
or if the right supplier doesn't exist
locally, suddenly the entire production
schedule becomes more complicated.
That's why some companies have adopted a
hybrid strategy. They expand assembly
and simpler production stages into new
manufacturing countries while continuing
to rely on established Asian supply
networks for more specialized processes.
And that reveals something important
about modern manufacturing.
You can move a factory much faster than
you can recreate the ecosystem
surrounding it. But there's another side
to this story.
Even when final production moves to a
new country, some of the most difficult
manufacturing processes may still be
outsourced to specialized suppliers
elsewhere.
A company might perform final assembly
in one location while precision
machining, tooling, surface treatment,
or other complex processes are handled
by suppliers with deeper technical
experience.
From the outside, the supply chain
appears to have moved. In reality, it
may simply have become more fragmented.
And for small CNC shops, that creates a
serious problem.
Instead of working directly with an
international customer, they may become
subcontractors several layers down the
supply chain.
That means less control over pricing,
less visibility into future demand, and
often thinner margins.
But here's the surprising part. A very
low hourly machining rate doesn't
automatically mean a factory is losing
money.
Under the right conditions, low-cost
machining can still work.
Imagine receiving one large order that
runs continuously for 6 months.
The engineering is completed once. The
CNC program is written once. Fixtures
are built once. The machines are dialed
in once.
Then the same parts are produced again
and again, potentially hundreds of
thousands of times.
Spread those setup costs across a
massive production run, and the cost per
part can become extremely low.
Keep the machines running around the
clock, minimize tool failures, control
scrap rates, and even a thin margin can
generate a profit through sheer volume.
But small subcontractors often don't get
that kind of work.
They might receive one batch today,
another completely different job next
week, and nothing at all after that.
Every new order means new drawings, new
programming, new tooling, new set-ups,
and new risks. And that's where the real
problem begins.
For a CNC shop, a low price isn't always
fatal. Unpredictable demand can be, and
this is exactly what makes unstable
demand so expensive.
A shop might suddenly receive an order
for several thousand parts.
Engineers work late preparing drawings,
programmers build new tool paths,
machinists install fixtures, test
cutting parameters, and produce sample
after sample until everything finally
runs correctly.
During that process, a CNC machining
center worth tens or even hundreds of
thousands of dollars may spend days
generating almost no productive output.
Then everything finally works. Cycle
times improve, production speeds up, the
machines are ready to make money, and
suddenly the order is finished.
The next customer arrives with a
completely different part, and the
entire set-up process begins again.
Programming, tooling, fixtures, testing,
more machine down time. When margins are
already extremely thin, every changeover

One new customer,

ecosystem.

and turn the country into a global
manufacturing powerhouse.

enormous production capacity.

prices can fall to levels that seem
almost impossible.

relentlessly improving efficiency.
The problem is bigger than any
individual machinist.
Global supply chains are changing.
Manufacturing investment is moving.
And the economics that once made owning
a few CNC machines incredibly attractive
are changing with them.
CNC machining isn't disappearing.
The world will always need precision
components.

But the era when simply owning a CNC

segments.text: - Today, we're gonna see how aluminum parts
like this one are made.
This is a CNC mill,
which stands for computer numeric control,
but think of it as the opposite of a 3D printer.
Instead of adding material to make the shape that we want,
it removes material from a block using a tool
similar to a drill bit to give us the shape that we want.
I'm gonna show you how all of this works
from start to finish.
I'm here at JLCCNC Factory in Zhuhai, China.
A huge thanks to them for flying me out
and giving me such complete access to the factory.
They have a variety of machines here, 75 in total.
We're gonna start with one of their simpler machines
that they run 80% of their jobs on,
and then we'll go look at some of the more complicated
and cool machines that they have.
(upbeat music)
(upbeat music continues)
But, first, let's head upstairs
and talk to the engineers
to see the very first step in this process.
I'm here with Mr. Young,
who's one of the engineers here at the CNC Factory.
(Mr. Young speaking in foreign language)
(Mr. Young speaking in foreign language)
(Mr. Young speaking in foreign language)
(Mr. Young speaking in foreign language)
(Mr. Young speaking in foreign language)
Mr. Young, thank you so much for spending all the time
to explain this to us.
This has been super helpful.
We're gonna leave you to work and head off
and go see the next step here.
So thank you very much.
Parts start their life here in the materials warehouse,
they have all sorts of materials.
This is brass.
They've got large blocks of aluminum down here,
copper here.
And then, over here, we've got polycarbonate.
This is acrylic.
We have FR-4 fiberglass, like in circuit boards.
This is POM, another plastic.
Bakelite here.
This is really common to see fixtures
in factories made out of this,
I think 'cause it's cheap and easy to machine,
but I'm not totally sure.
And then, this is all ABS plastic here.
They pull the raw stock here from the warehouse,
and then it gets sent over to the saws for cutting down
to rough size of the part.
(upbeat music)
(upbeat music) (machine whirs)
(upbeat music) (air whooshes)
(upbeat music)
That was super fast.
I thought this was a band saw,
it was gonna take a long time.
No, it's actually a circular saw underneath this guard.
It's a blade about this big,
and they can move real quick with it.
And then, this gets sent downstairs to get put in a mill.
So one of the first steps is going ahead
and making sure that the right tools are in the machine.
There's a special drill bit for this job
that he's loading right now.
He's taking out the old drill bit out of the toolholder.
This is what the machine will grab,
the spindle will grab this,
but the bit actually goes into the collet here,
and he's swapping those out.
(machines droning faintly in background)
This machine actually has a bunch of standard tools in it,
and this is the list
of what should be in this machine the whole time.
From 15 to 21, it's whatever the job requires.
So those are open slots that they can put specific tools in.
So he's putting this specific drill bit in 17.
And then, I think there's also a tool
that goes in 21 that's not normal.
Yeah, here, so this is a big facing cutter,
big facing mill.
We'll see it'll cut the top of the face
real flat very quickly.
The next step is to check that the raw material
he has is actually cut to the right size
to make sure he didn't grab one from a different job
or something like that.
I assume he's also checking that it's the right material.
Now he's loading the material in the vise.
This is workholding.
This is an art when it comes to CNC.
How are you gonna hold the material?
This particular part here has a very square bottom
and so that makes it very easy to hold in a vise
like they're using right now.
But you can imagine part shapes where the jaws
of the vise would get in the way of cutting that sidewall,
so there are other clever mechanisms to use for this,
and this is something the engineers upstairs specify.
So now he's loading the G code.
He's loading the program
that the engineers generated upstairs,
which actually tells the machine what movements to make,
at what speed should the end mill be spinning,
et cetera.
And it's actually the same programming language
as runs on your home 3D printer,
it's all the same commands more or less,
there's some variation between manufacturer.
But these are basically telling the machine
what tool to load, how fast to spin the spindle,
and where to move and how fast.
(machine whirs)
Oh, this is interesting.
So he's actually using an end mill
to measure where the part is.
So he's just bringing it in right up to the point
that it starts cutting,
I think he's listening to it,
and then hitting zero on the program.
And the machine doesn't know exactly
where in that vise the aluminum is sitting.
And so he's essentially telling the machine
where the corner of that block is in all of the dimensions.
So he's doing all four sides
and telling it the limits of the work.
And then, he's also gonna touch down on the top of it.
Oh, yeah, that one definitely spit chips.
Okay, it's funny 'cause there is actually
an edge finder in here, but he's not using it.
And this is actually pretty interesting,
I've never seen anybody do this before.
He's using another end mill of a known diameter
and doing a go/no-go check.
So he's basically trying to roll it underneath the end mill
to get the end mill zeroed to a known height.
Basically, the known diameter of the bit
he's using to check.
So there is an electronic tool setter here as well,
and the tool's probing off that.
So it's an electronic sensor that measures the height
of the tool off the spindle
so that the machine knows where the end of the tool is.
So he's using that for the tools,
but he's measuring the height of the block of aluminum
using this go/no-go test.
So he's bringing the tool down in little increments,
and then rolling this bit underneath it
to get an exact measurement of where the height
of that aluminum block is, very smart.
I've been learning a lot that I'm gonna apply
to my own CNC mill in my shop.
Lots of tricks of the trade here.
Our man here is very industrious,
and I'm having to ask him repeatedly to slow down
(chuckles) so that we can get footage of stuff.
He's ready to run this machine, which is good.
It's just making it hard.
Finally, we turn on the coolant here
to keep the chips out of the way,
and keep the cutter cool, and start the job.
So I had them pull off a panel here
so we could see in the side.
Normally, this would be all closed up
'cause this thing makes quite a mess.
The very first step here is this big face mill.
It's gonna come in and clean off the top of the part
and make sure it's totally parallel and flat.
And then, will come in and start roughing out material
with end mills.
(machine whirring)
We've milled the bottom of this part now.
The machine milled the top face here with a face cutter,
that big, huge block.
It then came in with a regular end mill
and carved out the edges here.
It did it in two passes.
So it did a roughing operation here
where it took out most of the material,
and then it did a finishing pass
where it came in and removed just a tiny bit
to get a really nice finish on this edge.
Then it came in and drilled these two holes.
And then, lastly, it used a chamfer bit
to put a countersink on the holes
where a screw head would fit in probably.
And then, finally, it came around this outside edge
with a chamfer bit and put a tiny bit of a chamfer here.
And the reason to do that is to remove any burrs
that might have been raised by the end mill.
It would raise a rough edge
that would be sharp on your fingers.
It would cause all sorts of other problems.
So they just take off a little bit
of an angled edge there so now this is nice and smooth.
Now he's gonna flip the part over
and hold it in the vise again.
This time he's gonna have known surfaces to register it in.
We know that this surface is parallel to this surface
at a right angle to this surface
and we have an exact width here.
When we have the rough stock,
we don't know exactly that everything's perfect.
It might be a little bit bigger,
a little bit smaller than it should be.
It might not be totally parallel.
But now we have a perfect reference surface
to finish the top of the part.
Now that he's flipped the part over,
he needs to remeasure where it is in the vise
'cause it undoubtedly has shifted.
And I was actually really curious how he was gonna do this,
because he's actually got under-hang
and I didn't know how he was gonna get around that.
It's pretty clever.
He's using a parallel,
which is a precision ground piece
of tool steel of a known width.
He's sticking that underneath the under-hang
and bumping it up against the wall.
And then, he's using an edge finder.
And an edge finder is a very cool tool.
It's very simple, but it's very brilliant.
So I've got an extra one here.
It's a cylinder of brass.
This is a very precise known diameter both here and here.
And it is attached to the shaft
that's in the toolholder via a spring
which allows it to move around off-center,
and the off-center part is very important.
You start with it off-center and you spin this,
and this will very visibly wobble.
And then, as you push it up against a wall and edge,
it gradually brings it into center
until it's perfectly centered.
And when it's perfectly centered on the shaft,
it'll stop wobbling.
And with a little bit of math,
you can subtract off the radius,
subtract off the width of that parallel,
and then you know exactly where that edge is.
And so he's doing that on all four sides
and, with that, he knows exactly where the part is.
It's really smart.
I'm not sure I would've known this,
which is why I'm not a full-time machinist.
(upbeat music)
(upbeat music continues)
And here's the finished part, this looks great.
The top of this has a lot more
complex geometry than the bottom did.
But this has some more organic shapes,
curves, things like that.
The top took about 45 minutes to mill,
while the bottom was only like four or five minutes,
and that's because, one, we're removing a lot more material,
but, two, we're carving along these organic curves,
and that takes a lot longer.
But, believe it or not,
this is actually a relatively simple part for CNC
and I'll show you why.
Just grabbing a random end mill they have laying around.
This is a 3-axis mill,
and what it means is the end mill or the bit
can move in three directions,
it can go up and down, it can move side to side,
and it can move forward and back,
and we can mill anything that it can reach
from that vertical position.
What it cannot do is it cannot come in sideways
and it cannot come in at an angle.
And so you could imagine if this part had holes in the side,
we'd have to do one of two things.
We either would have turn this on its side,
re-clamp it in the vise, and then do our holes.
Or we'd have to use a machine that has more axes, right?
That can move the part to a different position,
and then come in and mill it.
So this had two different setups,
the bottom where we milled this, and we milled the sides,
and we milled the holes,
and then we flipped it over and we did the top.
That's two setups.
Every time that has to be done,
a human has to come along, flip it,
they may be busy somewhere else
while this machine finishes up.
So ideally you minimize the number of setups on the machine,
maximize your machine time.
So we're gonna see some other machines
that can do things like mill holes in the side

If the part is a little bit more complex,
then they use what's called
a 3-axis plus 2-axis machine,
or a 3+2 machine.
This is the part they're running right now,
and you can see here it has holes drilled in the sidewalls

So they need to be able to hold this part
at a bunch of different orientations.
But once they get it to a given orientation,
they can just drill the hole and they're good to go.
The reason this is called 3+2 and not five

They can position the part anywhere they want,
but once they position it,
they need to hold it in that position

Then, once it's done with that operation, it comes back out.
They can reposition the part, hold it steady,
come in and do some more milling.
The last step, you've got something really complex,
is a 5-axis mill.
So this is an example of something

and this is because it has these really complex curves

So the only way to reach in here is by moving

They only have one of these machines right now.

That is so cool.

Something like say this.
Cylinder here, it's actually got a thread cut in it here,

For a part like this or like this,

You'd come in and spin the tool,

mill for anything that's not totally round.

they can load up a whole bunch of different tools.

Oh my god, this is so cool.
It's so smart.

This is one of those things

And this is where they store the more specialty tools

And then, it looks like they've got a bunch

This is easily tens of thousands of dollars

metadata.shortDescription:
Titan Gilroy tours Tongtai’s advanced CNC machining technology, showcasing a high-speed 160,000 RPM spindle, precision tooling, automation, and next-generation manufacturing capabilities. metadata.title: Don't Buy a Used CNC Machine Until You Watch This
metadata.author: Contend Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Used CNC machine salesperson exposes some of the dark truths of the industry.

In this video, Anthony Cerrito shares how manufacturers should navigate the used CNC machine tool and fabrication machine market.

He shares how to avoid purchasing a problem machine, what to look for during your inspection, and how to avoid unnecessary fees.

Partnering with Greg Paldino from Contend Capital, the two discuss how small business manufacturers can finance their CNC regardless of the age of the machine.

Key themes include having trusted partnerships within the manufacturing industry and leaning on these relationships when buying or selling machine tools.

For more information on financing a used machine tool, visit: 
https://contendcapital.com/machine-tool-financing/

For more insight on used machine buying and selling contact Anthony: https://www.linkedin.com/in/anthony-c-9a39b810b/

to a judgment. If the available

calendar days after notice from FMCSA,

suspension of operating authority to the

this a big deal? Well, according to
freight waves, apparently brokers used
to be able to maintain that bond with
the help of non-liquid assets like
personal loans, crypto, real estate
holdings, or unsecured financial
instruments as backing, but that is all
about to come to an end. According to
the FMCSA, beginning January 16th of
2026, so literally less than two months
from now, brokers, freight forwarders,
and financial responsibility providers
will need to comply with new rules
regarding broker freight forwarder
financial responsibility. These changes
are intended to protect motor carriers
and shippers by ensuring adequate funds
are available to satisfy unpaid freight
charges. So, the first big change on the
list, and I'm going to move right here
so you can see it as well. The only
acceptable assets for BMC85,
which is similar to the bond that
brokers are supposed to maintain, and
we're going to talk about it in just a
second. The only acceptable assets for
this are cash, irrevocable letters of
credit issued by federally insured
depository institutions or US Treasury
bonds. So, let me clarify. There are two
ways a broker can choose to maintain
bond. Either through BMC84
or BMC85.
BMC84
bonds are basically underwritten by
shity companies that end up taking the
financial risk. It's very similar to the
underwriting that happens with insurance
for a carrier. And basically the broker
splits up that $75,000
into monthly payments. BMC85,
however, is a little bit different. It's
like a trust fund, and it requires the
to be deposited with a trust company in
the form of collateral. Freightwave said
that BMC85
bonds are like the Wild West because
there are no financial checks, no credit
checks, and no underwriting. And this is
what they say. For years, some of these
providers operated with little to no
liquidity, often outside the reach of US
regulators. That's one way how brokers
could default on payments, shut down,
and leave carriers holding the bag. And
that is now over. The next thing that is
changing, of course, is the fact that if
a broker's uh bond, the shity bond of
$75,000 falls below $75,000 and they do
not replenish that amount within seven
calendar days, the FMCSA has the
authority to revoke the broker's
operating authority. So, what does that
mean? Well, I'm going to give you a
very, very um obvious example, I
suppose, because I think a lot of people
have worked with this broker before. So,
we're going to use RNR Express as an
example. As you know, if you have worked
with them, RNR was a pretty decent
broker, but something happened over the
past few months where something happened
to their financial situation. They are
rated an F with RTS Factoring. Their
credit score is in the toilet, yet they
continue posting and selling loads to
carriers. RNR is still an active broker
and is able to sell those loads to
carriers. As I have said now, I don't
know what their situation with their
bond is like because I haven't worked
with RNR Express for over a year now.
But under the new rule, if their bond
falls below $75,000
because carriers are not getting paid
and they are filing against that bond in
order to get their money, RNR Express
would have its authority revoked and
would no longer be able to sell loads to
carriers. Now, what does this rule mean
for you and me, the carriers, the
truckers? Well, it's twofold. On one
hand, this new rule, again, it's set to
begin or be effective as of January 16th
It will eliminate the bad actors. And
I'm talking about the brokers who know
that they have financial issues. Their
bond is falling below the $75,000. As
you guys know, if the broker is very
crappy, the bond gets depleted to zero.
And then if you're too late filing on
that bond, yeah, you end up without
money for the load you hauled. So, the
good news about this rule is, of course,
it's going to limit the amount of
brokers who have financial issues and
will not allow those brokers to continue
selling loads to carriers who perhaps
don't do significant vetting when
working with a broker. and just trust
that this broker is going to pay. So
those brokers are going to leave the
market. Their authority is going to get
revoked and it's going to limit
theoretically the amount of carriers who
end up holding the bag after hauling a
load and not getting paid. The flip side
is that there is some risk according to
freight waves. Some carriers may find
out after a broker authority is
suspended, after they hauled the load,
after the invoice is sitting unpaid.
FMCSA is not going to text you when a
broker's bond drops below $75,000.
So, it will basically be up to you to
start vetting these brokers like crazy.
It's not going to be a situation where,
oh, the FMCSA is regulating the
financial shy bonds right now, so I
don't have to vet. No, on the contrary,
you will start vetting more. Now, if
you're using a factoring company, it's a
little bit easier because factoring
companies do their own vetting and you
are just able to check what is going on
with their credit score, their days to
pay. Uh, so that's a little bit easier.
Now, if you're not using a factoring
company, Freightwaves actually
recommends several steps. Number one,
check Safer and FMCSA licensing and
insurance portal. Number two, confirm
that their BMC84 or BMC85. These are two
ways that brokers can get that bond are
current and active. And if you can call
the bond agency to ensure that they have
present. Number three is of course be
wary of insurance cancellations. So yeah
guys, I just wanted to update you on
this because again this is going to on
one hand provide a little bit more
financial security but on the other hand
it can drive a lot of brokers out uh
unexpectedly and we really don't want to
be in a situation where like freight
wave said you hold a load and then you

course to double check everything. Vet
those brokers like crazy. If you have
the DAT or truck stop higher tier load
board, you're able to take a look at how

And I would just be very careful. And
again, if you have a factoring company,

fantastic rest of your day. Stay safe,
stay healthy, and keep learning. See you

metadata.title: New FMCSA Rule to Protect Truckers from Unpaid Broker Claims
metadata.author: AFT Dispatch
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you a trucker who has been burned by freight brokers who don't pay you for your services? Do you have unpaid broker claims? Do you want to know how the new FMCSA rule will affect your business and your rights? If so, this video is for you.

The FMCSA has issued a new rule that will protect trucking companies from unpaid broker claims, effective from January 16, 2024. The rule is supported by both the Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) and the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association (OOIDA). The rule amends the broker and freight forwarder regulations, tightening the oversight in five areas of broker financial responsibility.

In this video, we will explain what these five areas are and how they will impact the trucking industry. We will also discuss who won and who lost in this rulemaking process, and whether it is fair for all parties involved. Some of the key points we will cover are:

- Brokers who do not respond after a drawdown will be immediately suspended, starting from January 2025.
- A broker's authority may be suspended if their security falls below $75,000, starting from January 2025.
- Surety providers can cancel a bond or trust due to broker insolvency, starting from January 2025.
- Acceptable trust fund assets (liquid and readily available) are cash, irrevocable letters of credit (ILOCs) and treasury bonds, starting from January 2026.
- No real estate, stocks, non-treasury bonds, or other securities are allowed, and loan and finance companies are no longer eligible as trust fund providers or trustees, starting from January 2026.

Don't miss this important update on the new FMCSA rule and how it will affect your trucking business. Watch the video now and leave your comments below.

metadata.title: FMCSA Complaint Center: Report Broker Problems, Fraud & Bad Chassis
metadata.author: Freight Pro Hub
metadata.shortDescription:
FMCSA expanded its Complaint Center on November 6, 2026. Truckers, owner-operators, and small fleets can use the updated system to report certain property broker violations, registration fraud, identity theft, and problems involving intermodal equipment providers.

In this video, I explain what changed, the types of complaints FMCSA accepts, and how to file a complaint with supporting documentation.

WHAT WE COVER:
• Broker authority and misrepresentation complaints
• DOT registration fraud and company identity theft
• Chassis and intermodal equipment provider problems
• CDL training providers and other eligible complaints
• How to file and what happens afterward

OFFICIAL FMCSA RESOURCES
File a complaint: https://complaint.fmcsa.dot.gov/
How to file: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/complaint-center/how-to-file
Eligible complaints: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/complaint-center/eligible-complaints

IMPORTANT: A complaint does not automatically trigger an investigation or fine. Filing through FMCSA does not guarantee payment of an unpaid freight invoice.

More trucking news and compliance resources for owner-operators and small fleets: https://freightprohub.com/

Have you dealt with broker misrepresentation, identity theft, or unsafe chassis equipment? Tell us about it in the comments.

I'm Carlton, Mr. Freight Pro Hub. Stay informed and protect your business.

#FMCSA #TruckingNews #OwnerOperators

metadata.title: Trucker Regs Daily: FMCSA Shuts Down YMC Transport, Trucking Jobs Flat, Reefer Rejections Hit 21%
metadata.author: the funny farm
metadata.shortDescription: Bob covers the newest trucker news for November 12, 2026: FMCSA orders YMC Transport out of service while its trucks keep running under a new carrier name, October trucking jobs come in flat at 1,471,300 while spot linehaul runs up to 35 percent higher than a year ago, reefer tender rejections hit 21 percent ahead of Thanksgiving, Knight-Swift seeks double-digit rate increases in contract talks, westbound SR-60 ramps close to trucks in Riverside County through spring 2027, and this morning's Love's diesel prices.

trucking news.

Administration shut down a carrier on

Line on November 9th.

higher.

buying new iron to fix it. Preliminary
class 8 truck orders totaled 13,500 in

meaningful demand build heading into the

are calling the strongest in over 100
years
as a potential additional pressure on
reefer capacity this winter,

double-digit rate increases in the

loaded mile, excluding fuel, had risen
5.6% year-on-year in the second quarter
Its chief executive, Adam Miller, linked
the tighter market to regulators
removing carriers that break the rules,
calling the change durable and saying it
raises the floor for rates.
That is the same enforcement squeeze
behind the numbers in the rest of this
show. And a road closure to know about

Monday, November 9th, the westbound
State Route 60 on and off ramps at

interchange project that includes six

Boulevard to six lanes.

Alabama, in the Mobile area, at $5.59.
That is Trucker Regs Daily for Thursday,
November 12th. We post at 7:00 a.m.
Central every day. Drive safe, and we
will talk to you tomorrow morning.

metadata.shortDescription:
FMCSA Personal Conveyance Rules EXPLAINED! (What Truckers MUST Know!)

Personal conveyance is one of the most confusing FMCSA rules for truck drivers and getting it wrong could put you out of service. In this video, I break down exactly what personal conveyance really means, what the FMCSA regulations actually say, and how DOT inspectors and CVSA officers enforce it.

You’ll learn:
✅ The official FMCSA definition of personal conveyance
✅ Situations where you can and cannot use it
✅ Common mistakes that lead to violations
✅ Real-world examples from inspections
✅ How to protect your CDL and avoid fines

Most drivers think they know this rule...but trust me, this is the one that gets truckers in trouble the most.

👉 Drop a comment: Do you think personal conveyance should have stricter limits, or do drivers need more flexibility?

If you’re a CDL driver who wants to stay compliant and keep rolling without stress, make sure to watch this all the way through.

📌 Subscribe for weekly videos on FMCSA rules, DOT inspections, CDL compliance, and trucking news that every driver needs to know.





Welcome to That DOT Cop — your go-to channel for real, no-fluff trucking advice straight from a State DOT Officer.

Here you’ll learn how to pass DOT inspections, avoid costly violations, keep your rig compliant, and stay safe on the road. I break down Level 1 inspections, weigh station myths, and truck maintenance tips that every driver and owner-operator needs to know.

Subscribe for weekly videos that help you stay rolling clean and legal.

metadata.title: What Happens to MRI Scanners When Hospitals Replace Them?
metadata.author: Reclaim Atlas
metadata.shortDescription:
Who buys a hospital’s old MRI scanner—and what happens before it can scan patients somewhere else?

Replacing an MRI machine does not automatically end its useful life. This documentary explores the market for used and refurbished MRI scanners, following the journey from a hospital’s replacement decision to specialist refurbishment and a potential new home.

We examine why another healthcare provider might consider a refurbished system, what refurbishment involves, and why buying the machine is only one part of the decision. Removal, installation and ongoing support also matter.

Manufacturer programmes such as Siemens Healthineers ecoline and GE HealthCare GoldSeal show how pre-owned imaging equipment can return to service. However, the condition and suitability of each system determine its next chapter.

Reclaim Atlas explores the second lives of machines, materials and products—and the businesses behind them.

What would you want to know before a hospital bought a refurbished MRI scanner?

#MRI #MedicalEquipment #CircularEconomy

segments.text: Imagine a hospital preparing to remove
its MRI scanner. The appointments have
stopped. Engineers are measuring the
exit route. Soon, the machine that
helped doctors look inside thousands of
people will leave the building. But
somewhere else, someone may be preparing
a room for its arrival. Who buys a
hospital's old MRI scanner and what
makes it worth trusting with another
patient? The next owner, the buyers can
be other hospitals, outpatient imaging
centers, and specialist healthcare
providers. But the person buying from
the original hospital may be an
equipment dealer or a manufacturer's
refurbishment business. They connect a
machine leaving one service with a
customer who can use it again. That
distinction matters. A hospital can sell
equipment without its next clinical
destination being ready. Between the two
owners, it's a business of inspection,
repair, logistics, installation, and
support. And this market is not limited
to places that cannot afford anything
else. In Finland, healthcare provider
Terveystalo describes choosing a
refurbished MRI system for its Tikkurila
location. In an article published in
December 2025, it explains that selected
components and software were modernized.
The provider presents the decision as
part of combining clinical needs,
cost-effectiveness, and sustainability.
That is a real buyer describing a real
installation. It does not tell us the
price, the machine's complete history,
or whether the same choice would suit
another clinic. But it answers the first
question. An older scanner can be a
deliberate investment rather than an
emergency compromise. The hard other
question is what has to happen before
that investment becomes useful. Why a
working scanner leaves a hospital
replacing a machine is not necessarily
declaring it broken. Its requirements
may have changed. It may want
capabilities its existing system cannot
deliver or a different workflow. An
equipment purchase can be driven by the
service a hospital wants to build next,
not simply by whether yesterday's
machine still operates. Think of two
hypothetical facilities. One needs to
expand a specialized imaging service,
the other needs dependable capacity for
examinations that an appropriately
configured older system can already
perform. The same scanner could be a
poor fit for the first facility and a
useful candidate for the second, but
nobody should decide that from the
machine's age or a photograph. Buyers
need to match its documented
capabilities to the examinations they
intend to provide. They also need to ask
what is actually being sold. A complete
system? A magnet with some accessories
missing? Equipment sold as it stands or
a package that includes refurbishment
and installation? Those descriptions can
refer to very different purchases, even
when the listing photographs look almost
identical. A second-hand listing also
captures just one moment. The buyer
needs to think ahead. If the service
grows, can the system still meet its
needs? If an essential component fails
later, is there a realistic repair path?
A machine that suits today's plan may
not suit the plan that justified buying
it. That is why remaining usefulness is
a better question than age alone. More
than the giant magnet. The recognizable
white tunnel is only the visible part of
the system. MRI uses magnetic fields and
radio frequency energy to obtain signals
from the body. Computers turn those
signals into images. Unlike a CT
scanner, MRI does not use ionizing
radiation to make those images. Inside
and around the scanner are components
with different jobs. The main magnet
provides a strong field. Gradient coils
vary that field in controlled ways,
helping locate where signals come from.
Radio frequency coils help transmit or
receive the signals used for imaging.
There are also electronics, software, a
patient table, and supporting equipment.
Imagine buying an expensive camera body
without checking its lenses, computer
connection, or available software. The
central object might be valuable, while
the complete setup cannot do your
particular job. With MRI, the
consequences of missing that distinction
are much greater. A buyer needs to know
which coils and software capabilities
are included, whether they are
compatible, and who will support the
system. A working magnet does not
establish that every examination the
buyer wants is possible. This is why
service records and a detailed equipment
inventory belong in the story alongside
the impressive machinery. The paperwork
helps reveal what the machine can become
and what it might still need. The room
becomes part of the purchase. Then comes
a problem that a normal second-hand
purchase rarely creates, the building
itself. A scanner needs a suitable route
out of its old location and into its new
one. Engineers must consider access and
structural support, including the weight
moving along that route. Equipment this
substantial cannot be treated like
office furniture. At the destination,
the project can involve electrical
supply, cooling, ventilation, and a room
designed for the particular system.
Radio frequency shielding helps keep
unwanted interference from affecting
imaging. Magnetic field considerations
also influence the layout and
surrounding space. The details vary by
scanner and site. A floor plan that
worked for one installation is not
automatically suitable for another. Nor
does disconnecting an ordinary power
cable establish that an MRI magnet is
safe to approach. Magnetic field hazards
require their own assessment, an
inactive screen is not proof of a safe
working area. Removal and transport
requires specialists following the
applicable procedures. For a buyer, all
of this becomes part of the cost and
schedule. Picture a clinic that has
found an attractive scanner, but has not
checked its building. The equipment
quote looks manageable. Then the
installation survey reveals additional
work. Nothing about the scanner's
advertised price has changed, yet the
actual project is now a different
proposition. What refurbishment has to
prove. Before an older system returns to
clinical work, someone has to establish
its condition and address the work it
requires. Siemens Healthineers describes
its refurbishment program in five
stages: selection, removal,
refurbishment, installation, and
services. Its selection criteria include
condition, service history, performance,
and technology level. That means a
professional refurbishment program
starts before the cleaning or
repainting. It begins by deciding
whether a particular machine belongs in
the program at all. The company
describes component checks, replacement
of worn parts, and suitable updates
within its process. These are the
suppliers' stated procedures, not a
promise that every seller follows the
same approach. The buyer still needs the
actual scope of work, configuration,
test results, and contract. A fresh
exterior cannot answer those questions.
Neither can the word refurbish on its
own. There is also a regulatory
distinction. In the United States, the
FDA distinguishes servicing from
remanufacturing that significantly
changes a device's performance or safety
specifications or its intended use. The
work performed matters, not simply the
label attached to the sale. Restoring a
system to specified performance is also
different from giving it every feature
of the latest model. Credible second
life depends on clear limits as much as
successful repairs. The cheap machine
and the expensive service. Now, imagine
two hypothetical offers for the same
clinic. The first has a lower equipment
price, the second costs more, but
includes a broader installation and
support package. Which is cheaper? You
cannot tell yet. The clinic needs
comparable totals, equipment, necessary
repairs, removal, transport, site
preparation, installation, and testing.
Then come the costs of operating and
maintaining the service. Even that
comparison is incomplete if the two
systems cannot perform the same required
examination. Here is the practical test.
Could this clinic use this configuration
in this building with the staff and
support it can actually obtain? A low
purchase price cannot compensate for a
missing capability essential to the
service. Nor does it solve a shortage of
trained staff or an unsuitable room. And
a service contract needs more than a
reassuring heading. What is covered?
Which parts are excluded? Who responds
when the system develops a fault, are
the promised services available at the
buyer's location? Philips, for example,
advertises warranty and service support
for its circular edition MRI systems.
That shows how support can be part of
the refurbished offering. It does not
mean every used scanner comes with
equivalent terms. For our hypothetical
clinic, downtime is another uncertainty.
A scanner awaiting repair occupies a
room while appointments may need to be
rearranged. An operating plan that
assumes uninterrupted service can make
an attractive purchase look better on
paper than it works in practice. So, the
buyer is evaluating more than a machine.
It is evaluating the ability to keep an
imaging service available. That is where
some apparent bargains disappear and
where a well-supported refurbished
system can make sense. Consider one more
detail in those two hypothetical offers,
the handover point. Does the seller's
responsibility finish when the equipment
is collected, when it reaches the
building, or after agreed installation
tests? The answer affects who must solve
an unexpected problem. A buyer comparing
only the headline prices could miss that
difference entirely. The contract
connects the promises in the sales
conversation to the work someone is
actually expected to complete. For
equipment that depends on a whole room
and a trained team, that connection can
shape the entire purchase. The first
scan is not the finish line. Once the
scanner arrives, producing an image is
only the beginning of proving that the
installation performs as intended. In
its MRI quality guidance, the American
College of Radiology calls for a
complete performance evaluation by a
qualified medical physicist or me a
scientist after installation and before
patient imaging. One tool used in MRI
quality assessment is a phantom, a
specially designed test object with
known features. Scanning something known
helps assess the system's performance
against expected results. A patient's
anatomy is not a convenient calibration
ruler. A test object gives specialists a
controlled reference. The ACR's
accreditation process includes both
phantom and clinical image quality
testing. These are elements of a
particular accreditation framework, not
a single worldwide permission slip. The
broader point is straightforward. A
machine has to be evaluated in the
service where it will operate. An
impressive photograph from its previous
location cannot establish its
performance after relocation, and checks
do not end when the opening day
photograph is taken. Ongoing quality
control is part of keeping the service
dependable. When another scanner needs
the parts, of course, not every retired
MRI system finds another clinical home.
Sometimes the work needed, available
support, or demand for that
configuration makes a complete resale
unattractive. Another potential buyer is
a business dealing in imaging equipment
parts. A compatible component with
documented condition in another system.
That does not mean every removed part is
reusable, or that a part from one model
will fit another. There is a difference
between recovering a useful component
and simply keeping a warehouse full of
unverified hardware. The rest of the
equipment still needs appropriate
handling. Its possible value as spare
parts does not make uncontrolled
dismantling sensible. There is another
outcome worth remembering, too. An older
scanner may stay where it is. Where an
appropriate upgrade exists, a provider
can retain valuable hardware and improve
the system around it. A second life does
not always require a second address. So,
who buys a hospital's old MRI scanner?
Sometimes a manufacturer or equipment
specialist buys it first. Sometimes
another health care provider becomes its
next operator. Sometimes a parts
business finds value in what can support
other machines. The deciding question is
not whether it once belonged to a
hospital. It is whether its remaining
capabilities, condition, support, and
total cost fit a real need. An MRI
scanner's second life succeeds when all
of those pieces come together, and the
next patient enters a service that is
ready for them.

A buyer needs to know which coils and software capabilities are included, whether they are compatible, and who will support the system. A working magnet does not establish that every examination the buyer wants is possible. This is why service records and a detailed equipment inventory belong in the story alongside the impressive machinery. The paperwork helps reveal what the machine can become and what it might still need. The room becomes part of the purchase. Then comes a problem that a normal second-hand purchase rarely creates, the building itself. A scanner needs a suitable route out of its old location and into its new one. Engineers must consider access and structural support, including the weight moving along that route. Equipment this substantial cannot be treated like office furniture. At the destination, the project can involve electrical supply, cooling, ventilation, and a room designed for the particular system. Radio frequency shielding helps keep unwanted interference from affecting imaging. Magnetic field considerations also influence the layout and surrounding space. The details vary by scanner and site. A floor plan that worked for one installation is not automatically suitable for another. Nor does disconnecting an ordinary power cable establish that an MRI magnet is safe to approach. Magnetic field hazards require their own assessment, an inactive screen is not proof of a safe working area. Removal and transport requires specialists following the applicable procedures. For a buyer, all of this becomes part of the cost and schedule. Picture a clinic that has found an attractive scanner, but has not checked its building. The equipment quote looks manageable. Then the installation survey reveals additional work. Nothing about the scanner's advertised price has changed, yet the actual project is now a different proposition. What refurbishment has to prove. Before an older system returns to clinical work, someone has to establish its condition and address the work it requires. Siemens Healthineers describes its refurbishment program in five stages: selection, removal, refurbishment, installation, and services. Its selection criteria include condition, service history, performance, and technology level. That means a professional refurbishment program starts before the cleaning or repainting. It begins by deciding whether a particular machine belongs in the program at all. The company describes component checks, replacement of worn parts, and suitable updates within its process. These are the suppliers' stated procedures, not a promise that every seller follows the same approach. The buyer still needs the actual scope of work, configuration, test results, and contract. A fresh exterior cannot answer those questions. Neither can the word refurbish on its own. There is also a regulatory distinction. In the United States, the FDA distinguishes servicing from remanufacturing that significantly changes a device's performance or safety specifications or its intended use. The work performed matters, not simply the label attached to the sale. Restoring a system to specified performance is also different from giving it every feature of the latest model. Credible second life depends on clear limits as much as successful repairs. The cheap machine and the expensive service. Now, imagine two hypothetical offers for the same clinic. The first has a lower equipment price, the second costs more, but includes a broader installation and support package. Which is cheaper? You cannot tell yet. The clinic needs comparable totals, equipment, necessary repairs, removal, transport, site preparation, installation, and testing. Then come the costs of operating and maintaining the service. Even that comparison is incomplete if the two systems cannot perform the same required examination. Here is the practical test. Could this clinic use this configuration in this building with the staff and support it can actually obtain? A low purchase price cannot compensate for a missing capability essential to the service. Nor does it solve a shortage of trained staff or an unsuitable room. And a service contract needs more than a reassuring heading. What is covered? Which parts are excluded? Who responds when the system develops a fault, are the promised services available at the buyer's location? Philips, for example, advertises warranty and service support for its circular edition MRI systems. That shows how support can be part of the refurbished offering. It does not mean every used scanner comes with equivalent terms. For our hypothetical clinic, downtime is another uncertainty. A scanner awaiting repair occupies a room while appointments may need to be rearranged. An operating plan that assumes uninterrupted service can make an attractive purchase look better on paper than it works in practice. So, the buyer is evaluating more than a machine. It is evaluating the ability to keep an imaging service available. That is where some apparent bargains disappear and where a well-supported refurbished system can make sense. Consider one more detail in those two hypothetical offers, the handover point. Does the seller's responsibility finish when the equipment is collected, when it reaches the building, or after agreed installation tests? The answer affects who must solve an unexpected problem. A buyer comparing only the headline prices could miss that difference entirely. The contract connects the promises in the sales conversation to the work someone is actually expected to complete. For equipment that depends on a whole room and a trained team, that connection can shape the entire purchase. The first scan is not the finish line. Once the scanner arrives, producing an image is only the beginning of proving that the installation performs as intended. In its MRI quality guidance, the American College of Radiology calls for a complete performance evaluation by a qualified medical physicist or me a scientist after installation and before patient imaging. One tool used in MRI quality assessment is a phantom, a specially designed test object with known features. Scanning something known helps assess the system's performance against expected results. A patient's anatomy is not a convenient calibration ruler. A test object gives specialists a controlled reference. The ACR's accreditation process includes both phantom and clinical image quality testing. These are elements of a particular accreditation framework, not a single worldwide permission slip. The broader point is straightforward. A machine has to be evaluated in the service where it will operate. An impressive photograph from its previous location cannot establish its performance after relocation, and checks do not end when the opening day photograph is taken. Ongoing quality control is part of keeping the service dependable. When another scanner needs the parts, of course, not every retired MRI system finds another clinical home. Sometimes the work needed, available support, or demand for that configuration makes a complete resale unattractive. Another potential buyer is a business dealing in imaging equipment parts. A compatible component with documented condition in another system. That does not mean every removed part is reusable, or that a part from one model will fit another. There is a difference between recovering a useful component and simply keeping a warehouse full of unverified hardware. The rest of the equipment still needs appropriate handling. Its possible value as spare parts does not make uncontrolled dismantling sensible. There is another outcome worth remembering, too. An older scanner may stay where it is. Where an appropriate upgrade exists, a provider can retain valuable hardware and improve the system around it. A second life does not always require a second address. So, who buys a hospital's old MRI scanner? Sometimes a manufacturer or equipment specialist buys it first. Sometimes another health care provider becomes its next operator. Sometimes a parts business finds value in what can support other machines. The deciding question is not whether it once belonged to a hospital. It is whether its remaining capabilities, condition, support, and total cost fit a real need. An MRI scanner's second life succeeds when all of those pieces come together, and the next patient enters a service that is ready for them.

metadata.title: MXR Imaging Webinar Series: Purchasing Platinum Certified Pre-Owned MRI and CT Equipment
metadata.author: MXR Imaging
metadata.shortDescription:
With the emerging technologies, there has been an increasing trend of "affordable buying". For example, today a customer is looking for a CT scanner that is reconditioned, rather than a brand new system. The reconditioned option allows the purchasing of necessary diagnostic imaging devices at affordable prices without compromising quality or safety.  There is a lack in standardization of policies for reconditioned devices and a question of quality within the market.  This webinar will examine the risks and benefits of buying a reconditioned MRI or CT versus new. 

Charlie Lewis is a widely known technical expert in the Diagnostic Imaging industry.  Over the last 40 years, he has held various leadership roles in Technical Service and Sales, including Senior Management positions at In-House Service Organizations (IHO), Independent Service Organizations (ISO’s), and with Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM’s). Charlie is highly respected for his technical expertise and experience within the industry.

segments.text: Hey everybody, I’m Jordan with Block Imaging, and today we’re going to talk about what
you get when you buy medical imaging equipment new, used, or refurbished.
Stick around and find out what each of these experiences looks like.
Let’s begin with the most self-explanatory category: new.
When you buy new medical imaging equipment it’s coming to you right from the factory
with a possible stop at a distributor’s warehouse along the way.
A new system has never seen service scanning patients, so there’s no wear and tear on
any of the components, and its cosmetic condition is pristine.
The price of a new system often includes a manufacturer’s warranty, so functional problems
or defects discovered in the early days of system use are covered by the manufacturer.
These are all fantastic benefits, but they will cost you.
Depending on which modality and manufacturer you’re working with, a new system could
cost twice as much as systems from the other categories.
On the other end of the spectrum, you’ll find used systems.
When you buy a used medical imaging system it’s coming from a facility where it’s
been in use scanning patients, or from a warehouse where it’s been stored since its deinstallation.
The system is sold in “as-is” condition, with all the wear, tear, bumps, and bruises
it earned in its previous home.
Manufacturer’s warranties are out of the picture with used equipment but, if you’re
working with a reputable provider, service parts and labor coverage can be added at a
cost in addition to the purchase price of the equipment.
The major pro for buying used equipment is its significantly lower price point.
The major con is the risk you assume by accepting it in “as-is” condition.
Still, with due diligence, a used purchase can be a strong value.
Right in the middle are refurbished imaging systems.
Not all refurbishment processes look the same.
You can find out more about that in some of the other videos in this playlist but, for
now, we’ll use our own as an example.

segments.text: First time buying on IronPlanet? Here's how you get started.
Step 1 - Create your account
Go to IronPlanet.com and click 'Create Free Account' in the top right corner.
Enter your details in the form and click the ‘Create Free Account’ button.
Go to your email inbox and open the confirmation email.
Confirm your email address by clicking the 'Confirm email' button.
Please note your personal password is included in this email.
Step 2 - Verify your phone number
To verify your account, please provide your phone number.
A code will be sent to your phone, which you need to enter on the verification page.
Click 'Confirm Code" on the page and your account is now verified!
Step 3 - Get bidding privileges
In order to buy on IronPlanet, you need to have bidding privileges. This can be seen as an approved buying limit.
Click on the 'Get bidding privileges' button and fill out your company details as accurately as possible.
Is your company located in the EU region? Then make sure to provide your VAT country and VAT number.
Are you based outside the EU region? You might be required to place a deposit.
Submit your information and your request will be processed immediately.
This should take no longer than 30 minutes.
Once approved you can start placing bids!
How to buy on IronPlanet & Marketplace-E
There are two easy ways to buy: 'Online Auctions' and 'Make Offer'.
With ‘Online Auctions’ you can place bids on items and compete against other bidders until the auction closes.
You can also place a maximum bid and the system will keep you in the lead with the smallest possible increment.
With 'Make Offer', you can place offers on items of interest and the seller of the item can accept, decline or counter-offer.
The system will keep you updated on your activity via email notifications. You can also see your activity in the 'My Account' section.
You're now ready to start buying on IronPlanet!
Go to ironplanet.com and create your free account.

metadata.title: How To Do A Ucc Lien Search?
metadata.author: County Portal
metadata.shortDescription:
How To Do A Ucc Lien Search?

To conduct a UCC lien search, first accurately identify the precise legal name of the debtor, whether an individual or business entity. Next, determine the correct jurisdiction, which is typically the state where the debtor is located or incorporated. Most states provide an online UCC search portal through their Secretary of State's website. Navigate to this portal and enter the exact debtor name into the search field; precise matching is crucial, as minor variations can yield no results. The system will then display any active UCC financing statements filed against that debtor. Review these results carefully, noting the secured party, collateral described, and filing date. While some states offer free basic searches, others may charge a fee for more detailed or certified results, which are often necessary for official or legal purposes.

We explain what a UCC lien is and how they can impact your business. UCC stands for uniform commercial code. With a UCC lien, a lender can lay claim to collateral that a borrower pledges to secure their financing. If the borrower can’t pay back the loan, the lien gives the lender the right to seize the assets that are secured and sell them to repay the loan. Let’s learn more about how a UCC lien works.

What Is a UCC Lien? (1:08)

How to Know If There’s a Lien Against Your Business (1:25)

Types of Loans That Have Liens (2:27)

How Do UCC Loans Affect Access to Capital? (3:00)

How Do I Remove a Lien? (4:15)

segments.text: UCC Liens: What Do They Mean For Your Business?
In today’s video, I’m going to explain what a UCC lien is and everything you need
to know about it.
I’m Priyanka Prakash, senior staff writer and small business expert at Fundera.
UCC stands for Uniform Commercial Code.
When you apply for a business loan, chances are high that the lender will place a UCC
lien on one or more of your business assets.
What exactly does that mean, and why should you care?
Let’s dig into the details.
What Is a UCC Lien?
A UCC lien is used by a lender to show that they have certain legal rights to your business’s
property.
A lien can be filed against a specific piece of property or collateral—like a particular
piece of equipment or your inventory—or a lender can file a blanket UCC lien against
all of your business assets.
Whichever the type of lien, here’s the important part.
If for some reason you can’t pay your loan back, the lien gives the lender the right
to seize the assets that are secured and sell them to repay the loan.
While this might sound scary, liens are actually a pretty routine part of getting a business
loan.
It’s just important that you understand how the lien works and how it can affect you
as a business owner.
For more information on business loans, head over to our video where we cover eight different
types of loans.
How to Know If There’s a Lien Against Your Business
If you already have a business loan, you might be wondering how you can know whether a lender
has already filed a lien against your business.
A lien is public record information, and you can find out if there’s a lien against you
(or another business for that matter) by contacting your state’s secretary of state office.
Many states also have an online UCC search database that’s open to the public.
Here’s New York State’s UCC database as an example.
If I type in the word “baked,” I get a full list of all businesses operating in the
state which have “baked” in their name and a UCC filing on their record.
Clicking a business’s name shows more detail about which lender or lenders have a claim
to which assets.
You can even see a copy of the UCC financing statement (called a UCC-1 financing statement)
that the lender filed against the business.
As an alternative, you can also check your business credit report to see if a lien has
been filed against your business.
Types of Loans That Have Liens
Almost all types of business loans require a UCC lien, including:
* Conventional bank loans * SBA loans
* Online business loans * Asset-based financing, such as inventory
loans * Commercial real estate loans
* Invoice financing * … and more
Only some merchant cash advance providers don’t require UCC liens, but merchant cash
advances can be very expensive for small businesses, so be cautious if you’re applying for this
type of financing.
How Do UCC Loans Affect Access to Capital?
Having a UCC lien on your record signals to a lender that you have already borrowed money
and that another lender has legal rights to some or all of your business property.
This means that the new lender might hesitate to lend money to you.
Every lender wants to be paid back, with interest and on time, but the lender with the oldest
UCC lien, called first position in the lending world, gets highest priority to your assets.
For example, assume that three lenders all have filed a UCC lien against a refrigerator
that your restaurant owns.
Lender A filed the lien in 2017, lender B in 2018, and lender C in 2019.
If you default on all three loans, lender A gets first dibs on the refrigerator and
can sell it off to be compensated for their loss.
Lender A is in first position.
Most high-profile lenders prefer to be in first position and won’t extend you a loan
if another lender has already filed a UCC lien against your business assets.
That said, online business lenders are more likely than bank lenders and SBA lenders to
accept a second or third position.
Since having a UCC lien on your record can affect your access to business capital, it’s
important to remove liens as soon as you pay off a loan.
A UCC filing is generally active for five years, after which a lender needs to renew
the filing to retain their rights in your property.
Most lenders just allow the lien to expire on its own.
If you want to have the lien removed before that, you need to file a UCC-3 financing statement.
Some unscrupulous lenders look through public records, searching for businesses with a bunch
of UCC liens filed against them.
They know that these businesses are in need of capital and may send them offers of pre-approval.
If you receive such offers, make sure you clearly have planned how much financing your
business can afford before agreeing to take on an additional business loan.
That’s the story on UCC liens and what they can mean for your small business.
For more information on small business loans or to apply for a business loan with a group
of vetted, reputable lenders, visit fundera.com.
You can also go to youtube.com/funderaloans, and subscribe to our channel for more videos.
Thanks for watching!

metadata.title: UCC 101 for Lenders: The Basics of UCC Searching and Filing
metadata.author: CSC
metadata.shortDescription:
https://www.cscglobal.com/service/webinar/ucc-101/

Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) filing, searching and monitoring can be complicated between debtor name variation, search logic differences, and various filing procedures. But filing, searching and monitoring properly can ensure your security interests remain perfected. Getting and staying organized, paying attention to detail and keeping close track of the changes that may impact your filing position can be easy with the help of a few best practices. 

Intended for lenders, this webinar provides valuable guidance to loan clerks, loan processors, commercial loan officers, and others responsible for the day-to-day management of UCC portfolios (i.e. UCC search and filing). 

Join Russ Lash of CSC to learn:
• Debtor name ins-and-outs
• Common UCC pitfalls
• Hints for better UCC-1 and UCC-3 forms
• Easier options for successful debtor tracking

metadata.author: Garden Shop Pro
metadata.shortDescription:
https://gardenshop.pro https://semenata.shop https://xn--80aahfu4ar.net https://xn--80aahfu4ar.com https://gardenbg.com https://semenata.org https://semenata.bg Need to search New York UCC filings step by step but don’t know where to begin? In this video, we explain how New York UCC filings work, why they matter, and how to search public UCC records online before making business, lending, or asset-related decisions.

You’ll learn what a UCC filing is, what a financing statement means, why lenders file UCC liens, and how these records can affect businesses, borrowers, equipment, inventory, accounts receivable, and other collateral. We also explain the difference between UCC-1 filings, amendments, continuations, assignments, and terminations so beginners can understand what they are seeing in public records.

This guide covers how to search New York UCC filings by debtor name, business entity name, individual name, filing number, and secured party information. You’ll also learn how to review filing dates, collateral descriptions, filing status, debtor information, secured party details, and how to recognize whether a filing appears active, amended, continued, assigned, or terminated.

We also cover practical real-world uses for UCC searches, including checking a business before buying it, reviewing equipment financing, researching commercial loans, verifying liens on assets, checking inventory financing, and improving due diligence before signing business agreements.

You’ll discover useful research strategies used by lenders, business buyers, attorneys, investors, and entrepreneurs, including checking spelling variations, reviewing historical filings, comparing business records, watching for blanket liens, and understanding red flags before transactions.

Whether you are a business owner, lender, investor, buyer, seller, legal researcher, or simply trying to understand public business records in New York, this video is designed to provide practical, detailed, beginner-friendly educational value that remains useful long term.

Disclaimer:
UCC filing systems, search tools, public record rules, fees, filing procedures, and legal requirements may change over time. This video is for educational and informational purposes only and should not be considered legal, lending, financial, or transaction-specific advice. Always verify important UCC information through official sources or qualified professionals before making decisions.

metadata.shortDescription:
Shipping #heavyhaul or an #oversizeload? This type of #freight #shipping can be complicated. We’re here to help you understand the regulations that go into these shipments so you can navigate them with ease.
