segments.text: From tree trunks that turn into lumber for construction, manufactured homes that provide
shelter, or solar panels that create energy for our homes; oversized shipments are needed
to keep the world running.
But they can have some of the most complex requirements. Oversized loads may need safety
equipment, escorts and permits for their travel alone. And regulations vary from state to
state.
We re here to simplify what you need to know for your oversized shipments.
An oversized load exceeds the maximum legal weight or dimensions. Each state has different
legal limits, however federal guidelines are as follows:
* Length: Maximum of 75 from front of truck to the end of the load
* Width: Maximum of 8 6 * Height: Maximum of 13 6 from ground to top
of load and * Weight: 80,000 lbs including truck, trailer
and cargo. It s important for you to know the exact dimensions
of your oversized freight to determine if a permit and/or support services are required.
Besides meeting legal regulations, oversized freight also needs the right equipment to
move it.
You need to know your equipment limits and to not overload it. Overloading can have bad
effects on steering, braking, and speed control, not to mention causing damage to the truck
itself.
Your freight should be positioned correctly on the flatbed for even weight distribution.
Poor positioning and being too top heavy can mean higher risk for a rollover.
Oversized freight can cause big problems if not secured properly. Loose cargo that falls
off can cause traffic problems. Make sure the right materials are used to tiedown the
freight or equipment to keep it from moving during transport.
Depending on the type and size of your shipment, you may require one or two escort vehicles.
The rule of escort vehicles differ by state. If the load is extra wide, some states demand
that there also be law enforcement escorts, with their time usually paid for by the hauling
company. Safety equipment includes warning signs, flags,
and lights to give visibility to drivers of the oversized load and its edges.
Most states call for a yellow and black sign or banner that states WIDE LOAD or OVERSIZED
LOAD on the back and/or front of the vehicle.
If the load is permitted to move at night, amber or red lights are required, as well
as whenever there may be reduced visibility, such as fog or rain.
All safety equipment is required to be removed or turned off when the truck is not hauling
the load.
Even though oversize load regulations vary by state, any load that exceeds legal limits
in weight or size MUST get a permit for the state being traveled through.
Permit fees can range to as little as $15 or over $70, depending on the state and size
of the load. Some states charge permit application fees, but if you frequently move oversized
loads, they may offer you to set up an account, reducing or dropping future application fees.
For an oversized shipment traveling through multiple states, that may mean multiple permits.
Permits can be purchased for one-time moves, multiple moves of similar hauls, or even an
annual permit for the movement of similar hauls.
Exact routes need to be specified on the state permit for oversized loads. Penalties for
not adhering to the conditions of the permit, or for not having the permit can result in
significant fines.
The most important takeaway, and most challenging aspect of oversized loads, is that every state
has different regulations.
If you re looking for an extensive guide with a list of state-by-state regulations to keep
on hand, check out our Over-Dimensional Shipping guide linked in the description below.
It's easy to see the complicated aspects of an oversized shipment.
You can simplify the process by finding a reliable and experienced logistics provider.
Here at Trinity Logistics, we specialize in complex oversize shipments.
To learn more or request a quote on your shipment visit trinitylogistics.com. Don to forget to
subscribe to our Youtube channel to stay up to date on the latest logistics news and education.

metadata.title: What Is a CTS Inspection? | Dozer Undercarriage Wear Explained | Track Talk Tuesday | HVT
metadata.author: Hunter Valley Tracks
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a CTS inspection, and why is it important for your dozer undercarriage?

CTS stands for Custom Track Service. It is an undercarriage inspection and measurement process used to accurately monitor component wear, identify wear patterns and help predict the remaining life of your undercarriage.

In this Track Talk Tuesday video, the Hunter Valley Tracks team explains how CTS inspections help operators, maintenance planners and equipment owners:

▪️ Measure undercarriage component wear
▪️ Monitor changes between inspections
▪️ Identify uneven or excessive wear early
▪️ Estimate remaining component life
▪️ Plan pin and bush turns, repairs and rebuilds
▪️ Reduce the risk of unexpected downtime
▪️ Make informed repair-or-replacement decisions

Undercarriage wear is affected by machine application, operating techniques, ground conditions and maintenance practices. Regular CTS inspections provide valuable data to help you plan maintenance at the right stage and get the best possible life from your undercarriage components.

Have a question about CTS inspections, undercarriage wear or asset management? Leave it in the comments or contact the Hunter Valley Tracks team.

ABOUT HUNTER VALLEY TRACKS

Hunter Valley Tracks provides complete undercarriage asset management solutions for mining, civil and heavy equipment. Our services include CTS inspections, wear monitoring, asset management software, track frame rebuilds, repairs, parts and sales.

Based in Rutherford, NSW, we support customers throughout the Hunter Valley and beyond.


Subscribe for more Track Talk Tuesday videos and practical undercarriage advice.

#CTSInspection #UndercarriageMaintenance #HunterValleyTracks

With the lab measuring particles smaller than a human hair, those taking samples need to take extra care in cleanliness to ensure accurate results. 
In this episode of The Dirt, you’ll learn the proper way to collect an oil sample, especially protecting it from contamination. She also demystifies oil sampling and analysis to give a down-to-earth explanation of how important this often-overlooked maintenance step is.
So to learn more about how to sample your equipment’s oil and take care of your machinery, check out the latest episode of The Dirt.

metadata.title: Fleet Strategy for Contractors: Preventive Maintenance, KPIs & CFO Insights (Yvette Aubin)
metadata.author: Beiing Human
metadata.shortDescription:
Heavy equipment is one of the largest financial levers in construction — and most contractors don’t manage it like a CFO should.

In this episode of Finance at the Jobsite, host Rishi Srivastava (CEO of Beiing Human) sits down with Yvette Aubin, CFO of Ebsary Foundation Company, to unpack how the best heavy contractors think about:

🚜 Fleet utilization
📉 Equipment downtime risk
🔧 Preventive + predictive maintenance
📊 Benchmarking with CFMA’s Heavy Equipment Comparator (HEC)
💰 Equipment rate-setting and bid accuracy
🤖 The future of AI + telematics in fleet management

Yvette brings nearly 25 years of construction accounting leadership, including auditing government entities, overseeing risk management, and serving as Chair of CFMA’s National Heavy Construction Committee. 

Whether you’re a contractor under $100M or scaling into heavy civil growth, this episode will give you a CFO-grade framework for turning equipment into a competitive advantage.

📩 Subscribe to the Finance at the Jobsite Newsletter (weekly insights for construction CFOs and contractors):
https://www.beiinghuman.com/newsletter-signup

⏱️ Chapters

00:00 Introduction
01:00 Yvette’s journey from auditor to construction CFO
02:30 Government contracting insights: the “checklist mindset”
05:20 CFMA leadership and national heavy construction trends
07:00 Top financial risks of owning heavy equipment
09:45 Preventive vs reactive maintenance (and why it matters)
10:50 Utilization, idle fleet costs, and rate-setting for bids
12:00 The Heavy Equipment Comparator (HEC) and benchmarking KPIs
14:30 Predictive maintenance, downtime tracking, and telematics
16:30 Translating fleet KPIs into margin improvement
19:40 What to do when fleet underperforms peers
21:00 Getting buy-in + training field teams on systems
24:00 Long-term fleet strategy: finance + ops alignment
27:00 AI, IoT, and the future of equipment finance
29:15 Closing thoughts

🔖 Hashtags

#ConstructionFinance #HeavyEquipment #ConstructionCFO #CFMA #FleetManagement #PreventiveMaintenance #Telematics #HeavyCivil #ConstructionAccounting #AIinConstruction #FinanceAtTheJobsite

metadata.title: How to Build A Fleet with Rent to Own Construction Equipment
metadata.author: RDO Equipment Co.
metadata.shortDescription:
At the end of the day, most contractors share a common goal: to hit their bottom line and grow their business. Rental purchase options (RPOs) are a great way to achieve that. 

When comparing an RPO to just renting, the advantage lies in the equity you build. Renting equipment is like renting an apartment, while renting to own allows you to gain equity, like you would as a homeowner. 

But that’s not all — there’s the service element that comes with the equipment. With RPOs, customers can be confident that any repair or service needs will be handled by RDO Equipment Co. Matthew Gillum, one of Five Star Civil Construction’s managing partners, calls it a win-win. 

“I couldn’t ask for anything else. Being an owner, managing a fleet and trying to be involved in other meetings, if I have a question, I know I can call RDO and have an answer in minutes,” Matthew says. 

Watch this episode of The Track to learn more about how Five Star Civil Construction transformed from a small team with limited resources into a sought-after company with a significantly expanded operation.

metadata.title: This Contractor Salvages Flood-Damaged Equipment to Boost Fleet
metadata.author: EquipmentWorld
metadata.shortDescription:
Jason Guelig Excavating of Mount Calvary, Wisconsin, is one of Equipment World’s 12 finalists for the 2021 Contractor of the Year award.

Jason Guelig started the company in 2004 with an $81,000 loan to buy a dump truck and a backhoe. Since then he has grown his business to 20 employees and 80 pieces of construction equipment.
In this video, he discusses a tactic that has helped him add used equipment to his fleet at a low purchase price. He searches around for salvaged equipment, like those that have been flooded. He then repairs them and puts them back into service.

He also focuses on new technology for his equipment, increasing the number of machines he has with 3D machine control. The technology has helped him boost productivity to the point where he would never go back.

Jason also discusses his involvement with the School to Work program. He reaches out to local high school seniors to offer them an opportunity to learn the construction business. He enjoys teaching the students about the industry, and in turn, some participants have stayed on with his company after graduation.

The Equipment World Contractor of the Year program, now in its 21st year, has been sponsored by Caterpillar since its start. It recognizes contractors who display the highest standards of business acumen, equipment management expertise, attention to safety and community involvement.

Equipment World serves up weekly videos on the latest in construction equipment, work trucks and pickup trucks – everything contractors need to get their work done. Subscribe and visit us at equipmentworld.com!

metadata.title: UCC Performance & Warranties — Contracts
metadata.author: BARGO NextGen Bar Prep
metadata.shortDescription:
A truckload of seed overturns on the highway, and the buyer who never touched a single bag still owes every dollar of the price.


Practice this topic with exam-style questions: nextgenbargo.com (https://nextgenbargo.com/nextgen-bar-exam/contracts?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=k-08-ucc-performance-warranties) 


In this episode:

  •  Silence means shipment contract; risk passes at the carrier
  •  Run agreement, carrier, bailee, then merchant status
  •  Perfect tender before acceptance, substantial impairment after
  •  Merchantability needs a merchant; fitness needs reliance
  •  As is kills implied warranties, never express ones or title

Narrated by an AI voice from a script written and checked by the editors at nextgenbargo.com. Educational content only — not legal advice. BARGO is not affiliated with or endorsed by the NCBE or any bar examining authority.

segments.text: Franklin Farm Supply loads 200 bags of
seed onto a carrier's truck bound for
Olsen in Colombia. The contract says FOB
Franklin. Halfway there, the truck
overturns and every bag is ruined.
Nobody was careless. Olsen never touched
the seed. Does Olsen still have to pay?
Yes, every dollar. His only comfort is a
claim against the carrier or an insurer.
Change one word in that shipping term
and the seller eats the loss instead.
Article two of the UCC decides who pays
when goods die in transit and it never
asks who owned them. By the end of this
episode, you will run that question and
the warranty question behind it on any
set of facts. Here is the route. First
the core bargain tender and the shipment
or destination split everything hangs
on. Then risk of loss in the order you
must run it. Then the buyer's path after
the goods arrive. Perfect tender,
rejection, cure, acceptance, and
revocation. [clears throat] Then the
warranty family. And finally,
disclaimers and the seller's defenses.
strip a sale of goods to its bones and
it is a swap. The seller transfers and
delivers conforming goods. The buyer
accepts and pays. Conforming means the
goods match what the contract called
for. The seller's pivotal act is tender
of delivery. Under section 25503, put
conforming goods at the buyer's
disposition and give whatever notice the
buyer needs. Tender is not the buyer
getting the goods. It is the seller
doing everything needed to make delivery
happen. Under a duty of good faith,
nobody can contract away. Now, the split
everything hangs on. Most goods travel
by carrier, and article 2 sorts those
into two boxes. In a shipment contract,
the seller must get the goods to a
carrier and make a reasonable contract
for their transport. In a destination
contract, the seller must get them to a
named place and tender them there. Here
is the trap. If the contract is silent
about how far the seller must deliver,
it is presumed to be a shipment
contract. A tile contract says shipped
by motor freight and names no delivery
point shipment or destination shipment.
Sellers deliver to the carrier, not the
buyer's door. Shipping terms abbreviate
all this. FOB,
free on board, is the workhorse.
F O the seller's city is a shipment
contract. F O the buyer city is a
destination contract. FAS free alongside
a named vessel is a shipment term and
the sneaky one is C IF cost insurance
and freight. It looks like destination
delivery. It is not. Risk of loss asks a
stark question. The goods are destroyed.
Nobody is at fault and someone still has
to pay. Who? Two ideas. Keep this clean.
The code divorces risk from title. So
never ask who owned the goods. And check
for breach first. Absent breach, run
four steps in order. One, did the
parties agree who bears risk? Honor it.
Two, are the goods moving by carrier?
Shipment contract. Risk passes when
conforming goods are duly delivered to
the carrier. Destination contract only
on tender at the destination. Three. Are
the goods sitting with a bailey not
moving? Under section 259,
risk passes when the buyer takes a
negotiable document of title or the
bailey acknowledges the buyer's right.
No wheat has to move. The document does
the work. Four, no carrier and no
bailey. The residual rule turns on one
fact. If the seller is a merchant, risk
passes only when the buyer actually
receives the goods. If the seller is not
a merchant, risk passes on tender. That
one decides cases. A professor sells her
personal grand piano to a neighbor for
tells him it is ready, and leaves it
awaiting his movers. A pipe bursts and
ruins it. Merchant or not. Not a
merchant in pianos. Risk passed on
tender. The neighbor bears the loss.
Breach flips the picture. Ship goods bad
enough to give the buyer a right to
reject. And section 2510 keeps risk on
the seller until cure or acceptance.
Back to Olsen. Make it F O Colombia. and
the seller eats the ruined seed. Make
those bags moldy and the seller eats it
anyway. Now, the buyer's path after the
goods arrive. And here, article 2 breaks
from the common law. At common law,
substantial performance is enough. Not
for goods. Under the perfect tender rule
in section 2601,
the goods or the tender need only fail
to conform in any respect. Then the
buyer may reject the whole, accept the
whole or accept some units and reject
the rest. Any respect means any a late
shipment, the wrong color, a short
count. The buyer normally inspects
first. The exception is cash on delivery
where you pay first and inspect after.
To reject, act within a reasonable time
and seasonably notify the seller. Then
hold the goods with care so the seller
can reclaim them and state the defect
because a buyer who hides a curable
defect may be barred from relying on it.
Perfect tender sounds brutal. So two
things soften it. First, cure. Under
section 25508,
if the performance time has not expired,
the seller notifies the buyer of an
intent to cure and delivers conforming
goods in time. Even after that time has
run, the seller gets a further
reasonable time if it reasonably
believed the tender would be acceptable.
Second, installment contracts goods in
separate lots, each separately accepted.
perfect tender does not apply lot by
lot. Reject one installment only if its
nonconformity substantially impairs the
value of that installment and cancel the
whole only if it impairs the value of
the whole. Then acceptance and this is
where buyers get caught three ways. the
buyer inspects and signifies the goods
conform or that it will keep them anyway
or the buyer fails to make an effective
rejection. So, silence past a reasonable
time is acceptance. Or the buyer acts
inconsistently with the seller's
ownership. Accept and four things
follow. You pay the contract price. You
lose the right to reject. The burden
flips, so you must prove the breach. and
a clock starts. Notify the seller of a
breach within a reasonable time after
discovering it or be barred from every
remedy. So what is left after
acceptance? Revocation under section
and the bar is far higher. The
nonconformity must substantially impair
the value of the goods to that buyer.
And the buyer must fit one of two boxes.
Accepted expecting a cure that never
came or accepted without discovering a
defect that was hard to find. Dileia
orders a refrigerator. Delivery due
Friday. It arrives Wednesday with a
dented door. Can she cancel? No. The
time has not run, so the dealer may cure
by Friday. Now change it, she accepts,
and 3 weeks later, the cooling system
dies. That substantially impairs the
value. No inspection would have caught
it. And she tells the dealer at once.
She may revoke. Now the second half, and
this is the part to know cold. A
warranty is a promise about the goods
that the seller is strictly bound to. No
proving carelessness, no proving a lie.
The goods fell short that caused harm.
The seller pays. Express warranties
under section 2-313.
Three ways to create one. An affirmation
of fact or a promise about the goods, a
description of the goods, or a sample or
model. Each must become part of the
basis of the bargain. and courts presume
the buyer relied. No magic words and no
intent to warrant. But sales talk does
not count. A statement of value or the
seller's opinion or commendation is
puffery. This is a terrific little car.
Best boots around. Warranty or puffery?
Puffery. This engine was rebuilt last
year. Is a warranty. The line is fact
against opinion. Then the big one,
merchantability. Under section 2-314,
in any sale by a merchant who deals in
goods of that kind, the law implies the
goods are merchantable, fit for the
ordinary purposes such goods are used
for, of fair, average quality,
adequately packaged and labeled. The
trigger is the merchant in that kind of
good. A car dealer selling cars, a
grosser selling food. But a plumber
selling her used personal truck is no
merchant with respect to trucks, so no
merchant ability attaches. And serving
food or drink for value is a sale that
carries it. Fitness for a particular
purpose. Section 2-315
is narrower. And here is the twist. It
needs no merchant seller. any seller can
give it. It arises when the seller has
reason to know a particular purpose the
buyer wants the goods for and the buyer
must be relying on the seller's skill or
judgment to choose them. Particular is
the key word, a specific use beyond the
ordinary one. Boots are ordinarily for
walking and that is merchantability.
Boots that must keep your feet dry while
you wade a cold river are a particular
purpose. Name an exact brand though and
reliance is negated. Then ownership in
every sale unless specifically
disclaimed. The seller warrants that
title is good and its transfer rightful.
The goods must come free of any lean the
buyer did not know about. Every seller
gives it, not just merchants. A merchant
regularly dealing in such goods also
warrants against infringement. Sellers
try to shed all of this and section
sets precise rules different for each
warranty. Express warranties are nearly
impossible to disclaim. A court reads
the warranty and the disclaimer
together, and where they flatly
conflict, the disclaimer is inoperative.
You cannot guarantee a watertight hull
and then erase it in boilerplate. The
implied warranties are more
disclaimable, and each has its own
formality. To disclaim merchantability,
the language must actually use the word
merchantability, and in a writing, it
must be conspicuous.
It may be oral. To disclaim fitness, the
exclusion must be written and
conspicuous
or knock out both at once with asis or
with all faults. Also by the buyer's
examination or refusal to examine as to
defects it should have revealed and by
course of dealing or usage of trade. But
does asis reach title? No. Never. Even
with a warranty made and broken, sellers
have defenses. The heavy hitter is
notice. An accepting buyer who fails to
notify the seller within a reasonable
time after discovering the breach is
barred from every remedy. A seller may
also cap the buyer to repair or
replacement unless that limit is
unconscionable.
Privity is shrinking because section
extends warranties to the buyer's
family, household, and guests, and the
seller cannot contract out of it. And
the clock is 4 years from tender of
delivery whenever the buyer discovered
the breach. One last skill, where the
exam hands you the code, read the
supplied section, not your memory. The
Franklin Sales Act might demand written
notice within 90 days of discovery. Then
a phone call loses and day 100 loses. A
word on authorities. This episode named
no cases and there were none to name.
Article two is a statute and a sales
question sends you to a section number
not to a decision. When the code is in
front of you, read the section for what
it requires. When it is not, these
numbers are your pegs. If you keep only
three, keep these. Section 2-509,
the risk of loss ladder. Agreement, then
carrier, then bailey, then merchant
status. Section 2-601,
perfect tender, and the cure and
installment rules that soften it. and
section 2-316
which sets a different formality for
every disclaimer. Now the traps straight
from the examiner's favorites. One,
never solve risk of loss by asking who
held title. Run section 2-509
and check for breach first. Two, CIF
looks like a destination contract and is
a shipment contract. Three, the residual
rule turns on merchant status. A
merchant seller keeps the risk until the
buyer receives the goods. Four,
rejection uses perfect tender.
Revocation and installment problems use
substantial impairment. Do not swap
them. Five, a buyer can accept by
silence or by using the goods without
ever saying, "I accept."
Six, an accepting buyer who gives no
timely notice is barred from all
remedies and that quietly kills warranty
claims. Seven, fitness needs no merchant
seller. Merchantability does. Eight,
ASIS disclaims the implied warranties
but never an express warranty and never
title. Nine, a written fitness
disclaimer must be conspicuous and a
merchantability disclaimer must use the
word merchantability.
Time for the quick check. And this one
comes straight from the Bargo question
bank. A buyer buys a used motorcycle
from a private seller. The handwritten
bill of sale reads in bold letters,
"Sold as with no warranties of any
kind." Months later, the police sees it.
The motorcycle had been stolen before
the seller ever acquired it. The buyer
sues for breach of the warranty of title
and the seller points to that bold ASIS
language. Option one, the seller wins
because ASIS excludes every warranty
including good title. Option two, the
seller wins because a private seller
gives no title warranty at all. Option
three, the buyer wins because ASIS
disclaims the implied quality warranties
but not title. Pause here if you want a
moment. The answer is option three. The
warranty of good title under section
is given by every seller, merchant or
not, and it is not disclaimed by asis or
with all faults. Those words knock out
the implied warranties of quality. Title
goes only by specific language or by
circumstances telling the buyer the
seller claims no full title. Neither is
here. Option two fails because private
non- merchant sellers do give the title
warranty. It is the separate warranty
against infringement that is limited to
merchants. There are 30 plus more
questions on this topic alone. each with
every option explained like that. Five
things to take away. One, silence means
shipment contract. So the seller
delivers to the carrier and risk passes
there. Two, for risk of loss run
agreement, then carrier then bailey then
merchant status and check for breach
before any of it. Three, before
acceptance, the standard is perfect
tender. After acceptance, substantial
impairment. Four, merchantability needs
a merchant in that kind of good and
covers ordinary use. Fitness needs no
merchant but needs a known particular
purpose and the buyer's reliance.
Five asis kills the implied warranties,
not the express one and not title. And a
buyer who accepts and stays silent loses
everything. Which is why Olsen pays for
a truckload of seed he never touched.
Fob Franklin put the risk on him at the
carrier's door. Next time, breach,
repudiation, and excuse. Practice this
topic with more than 2,900 exam style
questions free to start at
nextgenbargo.com.
This episode is for education and exam
preparation only, not legal advice, and
we are not affiliated with or endorsed

or any bar examining authority. Ready?

videos.full_text: Franklin Farm Supply loads 200 bags of seed onto a carrier's truck bound for Olsen in Colombia. The contract says FOB Franklin. Halfway there, the truck overturns and every bag is ruined. Nobody was careless. Olsen never touched the seed. Does Olsen still have to pay? Yes, every dollar. His only comfort is a claim against the carrier or an insurer. Change one word in that shipping term and the seller eats the loss instead. Article two of the UCC decides who pays when goods die in transit and it never asks who owned them. By the end of this episode, you will run that question and the warranty question behind it on any set of facts. Here is the route. First the core bargain tender and the shipment or destination split everything hangs on. Then risk of loss in the order you must run it. Then the buyer's path after the goods arrive. Perfect tender, rejection, cure, acceptance, and revocation. [clears throat] Then the warranty family. And finally, disclaimers and the seller's defenses. strip a sale of goods to its bones and it is a swap. The seller transfers and delivers conforming goods. The buyer accepts and pays. Conforming means the goods match what the contract called for. The seller's pivotal act is tender of delivery. Under section 25503, put conforming goods at the buyer's disposition and give whatever notice the buyer needs. Tender is not the buyer getting the goods. It is the seller doing everything needed to make delivery happen. Under a duty of good faith, nobody can contract away. Now, the split everything hangs on. Most goods travel by carrier, and article 2 sorts those into two boxes. In a shipment contract, the seller must get the goods to a carrier and make a reasonable contract for their transport. In a destination contract, the seller must get them to a named place and tender them there. Here is the trap. If the contract is silent about how far the seller must deliver, it is presumed to be a shipment contract. A tile contract says shipped by motor freight and names no delivery point shipment or destination shipment. Sellers deliver to the carrier, not the buyer's door. Shipping terms abbreviate all this. FOB, free on board, is the workhorse. F O the seller's city is a shipment contract. F O the buyer city is a destination contract. FAS free alongside a named vessel is a shipment term and the sneaky one is C IF cost insurance and freight. It looks like destination delivery. It is not. Risk of loss asks a stark question. The goods are destroyed. Nobody is at fault and someone still has to pay. Who? Two ideas. Keep this clean. The code divorces risk from title. So never ask who owned the goods. And check for breach first. Absent breach, run four steps in order. One, did the parties agree who bears risk? Honor it. Two, are the goods moving by carrier? Shipment contract. Risk passes when conforming goods are duly delivered to the carrier. Destination contract only on tender at the destination. Three. Are the goods sitting with a bailey not moving? Under section 259, risk passes when the buyer takes a negotiable document of title or the bailey acknowledges the buyer's right. No wheat has to move. The document does the work. Four, no carrier and no bailey. The residual rule turns on one fact. If the seller is a merchant, risk passes only when the buyer actually receives the goods. If the seller is not a merchant, risk passes on tender. That one decides cases. A professor sells her personal grand piano to a neighbor for $9,000, tells him it is ready, and leaves it awaiting his movers. A pipe bursts and ruins it. Merchant or not. Not a merchant in pianos. Risk passed on tender. The neighbor bears the loss. Breach flips the picture. Ship goods bad enough to give the buyer a right to reject. And section 2510 keeps risk on the seller until cure or acceptance. Back to Olsen. Make it F O Colombia. and the seller eats the ruined seed. Make those bags moldy and the seller eats it anyway. Now, the buyer's path after the goods arrive. And here, article 2 breaks from the common law. At common law, substantial performance is enough. Not for goods. Under the perfect tender rule in section 2601, the goods or the tender need only fail to conform in any respect. Then the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole or accept some units and reject the rest. Any respect means any a late shipment, the wrong color, a short count. The buyer normally inspects first. The exception is cash on delivery where you pay first and inspect after. To reject, act within a reasonable time and seasonably notify the seller. Then hold the goods with care so the seller can reclaim them and state the defect because a buyer who hides a curable defect may be barred from relying on it. Perfect tender sounds brutal. So two things soften it. First, cure. Under section 25508, if the performance time has not expired, the seller notifies the buyer of an intent to cure and delivers conforming goods in time. Even after that time has run, the seller gets a further reasonable time if it reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable. Second, installment contracts goods in separate lots, each separately accepted. perfect tender does not apply lot by lot. Reject one installment only if its nonconformity substantially impairs the value of that installment and cancel the whole only if it impairs the value of the whole. Then acceptance and this is where buyers get caught three ways. the buyer inspects and signifies the goods conform or that it will keep them anyway or the buyer fails to make an effective rejection. So, silence past a reasonable time is acceptance. Or the buyer acts inconsistently with the seller's ownership. Accept and four things follow. You pay the contract price. You lose the right to reject. The burden flips, so you must prove the breach. and a clock starts. Notify the seller of a breach within a reasonable time after discovering it or be barred from every remedy. So what is left after acceptance? Revocation under section 2-608 and the bar is far higher. The nonconformity must substantially impair the value of the goods to that buyer. And the buyer must fit one of two boxes. Accepted expecting a cure that never came or accepted without discovering a defect that was hard to find. Dileia orders a refrigerator. Delivery due Friday. It arrives Wednesday with a dented door. Can she cancel? No. The time has not run, so the dealer may cure by Friday. Now change it, she accepts, and 3 weeks later, the cooling system dies. That substantially impairs the value. No inspection would have caught it. And she tells the dealer at once. She may revoke. Now the second half, and this is the part to know cold. A warranty is a promise about the goods that the seller is strictly bound to. No proving carelessness, no proving a lie. The goods fell short that caused harm. The seller pays. Express warranties under section 2-313. Three ways to create one. An affirmation of fact or a promise about the goods, a description of the goods, or a sample or model. Each must become part of the basis of the bargain. and courts presume the buyer relied. No magic words and no intent to warrant. But sales talk does not count. A statement of value or the seller's opinion or commendation is puffery. This is a terrific little car. Best boots around. Warranty or puffery? Puffery. This engine was rebuilt last year. Is a warranty. The line is fact against opinion. Then the big one, merchantability. Under section 2-314, in any sale by a merchant who deals in goods of that kind, the law implies the goods are merchantable, fit for the ordinary purposes such goods are used for, of fair, average quality, adequately packaged and labeled. The trigger is the merchant in that kind of good. A car dealer selling cars, a grosser selling food. But a plumber selling her used personal truck is no merchant with respect to trucks, so no merchant ability attaches. And serving food or drink for value is a sale that carries it. Fitness for a particular purpose. Section 2-315 is narrower. And here is the twist. It needs no merchant seller. any seller can give it. It arises when the seller has reason to know a particular purpose the buyer wants the goods for and the buyer must be relying on the seller's skill or judgment to choose them. Particular is the key word, a specific use beyond the ordinary one. Boots are ordinarily for walking and that is merchantability. Boots that must keep your feet dry while you wade a cold river are a particular purpose. Name an exact brand though and reliance is negated. Then ownership in every sale unless specifically disclaimed. The seller warrants that title is good and its transfer rightful. The goods must come free of any lean the buyer did not know about. Every seller gives it, not just merchants. A merchant regularly dealing in such goods also warrants against infringement. Sellers try to shed all of this and section 2-316 sets precise rules different for each warranty. Express warranties are nearly impossible to disclaim. A court reads the warranty and the disclaimer together, and where they flatly conflict, the disclaimer is inoperative. You cannot guarantee a watertight hull and then erase it in boilerplate. The implied warranties are more disclaimable, and each has its own formality. To disclaim merchantability, the language must actually use the word merchantability, and in a writing, it must be conspicuous. It may be oral. To disclaim fitness, the exclusion must be written and conspicuous or knock out both at once with asis or with all faults. Also by the buyer's examination or refusal to examine as to defects it should have revealed and by course of dealing or usage of trade. But does asis reach title? No. Never. Even with a warranty made and broken, sellers have defenses. The heavy hitter is notice. An accepting buyer who fails to notify the seller within a reasonable time after discovering the breach is barred from every remedy. A seller may also cap the buyer to repair or replacement unless that limit is unconscionable. Privity is shrinking because section 2-318 extends warranties to the buyer's family, household, and guests, and the seller cannot contract out of it. And the clock is 4 years from tender of delivery whenever the buyer discovered the breach. One last skill, where the exam hands you the code, read the supplied section, not your memory. The Franklin Sales Act might demand written notice within 90 days of discovery. Then a phone call loses and day 100 loses. A word on authorities. This episode named no cases and there were none to name. Article two is a statute and a sales question sends you to a section number not to a decision. When the code is in front of you, read the section for what it requires. When it is not, these numbers are your pegs. If you keep only three, keep these. Section 2-509, the risk of loss ladder. Agreement, then carrier, then bailey, then merchant status. Section 2-601, perfect tender, and the cure and installment rules that soften it. and section 2-316 which sets a different formality for every disclaimer. Now the traps straight from the examiner's favorites. One, never solve risk of loss by asking who held title. Run section 2-509 and check for breach first. Two, CIF looks like a destination contract and is a shipment contract. Three, the residual rule turns on merchant status. A merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods. Four, rejection uses perfect tender. Revocation and installment problems use substantial impairment. Do not swap them. Five, a buyer can accept by silence or by using the goods without ever saying, "I accept." Six, an accepting buyer who gives no timely notice is barred from all remedies and that quietly kills warranty claims. Seven, fitness needs no merchant seller. Merchantability does. Eight, ASIS disclaims the implied warranties but never an express warranty and never title. Nine, a written fitness disclaimer must be conspicuous and a merchantability disclaimer must use the word merchantability. Time for the quick check. And this one comes straight from the Bargo question bank. A buyer buys a used motorcycle from a private seller. The handwritten bill of sale reads in bold letters, "Sold as with no warranties of any kind." Months later, the police sees it. The motorcycle had been stolen before the seller ever acquired it. The buyer sues for breach of the warranty of title and the seller points to that bold ASIS language. Option one, the seller wins because ASIS excludes every warranty including good title. Option two, the seller wins because a private seller gives no title warranty at all. Option three, the buyer wins because ASIS disclaims the implied quality warranties but not title. Pause here if you want a moment. The answer is option three. The warranty of good title under section 2-312 is given by every seller, merchant or not, and it is not disclaimed by asis or with all faults. Those words knock out the implied warranties of quality. Title goes only by specific language or by circumstances telling the buyer the seller claims no full title. Neither is here. Option two fails because private non- merchant sellers do give the title warranty. It is the separate warranty against infringement that is limited to merchants. There are 30 plus more questions on this topic alone. each with every option explained like that. Five things to take away. One, silence means shipment contract. So the seller delivers to the carrier and risk passes there. Two, for risk of loss run agreement, then carrier then bailey then merchant status and check for breach before any of it. Three, before acceptance, the standard is perfect tender. After acceptance, substantial impairment. Four, merchantability needs a merchant in that kind of good and covers ordinary use. Fitness needs no merchant but needs a known particular purpose and the buyer's reliance. Five asis kills the implied warranties, not the express one and not title. And a buyer who accepts and stays silent loses everything. Which is why Olsen pays for a truckload of seed he never touched. Fob Franklin put the risk on him at the carrier's door. metadata.title: You Bought a Dying Auction House for $175,000. Now It Earns $500K/Year Selling Other People’s Stuff.
metadata.author: Plain Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
You buy a dying equipment auction house after watching your father’s machine shop sell to an empty room, then make one promise that nearly breaks the business. This auction business story shows how matching industrial equipment to inspected buyers grows a $22K-a-year auction company into $500K a year in operating earnings, before debt and taxes. It also explains buyer premiums, consignment fees and why a guaranteed sale can cost you everything.

Chapters:
0:00 Three Hundred Names, No Hands: $175K Buy
2:51 The People Behind the Paddles: $150K Year
5:39 The Promise You Cannot Make: $520K Guarantee
8:21 The $150K Promise: The Room Fails
11:00 Selling Confidence: Back to $58K
13:58 The Hammer Without a Promise: $500K a Year

#BoringBusiness #AuctionHouse #BusinessStory

segments.text: 300 people are registered to
bid, and nobody is bidding.
The counter on the webcast screen says so
in bright green numbers,
a count that folds in every online
account, every phone line, and all 31
folding chairs in the room.
Mae Navarro lifts her gavel to try again.
"Do I hear $110,000? For the
best machine in the building?"
Nothing. No paddle, no nod.
Across the aisle, Joyce Tolland sits very
straight with an envelope on her lap.
Inside it is a page with your signature
at the bottom, promising
her $520,000 no matter what
this room does tonight. Your own
signature looks different
than it did when you wrote it.
You have heard this kind of quiet before.
14 years ago, your
father's machine shop closed
after one customer canceled one big
order, and at the
liquidation, the best thing he owned
was a specialized machine in perfect
working order. "It runs
like the day I bought it,"
he told the auctioneer. The people who
came to bid were bargain
hunters and a local scrap dealer,
and none of the factories that could have
used the machine were in the room.
The hammer dropped on a number that made
your father stare at his shoes.
"It's worth more than that,"
you said on the drive home.
"It is," he said. "To
somebody who wasn't there."
So you learned the other half of the
trade, valuing
industrial equipment for lenders
until you could tell a sound machine from
a tired one at a glance.
But an appraisal isn't a bid. You thought
you had learned that.
About 18 months before that night,
Baines Auction and
Appraisal is for sale,
with faded banners and a leaking
inspection bay. Hal Baines refolds the
sale papers along their
original creases while he explains the
terms. "Operating company only," he says.
"The building isn't mine to sell.
$55,000 from your savings,
and Hal carries the other $120,000 as a
note, about $2,900 a
month, for four years.
You put another $60,000 into the
company's bank account to run on. About
$110,000 of the price
is gear, the forklift and trailers the
house needs to run a
sale, and the rest is staff,
a calendar, and a name. Last year, the
house handled $3.2 million
of other people's equipment,
and, after commissions, event costs and
overhead, kept $22,000. That wouldn't
even cover the $35,000
a year the note will cost. In your first
month, a usable machine
sells at a small auction for
$7,900. The next afternoon, a rebuilder
in another state calls to
ask if it's still available.
"It sold yesterday." "Of course it did." You
can't unwind a sale, and
you begin to understand that
the room wasn't empty. The
right people just weren't in it.
Mae spreads two sheets of paper on the
counter, a buyer's invoice
and a seller's settlement.
"$20,000 machine," she says. "The
seller pays us 6%
$1,200. The buyer pays 10%
on top $2,000. $3,200, and we never
touched the machine." Diego
Santos, who runs the catalog
and the bidder list, writes serial
numbers on the back of his
hand. He opens the mailing list,
a long scroll of stale accounts and
people who only watched, with
a handful who have inspected
an industrial machine this year. "A list
of names isn't a list
of customers," he says.
"Then we pick one machine," you say, "and
find its buyers by hand."
The machine is a precision
grinder with an unusual control package,
the kind only a narrow
class of shops runs.
Diego posts clear photos, the serial
plate and an honest video,
and you call a rebuilder in Ohio
named Colm Rafferty, who works on that
exact family of machines.
"Does the spindle hold under
load?" Colm asks. "Diego's video shows it
running." "Running isn't loaded." He
measures the doorway from
your photos and hires a mechanic to
inspect it. Then, a second
shop asks for the same window,
and Mae makes room for both. On sale day,
the first bids come in
weak, and you feel your
father's room settle around you. Then the
two inspected buyers start
competing, a remote dealer
with confirmed transport joins them, and
the paddles keep rising. "Thirty-eight
thousand," Mae says.
The gavel falls. "Sold." The seller
accepts, the buyers settle,
and the house keeps six thousand
eighty dollars in fees for putting people
together. The seller
shakes Mae's hand and
never once looks at the floor, and you
remember where your father's
eyes went. Mae notices. She
says nothing. At the next sale, a
specialty lot never reaches
the price its seller approved,
and Mae lays her gavel on its side, the
way she does whenever a
lot fails to sell. "Unsold."
"Why not push it?" you ask afterward,
frustrated and not hiding it.
"Because the next seller is watching,"
she says. "An honest pass is how they
know our hammer means
something." You nod. You will remember
that standard exactly when
you need it, and you won't
follow it. By the end of the year, repeat
consignors are calling
before you call them,
and Mae slides the books across your
desk. "Four point two
million dollars handled," she says.
"One hundred fifty thousand kept after
event costs and overhead."
"Up from twenty-two," you say. That is
the company's earnings,
not your paycheck, but the market has
started returning your calls.
Five months into your second year, the
calls keep coming. Bankers
and sellers who once forgot
the Baines name now ask for you by yours,
and the webcast shows registrations
climbing every month.
"Names on a dashboard aren't hands in the
air," Mae says. She is
right, but you also just finished
a very good year, and after the note
payments, your draws, the
taxes, and new equipment,
the company's account holds $165,000.
Joyce Tolland is
retiring. She has to empty her
precision manufacturing plant before the
building changes hands on October 31st
because she owes her lender a payoff
before she can hand over the keys.
She straightens whatever is closest to
her, a pen, a stack of
papers, before she answers anything
about money. She isn't desperate, just
out of time, and other
auctioneers have already offered
her ordinary terms. "Five hundred twenty
thousand dollars, net to me,
whatever happens," she says.
"I need a number I can plan around." Mae
offers the careful answer:
ordinary terms, reserves on the best
lots, a plan to reach
qualified buyers and no promise
from the house. "That leaves me
guessing," Joyce says. You think of your
father looking at his
shoes. Your own comps say her plant is
worth six hundred twenty thousand
dollars, so you wouldn't
be promising her a miracle, only most of
what you believe is
already there. Diego brings the
inspection log to your desk. "About three
hundred registered
accounts," he says. "Three qualified
inspections across the six most valuable
lots." "Only three?" "One
dealer has no rigging crew.
Another hasn't finished his payment
arrangements. Neither has promised
anything." You look at your
comps, then at the registration count,
then at the three rows of
ink in Diego's log, and you
trust the first two. Over Mae's
objection, you sign. "A guaranteed sale
means no reserves," she says.
"If the building has to be empty,
everything sells to whoever is in the
room. And you owe Joyce the
difference." "My comps say there's room
for that." "Your comps aren't
bidders." She turns the bank
statement toward you. "You have one
hundred sixty-five thousand
dollars. You just promised five
hundred twenty." The house keeps a twelve
percent buyer premium and
anything above five hundred twenty
and pays fifty thousand dollars in event
costs. If the room fails,
you cover the difference.
The night before the sale, Mae stands in
the warehouse beside
the biggest machine on the
floor, which still has no second
inspection on the calendar, and she
doesn't repeat her warning.
You close the bidder tab and
look at your forecast instead.
The first hour goes well, with shop tools
and small machines
selling close to your comps
until you start to think the guarantee
was harmless. In the
second row, Joyce relaxes.
She shouldn't. Then Mae calls the best
machine in the
building, her cadence slows,
and she scans the room for a real bidder
she refuses to invent.
One paddle comes up. Then
nothing. "Selling,"
Mae says. "Last call."
Your comps said one hundred ninety
thousand dollars. The
hammer falls at eighty-four.
"One bidder is a price," Mae says
quietly. "Two is a market."
The other valuable machines go the same
way. The dealer without a
rigging crew can't bid on the
biggest lots because he couldn't move
them by Joyce's
deadline, and the shop that never
finished its payment arrangements isn't
allowed to bid at all. You
saw both problems before you
signed, and you didn't count them. By the
time the six valuable
machines are gone, they have
brought less than half of what your comps
said. The chairs are still
mostly empty, and the counter
still reads three hundred registered.
When the last lot is
gone, the totals come up.
Every machine in the plant has sold for
three hundred
seventy-five thousand dollars.
Joyce is owed five hundred twenty, so the
room fell one hundred
forty-five thousand short.
You pay her anyway. After the premium you
collect and the event bills,
the sale costs the house one hundred
fifty thousand dollars.
You sign Joyce's payment
yourself. She straightens the envelope on
her lap one last time, then
shakes your hand with both of
hers. "I can close on time," she says. "I
didn't think I could." It is
worse than anger would have
been, because your mistake bought a real
person certainty, and it
nearly cost your staff their
jobs. The next morning, the house has
fifteen thousand dollars in the bank,
down from one hundred
sixty-five. "Payroll is nine thousand,
due Friday," Mae says. You cancel your
owner draw and every
planned repair, and you ask whether
seller proceeds could cover one week.
"Those aren't ours," she says.
"Not one dollar." You think about selling
the forklift instead. "Then we
can't load a single machine,"
Mae says. "Sale day is the only day we
earn." She is right.
And from that morning on,
Mae stops leaving the reserve sheet on
your desk, so that when
you want it, you have to ask.
You can value steel. You can't promise
the person who will buy it. Ten days from
now, another auction
is on the calendar, and by the time it
starts, you will have five thousand
dollars left to run it.
This auction was booked long before
Joyce, and after payroll
and the first event bill,
you have $5,000 between the house and the
bank. "I'll run it clean," Mae says.
"But I can't rescue you twice." Marta
Fielding brings a
machining press to the sale,
and she introduces every
machine with the year she bought it.
"2004," she says, patting the frame.
"Never missed a day."
You know certain shops would pay well for
it. But Diego can
document only one buyer with both
an inspection and a removal plan, and
bidding stalls at $61,000
against Marta's approved
reserve of $72,000. Mae lays her gavel on
its side. "Unsold." You
refuse to cover the missing
$11,000. Marta's face hardens, the house
loses its fee, and the
press goes home with her.
$420,000 of winning bids, and the house
keeps 16% of it, $67,200 in fees.
The sellers' proceeds never touch your
account. After the rest of
the event bills are paid,
that leaves $58,200 in the bank. Not
$420,000. Only the fees are
yours. The lights stay on.
Over the next year, the buyer file
becomes an evidence trail.
You work out who runs each kind
of machine, and the same specialists turn
up at one sale after
another. "That's the same handful
of shops," Diego says, scrolling the log.
"And every one asked about
removal first." The calendar
stays at about 10 sales a year, but lots
that once got photographed,
cataloged, and pushed onto a
second sale now sell the first time.
Overhead grows by only
$50,000, one more coordinator and
a bigger weekend crew, while the winning
bids climb by more than $2 million. At
one booked inspection,
a rebuilder arrives with his own rigger
and a bank verified bidder account.
"Show me the control manual," he says,
and signs the log. He is one actual buyer
with a reason to bid.
Early in your third year, a plant owner
is deciding which auction
house will clear his factory.
You bring him results from comparable
sales, the names of
qualified buyers, and a plan for each
category. His plant isn't open to buyers
yet, so you promise
inspections after he signs,
and you don't pretend they have already
happened. "Now give me a number," he
says. "A guaranteed net."
"No," you say, and wait for him to walk.
He doesn't. He picks
the ordinary consignment,
with reserves on a few high-value
machines and clear
settlement terms. What won the job
wasn't a price, but a network he could
see. That night, there is a
reserve sheet on your desk.
Mae hasn't left one there since Joyce.
The night before the
sale, Diego's list shows real
inspections by qualified buyers. "Want to
promise him something
extra?" she asks. "Just in case?"
"No," you say. The unease doesn't go
away. But this time, you
have chosen to feel it.
Eighteen months after Joyce's sale, the
chairs are full and the
right people are in them:
machinists, rebuilders, buyers, who
inspected the plant.
"Looks like Joyce's
room," Diego says quietly.
"It isn't," Mae says.
"Look at the paddles."
One expensive specialist unit stalls
short of its reserve, and
Mae lays her gavel on its side.
The seller nods, prepared for this, and
you stand by the contract instead of
offering a promise.
The remaining lots draw real competition,
and the sale closes at
$1.8 million of winning bids
on equipment the house never owned, which
earns the house $288,000 in fees.
When the books close on your third full
year, you have run ten auctions
and handled $7.6 million of winning bids.
After event costs and
overhead, the house has earned
$500,000 in operating earnings, before
the note and the taxes.
Even without the big sale, the other nine

videos.full_text: 300 people are registered to bid, and nobody is bidding. The counter on the webcast screen says so in bright green numbers, a count that folds in every online account, every phone line, and all 31 folding chairs in the room. Mae Navarro lifts her gavel to try again. "Do I hear $110,000? For the best machine in the building?" Nothing. No paddle, no nod. Across the aisle, Joyce Tolland sits very straight with an envelope on her lap. Inside it is a page with your signature at the bottom, promising her $520,000 no matter what this room does tonight. Your own signature looks different than it did when you wrote it. You have heard this kind of quiet before. 14 years ago, your father's machine shop closed after one customer canceled one big order, and at the liquidation, the best thing he owned was a specialized machine in perfect working order. "It runs like the day I bought it," he told the auctioneer. The people who came to bid were bargain hunters and a local scrap dealer, and none of the factories that could have used the machine were in the room. The hammer dropped on a number that made your father stare at his shoes. "It's worth more than that," you said on the drive home. "It is," he said. "To somebody who wasn't there." So you learned the other half of the trade, valuing industrial equipment for lenders until you could tell a sound machine from a tired one at a glance. But an appraisal isn't a bid. You thought you had learned that. About 18 months before that night, Baines Auction and Appraisal is for sale, with faded banners and a leaking inspection bay. Hal Baines refolds the sale papers along their original creases while he explains the terms. "Operating company only," he says. "The building isn't mine to sell. $175,000." You pay $55,000 from your savings, and Hal carries the other $120,000 as a note, about $2,900 a month, for four years. You put another $60,000 into the company's bank account to run on. About $110,000 of the price is gear, the forklift and trailers the house needs to run a sale, and the rest is staff, a calendar, and a name. Last year, the house handled $3.2 million of other people's equipment, and, after commissions, event costs and overhead, kept $22,000. That wouldn't even cover the $35,000 a year the note will cost. In your first month, a usable machine sells at a small auction for $7,900. The next afternoon, a rebuilder in another state calls to ask if it's still available. "It sold yesterday." "Of course it did." You can't unwind a sale, and you begin to understand that the room wasn't empty. The right people just weren't in it. Mae spreads two sheets of paper on the counter, a buyer's invoice and a seller's settlement. "$20,000 machine," she says. "The seller pays us 6% $1,200. The buyer pays 10% on top $2,000. $3,200, and we never touched the machine." Diego Santos, who runs the catalog and the bidder list, writes serial numbers on the back of his hand. He opens the mailing list, a long scroll of stale accounts and people who only watched, with a handful who have inspected an industrial machine this year. "A list of names isn't a list of customers," he says. "Then we pick one machine," you say, "and find its buyers by hand." The machine is a precision grinder with an unusual control package, the kind only a narrow class of shops runs. Diego posts clear photos, the serial plate and an honest video, and you call a rebuilder in Ohio named Colm Rafferty, who works on that exact family of machines. "Does the spindle hold under load?" Colm asks. "Diego's video shows it running." "Running isn't loaded." He measures the doorway from your photos and hires a mechanic to inspect it. Then, a second shop asks for the same window, and Mae makes room for both. On sale day, the first bids come in weak, and you feel your father's room settle around you. Then the two inspected buyers start competing, a remote dealer with confirmed transport joins them, and the paddles keep rising. "Thirty-eight thousand," Mae says. The gavel falls. "Sold." The seller accepts, the buyers settle, and the house keeps six thousand eighty dollars in fees for putting people together. The seller shakes Mae's hand and never once looks at the floor, and you remember where your father's eyes went. Mae notices. She says nothing. At the next sale, a specialty lot never reaches the price its seller approved, and Mae lays her gavel on its side, the way she does whenever a lot fails to sell. "Unsold." "Why not push it?" you ask afterward, frustrated and not hiding it. "Because the next seller is watching," she says. "An honest pass is how they know our hammer means something." You nod. You will remember that standard exactly when you need it, and you won't follow it. By the end of the year, repeat consignors are calling before you call them, and Mae slides the books across your desk. "Four point two million dollars handled," she says. "One hundred fifty thousand kept after event costs and overhead." "Up from twenty-two," you say. That is the company's earnings, not your paycheck, but the market has started returning your calls. Five months into your second year, the calls keep coming. Bankers and sellers who once forgot the Baines name now ask for you by yours, and the webcast shows registrations climbing every month. "Names on a dashboard aren't hands in the air," Mae says. She is right, but you also just finished a very good year, and after the note payments, your draws, the taxes, and new equipment, the company's account holds $165,000. Joyce Tolland is retiring. She has to empty her precision manufacturing plant before the building changes hands on October 31st because she owes her lender a payoff before she can hand over the keys. She straightens whatever is closest to her, a pen, a stack of papers, before she answers anything about money. She isn't desperate, just out of time, and other auctioneers have already offered her ordinary terms. "Five hundred twenty thousand dollars, net to me, whatever happens," she says. "I need a number I can plan around." Mae offers the careful answer: ordinary terms, reserves on the best lots, a plan to reach qualified buyers and no promise from the house. "That leaves me guessing," Joyce says. You think of your father looking at his shoes. Your own comps say her plant is worth six hundred twenty thousand dollars, so you wouldn't be promising her a miracle, only most of what you believe is already there. Diego brings the inspection log to your desk. "About three hundred registered accounts," he says. "Three qualified inspections across the six most valuable lots." "Only three?" "One dealer has no rigging crew. Another hasn't finished his payment arrangements. Neither has promised anything." You look at your comps, then at the registration count, then at the three rows of ink in Diego's log, and you trust the first two. Over Mae's objection, you sign. "A guaranteed sale means no reserves," she says. "If the building has to be empty, everything sells to whoever is in the room. And you owe Joyce the difference." "My comps say there's room for that." "Your comps aren't bidders." She turns the bank statement toward you. "You have one hundred sixty-five thousand dollars. You just promised five hundred twenty." The house keeps a twelve percent buyer premium and anything above five hundred twenty and pays fifty thousand dollars in event costs. If the room fails, you cover the difference. The night before the sale, Mae stands in the warehouse beside the biggest machine on the floor, which still has no second inspection on the calendar, and she doesn't repeat her warning. You close the bidder tab and look at your forecast instead. The first hour goes well, with shop tools and small machines selling close to your comps until you start to think the guarantee was harmless. In the second row, Joyce relaxes. She shouldn't. Then Mae calls the best machine in the building, her cadence slows, and she scans the room for a real bidder she refuses to invent. One paddle comes up. Then nothing. "Selling," Mae says. "Last call." Your comps said one hundred ninety thousand dollars. The hammer falls at eighty-four. "One bidder is a price," Mae says quietly. "Two is a market." The other valuable machines go the same way. The dealer without a rigging crew can't bid on the biggest lots because he couldn't move them by Joyce's deadline, and the shop that never finished its payment arrangements isn't allowed to bid at all. You saw both problems before you signed, and you didn't count them. By the time the six valuable machines are gone, they have brought less than half of what your comps said. The chairs are still mostly empty, and the counter still reads three hundred registered. When the last lot is gone, the totals come up. Every machine in the plant has sold for three hundred seventy-five thousand dollars. Joyce is owed five hundred twenty, so the room fell one hundred forty-five thousand short. You pay her anyway. After the premium you collect and the event bills, the sale costs the house one hundred fifty thousand dollars. You sign Joyce's payment yourself. She straightens the envelope on her lap one last time, then shakes your hand with both of hers. "I can close on time," she says. "I didn't think I could." It is worse than anger would have been, because your mistake bought a real person certainty, and it nearly cost your staff their jobs. The next morning, the house has fifteen thousand dollars in the bank, down from one hundred sixty-five. "Payroll is nine thousand, due Friday," Mae says. You cancel your owner draw and every planned repair, and you ask whether seller proceeds could cover one week. "Those aren't ours," she says. "Not one dollar." You think about selling the forklift instead. "Then we can't load a single machine," Mae says. "Sale day is the only day we earn." She is right. And from that morning on, Mae stops leaving the reserve sheet on your desk, so that when you want it, you have to ask. You can value steel. You can't promise the person who will buy it. Ten days from now, another auction is on the calendar, and by the time it starts, you will have five thousand dollars left to run it. This auction was booked long before Joyce, and after payroll and the first event bill, you have $5,000 between the house and the bank. "I'll run it clean," Mae says. "But I can't rescue you twice." Marta Fielding brings a machining press to the sale, and she introduces every machine with the year she bought it. "2004," she says, patting the frame. "Never missed a day." You know certain shops would pay well for it. But Diego can document only one buyer with both an inspection and a removal plan, and bidding stalls at $61,000 against Marta's approved reserve of $72,000. Mae lays her gavel on its side. "Unsold." You refuse to cover the missing $11,000. Marta's face hardens, the house loses its fee, and the press goes home with her. $420,000 of winning bids, and the house keeps 16% of it, $67,200 in fees. The sellers' proceeds never touch your account. After the rest of the event bills are paid, that leaves $58,200 in the bank. Not $420,000. Only the fees are yours. The lights stay on. Over the next year, the buyer file becomes an evidence trail. You work out who runs each kind of machine, and the same specialists turn up at one sale after another. "That's the same handful of shops," Diego says, scrolling the log. "And every one asked about removal first." The calendar stays at about 10 sales a year, but lots that once got photographed, cataloged, and pushed onto a second sale now sell the first time. Overhead grows by only $50,000, one more coordinator and a bigger weekend crew, while the winning bids climb by more than $2 million. At one booked inspection, a rebuilder arrives with his own rigger and a bank verified bidder account. "Show me the control manual," he says, and signs the log. He is one actual buyer with a reason to bid. Early in your third year, a plant owner is deciding which auction house will clear his factory. You bring him results from comparable sales, the names of qualified buyers, and a plan for each category. His plant isn't open to buyers yet, so you promise inspections after he signs, and you don't pretend they have already happened. "Now give me a number," he says. "A guaranteed net." "No," you say, and wait for him to walk. He doesn't. He picks the ordinary consignment, with reserves on a few high-value machines and clear settlement terms. What won the job wasn't a price, but a network he could see. That night, there is a reserve sheet on your desk. Mae hasn't left one there since Joyce. The night before the sale, Diego's list shows real inspections by qualified buyers. "Want to promise him something extra?" she asks. "Just in case?" "No," you say. The unease doesn't go away. But this time, you have chosen to feel it. Eighteen months after Joyce's sale, the chairs are full and the right people are in them: machinists, rebuilders, buyers, who inspected the plant. "Looks like Joyce's room," Diego says quietly. "It isn't," Mae says. "Look at the paddles." One expensive specialist unit stalls short of its reserve, and Mae lays her gavel on its side. The seller nods, prepared for this, and you stand by the contract instead of offering a promise. The remaining lots draw real competition, and the sale closes at $1.8 million of winning bids on equipment the house never owned, which earns the house $288,000 in fees. When the books close on your third full year, you have run ten auctions and handled $7.6 million of winning bids. After event costs and overhead, the house has earned $500,000 in operating earnings, before the note and the taxes. Even without the big sale, the other nine auctions would have beaten any year before. A smaller seller asks you the old question. "Can you promise me a price?" She twists her hands in her lap, and for a moment she is Joyce, and then she is your father. You tell her whom you will call, which inspections you will arrange and what a reserve will protect, and you don't promise her a bid. "That's not what I wanted," she says. "I know. It's what's true." She nods slowly. Mae calls the next lot. A buyer in the room raises a paddle, a remote bidder answers, and the seller leans forward in her chair while you watch them compete and let it happen. The hammer comes down.
