metadata.title: Why the Pentagon Is Forced to Auction Brand-New Bulldozers as “Unserviceable Scrap”
metadata.author: Vantor Surplus
metadata.shortDescription:
A crawler tractor with factory paint still on its blade and single-digit hours on the meter, sitting behind a chain-link fence with a tag that says scrap. It sounds impossible, but one line in the Defense Materiel Disposition Manual makes it routine. In this video we break down Supply Condition Code H, why the Pentagon labels low-hour bulldozers "unserviceable," and what that means for contractors and farmers who know where to look on government surplus auctions. We also cover what to check in the listing photos before you bid, and why most civilian buyers scroll right past these machines.

Have you ever seen a low-hour military dozer behind an auction fence near your town? Tell me in the comments.

#MilitarySurplus #GovernmentAuction #Bulldozer #HeavyEquipment #SurplusAuction

segments.text: Supply condition code H designates
property that is unserviceable and does
not possess sufficient value to justify
repair, states defense materiel
disposition manual 4160.21-M.
That federal rule explains why the
Pentagon is forced to auction brand new
bulldozers as unserviceable scrap even
when their steel tracks have barely
touched dirt.
On a surplus yard gravel pad, a heavy
olive drab crawler tractor sits behind
chain link fencing with factory paint
still intact on its blade corners. The
windshield tag reads scrap.
Tell me in the comments, have you ever
spotted a low hour military dozer
sitting behind an auction fence near
your town? And subscribe if you want the
next breakdown.
Look inside the cab and the hour meter
often shows single digit or double digit
runtime. Civilian contractors stare at
those auction photos and assume the
engine block is cracked or the final
drives are stripped. They misread the
code.
Underneath that warning tag sits a 30
ton crawler condemned by procurement
schedules, emissions exemptions, and
depot labor math rather than mechanical
failure.
Factory paint tells the real story.
Blades never keep crisp primer if they
pushed rock. Tracks stay clean. Sprocket
teeth show zero rounding.
Watching a zero wear machine hit public
auction with a condemnation sticker
glued across its glass looks absurd at
first glance, yet the chain of rules
starts miles away from any dirt pit
inside supply depot accounting ledgers
that treat an expired inspection stamp
the exact same way a civilian shop
treats a shattered crankshaft.
Tracing how an unused 30 ton bulldozer
lands in a scrap heap requires following
the Pentagon supply chain from the day a
defense contract closes.
When the Department of Defense orders
tactical earth movers like armored
Caterpillar D7 crawlers, John Deere 850J
dozers, or air transportable tractors
for combat engineering battalions,
those machines enter inventory under
rigid life cycle
Active units run a fraction of the fleet
on training ranges while placing reserve
tractors into long-term dehumidified
storage or prepositioned staging depots.
Time moves forward even when tracks stay
parked.
Elastomer hydraulic seals slowly lose
flexibility. Radiator hoses pass shelf
life dates and diesel fuel sitting
inside injection lines begins swarming
sticky varnish through slow chemical
oxidation.
Once a stored tractor passes its
scheduled 36-month depot inspection
window without an active battalion
funding a complete teardown and reseal,
logistics clerks cannot legally classify
it as ready for issue.
Federal disposition regulations forbid
releasing uncertified hardware as
serviceable property.
Paperwork seals the fate.
Clerks push the intact crawler straight
down into condition code F or H. The
tractor never broke down on a job site.
A calendar date simply expired inside a
warehouse database, stripping the
machine of its active duty status
overnight.
Supply condition codes operate like a
one-way ratchet inside Defense Logistics
Agency liquidation portals.
Condition code A marks equipment as new
and ready for combat deployment, whereas
codes F and H label machines as
unserviceable, beyond economical repair,
or condemned under military maintenance
standards.
Here is the paradox civilian buyers
miss.
Military repair accounting never
compares a minor storage repair against
the real commercial auction value of a
bulldozer.
Depot estimators calculate burdened
government shop labor rates, mandatory
full system teardown hours, military
spec shielded wiring harnesses, and
environmental recertification testing
against an arbitrary replacement cap set
years earlier. Shop math is rigid.
If a tractor requires $40,000 in
scheduled storage seal replacements,
24-volt harness checks, and
administrative certification on paper,
the depot software flags it as beyond
economical repair. The engine never
knocked and the blade never bent, yet
the tractor still failed a depot
spreadsheet.
Once that flag enters the federal
property system, depot managers have no
budget line to reverse it, and the
bulldozer moves straight onto the public
disposal schedule, regardless of how
cleanly its diesel block turns over.
People ask where these supply condition
codes and depot repair rules are written
down. It is set down in the field manual
collection in chapter six, military
surplus vehicles and gear. Check the
description, the pinned comment, or
point your phone camera at the QR code
on your screen.
Federal emissions exemptions and
equipment type classification rules
tighten that bureaucratic trap even
further.
Bulldozers built under national security
exemptions often leave factories without
civilian Environmental Protection Agency
exhaust aftertreatment hardware, such as
diesel particulate filters or selective
catalytic reduction tanks.
While military engineering units operate
those tractors legally on defense
ranges, federal transfer statutes
restrict how an agency can release
non-certified engines into domestic
commercial fleets.
Procurement updates compound the problem
whenever a military branch standardizes
on a newer hydraulic pump layout or
modular cab armor package.
Once an older tractor series loses its
active national stock number support,
the Pentagon supply system treats
remaining spare parts and whole machines
as obsolete inventory.
Keeping an obsolete crawler inside an
active battalion motor pool creates
parts bottlenecks for mechanics during
overseas deployments.
Warehouse space costs money. Every
square foot counts.
Clearing the storage pad by downgrading
the machine to unserviceable scrap
becomes the fastest legal exit for the
logistics officer signing the release
order, even when the machine inside the
crate has fewer hours than a
demonstrator sitting on a civilian
dealer lot.
Notice what happens physically inside a
bulldozer while it sits waiting for
those disposition orders, because
storage physics explains why mechanics
love these lots.
On a crawler parked for four years,
hydraulic system pressure drops to zero
while daily temperature swings pull
humid air inside unvented fuel tanks and
battery boxes.
Rubber O-rings around hydraulic control
spools stiffen as plasticizers migrate
out, and 24-volt lead-acid batteries
suffer sulfate crystal buildup across
the plates until voltage collapses under
starter load.
Meanwhile, high-pressure fuel injectors
gum up around microscopic pintle
clearances from stagnant diesel
oxidation, preventing clean atomization
at startup.
None of that damages forged steel
crankshafts, induction-hardened cylinder
liners, or planetary final drive gears
bathed in heavy 90-weight gear oil.
Tracks stay tight, pins show zero wear.
Undercarriage rollers and drive
sprockets barely turned 20 mi since
leaving the assembly line.
Depot inspectors flip the master
disconnect switch, measure dead battery
voltage and a stuck fuel rack, and log
the tractor as non-operational scrap
without ever pulling a valve cover or
checking cylinder compression.
Even hydraulic oil inside sealed
reservoir tanks remains clean and
bright, protected from abrasive dust
until an operator drains the sump and
swaps a $10 filter element.
That brings up the central question
every heavy equipment buyer faces when
scrolling through government liquidation
listings.
If federal paperwork labels a low-hour
military dozer as unserviceable scrap,
how much real iron is actually broken
when a low-boy trailer arrives to haul
it home?
Compare both operating standards.
A combat engineering battalion requires
a bulldozer that fires on the first
crank at 20 below zero, pushes blasted
concrete under hostile fire, and passes
every military safety audit with zero
diagnostic fault codes.
A rural excavation contractor, ranch
owner, or timber operator runs under
completely different mechanical
priorities.
They need a diesel engine that builds 50
lbs per square inch of oil pressure, a
torque converter that pulls smoothly
under load, and a hydraulic blade that
holds grade without drifting.
Those two bars rarely align.
What fails a wartime readiness checklist
still delivers 20 years of heavy dirt
work.
Understanding that gap lets an informed
buyer separate genuine structural
wreckage from untouched military iron
trapped behind scary federal
terminology.
Military logistics clerks grade against
combat readiness checklists written for
overseas deployment, whereas private
earth movers evaluate cylinder
compression, frame straightness, and
hydraulic pump pressure.
Every one of these heavy equipment
checks is set down in the field manual
collection in chapter nine, Heavy
Equipment and Work Trucks. You will find
it in the description and the pinned
comment or aim your phone camera at the
QR code on your screen.
Inspecting a real surplus dozer after
the gavel falls exposes how minor those
condemning defects usually are in a
commercial repair bay.
Mechanics who win unserviceable lots
frequently unbolt engine side shields,
expecting seized pistons, cracked heads,
or metal shavings packed inside
transmission suction screens. Instead,
they find crisp factory yellow or tan
paint across the track frames, sharp
cutting edges on the moldboard, and dry
seals around the hydraulic track
tensioners.
The defect that triggered the scrap tag
often turns out to be a corroded 24-volt
battery disconnect switch, varnished
diesel inside a mechanical transfer
pump, or a cracked rubber hose feeding
the hydraulic pilot controls.
Dealer shelves stock every seal.
Commercial Caterpillar and John Deere
parts counters carry the exact filters
and gaskets needed. Half a day of
systematic troubleshooting, two fresh
12-volt batteries wired in series, and
clean diesel fuel frequently bring a
condemned 30-ton crawler roaring back to
life without touching a single internal
gear.
Shop owners routinely discover that the
total parts bill to wake up a scrap
tagged military tractor stays lower than
one monthly payment on a comparable new
machine.
Once fresh fuel primes the undercarriage
rail and clean hydraulic fluid cycles
through the control valve bank, blade
tilt and ripper cylinders respond
smoothly at normal operating pressure.
Looking at specific tactical models
shows why commercial dealer parts
counters match military crawlers so
easily.
Heavy Caterpillar D7G and D7R Series II
tractors built for military engineering
units use proven 3306 and C9 inline six
diesel blocks paired with standard power
shift transmissions and planetary final
drives.
Medium crawlers such as the John Deere
850J and Case M4K share hydrostatic pump
cores, track chains, and undercarriage
rollers directly with civilian
construction fleets across North
America.
Mechanical simplicity rules these
designs. Even when the Pentagon orders
olive drab paint, heavy brush guards, or
blackout switches, the internal engine
bearings, cylinder heads, and hydraulic
valve spools come straight off
commercial assembly lines.
Experienced auction buyers pair that
parts commonality with a disciplined
yard checklist before bidding. They
match the data plate serial number
against Defense Logistics Agency catalog
descriptions to verify engine family and
blade trim.
Check final drive drain plugs and
hydraulic sight glasses for milky water
contamination,
inspect track link pin bosses for sharp
internal wear, and measure grouser bar
height in inches to confirm genuine low
runtime.
Five minutes of checking track
tensioners and cylinder rods separates a
preserved reserve tractor with hardened
hoses from a worn-out range machine.
Treating every unserviceable scrap
listing like a guaranteed bargain is
still a dangerous mistake
because federal demilitarization rules
draw a sharp legal line between intact
unserviceable machines and mutilated
scrap.
Every catalog entry carries a D-mail
code alongside its supply condition
code.
Code A and code Q tractors transfer
intact to eligible civilian bidders
after routine end-use certificate
screening even when the condition line
reads unserviceable or salvage.
By contrast, higher demilitarization
codes assigned to specialized armor kit
dozers or mine-clearing rakes mandate
physical torch cutting, frame piercing,
or armor removal at the depot before
release.
Read the demil code first. Photos alone
never tell the whole story.
Moving a 50,000-lb crawler also demands
a multi-axle lowboy trailer, oversized
highway permits, and a yard winch
capable of dragging a dead tractor onto
a deck.
Scrapped tier bills of sale often
restrict registration to off-highway
dirt work in many states, blocking fast
retail flips through standard equipment
lenders and forcing buyers to match each
tractor to real earth-moving or
timber-clearing contracts where off-road
title rules apply cleanly.
Zooming out from a single auction yard
reveals what this pipeline says about
modern defense procurement and the
broader heavy equipment economy.
Military logistics networks are
engineered for instant wartime readiness
rather than squeezing 20,000 working
hours out of federal budgets and fleet
contracts.
This was never about deliberate waste.
Rigid lifecycle rules, shifting federal
emissions tiers, and burdened depot
labor formulas force the Pentagon to
purge intact machines whenever
compliance paperwork falls out of step
with active-duty standards.
Across the defense supply chain,
maintenance policy prioritizes immediate
deployability over commercial resale
value at every turn.
So what does this mean for the broader
economy and American taxpayers?
While defense appropriations absorb the
rapid depreciation of scheduled fleet
turnover, private construction firms,
agricultural operators, and regional
contractors gain access to durable
industrial capital at a fraction of
factory cost.
If you want every one of these codes and
inspection checks in one place, that is
what the field manual collection is. It
is in the description and the pinned
comment, or scan the QR code on your
screen to go right to it.
In the end, government policy designed
for combat urgency keeps shifting
billions in productive equipment from
defense inventory back into the wider
industrial economy.

Code A and code Q tractors transfer intact to eligible civilian bidders after routine end-use certificate screening even when the condition line reads unserviceable or salvage. By contrast, higher demilitarization codes assigned to specialized armor kit dozers or mine-clearing rakes mandate physical torch cutting, frame piercing, or armor removal at the depot before release. Read the demil code first. Photos alone never tell the whole story. Moving a 50,000-lb crawler also demands a multi-axle lowboy trailer, oversized highway permits, and a yard winch capable of dragging a dead tractor onto a deck. Scrapped tier bills of sale often restrict registration to off-highway dirt work in many states, blocking fast retail flips through standard equipment lenders and forcing buyers to match each tractor to real earth-moving or timber-clearing contracts where off-road title rules apply cleanly. Zooming out from a single auction yard reveals what this pipeline says about modern defense procurement and the broader heavy equipment economy. Military logistics networks are engineered for instant wartime readiness rather than squeezing 20,000 working hours out of federal budgets and fleet contracts. This was never about deliberate waste. Rigid lifecycle rules, shifting federal emissions tiers, and burdened depot labor formulas force the Pentagon to purge intact machines whenever compliance paperwork falls out of step with active-duty standards. Across the defense supply chain, maintenance policy prioritizes immediate deployability over commercial resale value at every turn. So what does this mean for the broader economy and American taxpayers? While defense appropriations absorb the rapid depreciation of scheduled fleet turnover, private construction firms, agricultural operators, and regional contractors gain access to durable industrial capital at a fraction of factory cost. If you want every one of these codes and inspection checks in one place, that is what the field manual collection is. It is in the description and the pinned comment, or scan the QR code on your screen to go right to it. In the end, government policy designed for combat urgency keeps shifting billions in productive equipment from defense inventory back into the wider industrial economy.

metadata.title: Who Buys Used Data Center UPS, Switchgear and Generators?
metadata.author: Reclaim Atlas
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens to the huge UPS systems, switchgear, generators, transformers and power-distribution equipment when a data center upgrades or shuts down?

Some equipment can still have a second life. Serviceable systems may be inspected, removed and resold for use at another facility, while older, damaged or obsolete equipment may be stripped for parts or recycled for valuable materials.

In this video, we follow data center power equipment after decommissioning, see which machines can attract second-hand buyers, and explore how age, condition, documentation, removal costs and transport can determine whether reuse still makes economic sense.

Subscribe to Reclaim Atlas for more documentaries about the hidden second-life market for valuable equipment.

segments.text: When a data center closes, you might
expect the owner to pay a demolition
contractor to tear out the electrical
equipment and haul it away. But in 2026,
a data center facility in Oakidge,
Tennessee, shut down, and something very
different happened. A specialist removed
a 225 kilo volt ampear PS system, a 180
kW standby generator, cooling equipment,
racks, and other infrastructure, cleared
the room in 10 days, and the facility
owner was paid $12,000 for the
equipment. That sounds backwards. Why
would anyone pay for machines that a
data center is trying to get rid of?
Because behind the servers is another
business almost nobody sees. A
secondhand market for the equipment that
keeps a data center alive when normal
power disappears. Giant UPS systems,
diesel generators, automatic transfer
switches, switch gear, transformers, and
power distribution equipment can still
have years of useful life after the
servers they protected have moved
somewhere else. And when a data center
closes, the question is not simply what
can be recycled. it is which parts of
that hidden power plant are still
valuable enough to become someone else's
infrastructure. Electricity enters a
data center through switch gear and
transformers before reaching UPS
systems. The UPS keeps the load stable
and bridges the gap when utility power
fails. Automatic transfer switches then
connect the site to standby generators
while distribution equipment carries
power deeper into the server rooms.
Large facilities can have several
complete power paths because redundancy
is part of the design. A data center
does not want one failed breaker or one
dead generator to take thousands of
computers offline. That means when the
facility closes, it can leave behind far
more than servers. A 2026D decommission
in Raleigh, North Carolina, removed four
225 kilovolt ampear UPS systems, two 750
kW colar generators, two transfer
switches, and two 2000 amp main service
lineups from one 8,000 ft data center.
Once the facility shut down, equipment
built for missionritical service
suddenly became used inventory. That
transition is where specialist buyers
enter. Companies that buy decommissioned
data center assets actively look for UPS
systems, generators, switch gear,
transformers, PDUs, transfer switches,
and busway. Their first goal is often
not scrap. It is to preserve enough
value to sell the equipment again. Start
with the generator. Data center standby
generators can be attractive secondhand
because many spend most of their lives
waiting. They run during testing,
maintenance, and real outages. But a
well-maintained unit may accumulate
relatively few operating hours compared
with an engine used everyday in
construction or industrial service. That
means a data center can retire an older
generator while the engine still has
substantial mechanical life. The next
buyer might be another data center, but
it could also be a hospital, factory,
university, or commercial building.
Before paying serious money, buyers want
the name plate, kilowatt rating,
voltage, fuel type, operating hours, and
maintenance history. A load bank test is
valuable because it forces the generator
to prove that it can carry electrical
demand instead of merely starting and
idling. If the engine, alternator, and
controls are healthy, the unit can be
refurbished rather than scrapped. Work
can include servicing the engine and
cooling system, repairing fuel
components, modernizing controls,
restoring the enclosure, and then
testing the generator again under load.
PS systems follow a similar path, but
with one major complication, batteries.
A giant UPS cabinet contains expensive
rectifiers, inverters, control
electronics, breakers, and sometimes
transformers. Those components can
outlive the battery strings connected to
them. Traditional sealed lead acid UPS
batteries often need replacement much
sooner than the main cabinet. So, a
buyer can look at a 10-year-old UPS and
see two different assets. The batteries
may be near the end and headed for
specialized recycling. The UPS itself
may still be worth refurbishing. That is
why used UPS buyers ask for the exact
model, KVA and kilowatt rating, input
and output voltage, age, service
history, battery date codes, and whether
matching bypass or paralleling equipment
is included. Voltage can end the
conversation quickly. A 480 volt 3-phase
UPS is only useful to a site that can
accommodate it. A bargain machine with
the wrong configuration can become
expensive. Inventory. Then technicians
inspect what years of operation have
done. Fans and capacitors are wear
items. Connections can show signs of
overheating. Power modules and control
boards have to function correctly.
Bypass operation, alarms, and monitoring
all need to work. And if the batteries
are old, the refurbisher may simply
replace them. That can produce something
that sounds strange. An old UPS with
brand new energy storage, tested, and
ready to protect another facility.
Switch gear looks less dramatic, but it
can be just as valuable. These large
electrical lineups contain breakers,
buses, and controls that distribute and
interrupt huge amounts of power. Buyers
care about manufacturer, voltage, class,
amperage, interrupting rating, breaker
type, and configuration. Specialist
brokers may ask for formal acceptance
test reports because the equipment has
to fit the next building's electrical
design, and fault current requirements.
Transformers create another set of
questions. Buyers want the rating and
voltage ratio, and older oil filled
units may need oil analysis, turns ratio
testing, and confirmation that
problematic PCB contamination is not
present. This is why the secondhand
power market is not simply used
equipment for sale. Every major asset
carries a technical identity, and the
better the records, the easier it is to
turn unknown surplus into credible
equipment. Then comes the hardest part,
getting everything out. Data center
power equipment is heavy, connected to
high energy electrical systems, and
often installed in rooms never designed
for casual removal. A UPS can weigh
tons. Switch gear may occupy an entire
wall. Transformers need specialized
rigging. Generators may sit behind
fences, on rooftops, or inside
enclosures connected to fuel systems and
exhaust. Before removal, the site has to
be sequenced safely. Loads are migrated
or shut down. Electrical systems are
deenergized and verified. Batteries are
isolated. Fuel can be removed from
generators. Cables are disconnected and
labeled. Equipment may have to be
separated into sections before riggers
can move it through the building. If
part of the facility is still operating,
the job becomes harder because crews may
be dismantling one powertrain while
another remains live. And this is where
resale value can disappear. A generator
may be desirable but expensive to remove
without a crane. A UPS may be valuable
but trapped in a basement with no
practical route out. Switch gear may
have strong demand, yet careless cutting
can destroy the exact bus sections and
breakers that make it worth reselling.
So, specialist buyers value the removal
project as well as the machine. That is
why some companies handle disconnecting,
rigging, and freight as part of the
deal. The owner sees a room that needs
to be cleared. The buyer sees equipment
whose resale value may be high enough to
pay for the removal. That is exactly
what happened in Oakidge. Instead of
paying someone to treat the equipment as
demolition debris, the owner received
money because the recovered generator
and UPS could be refurbished and resold.
But who buys them next? Sometimes
another data center needs compatible
equipment quickly. A facility may want a
replacement UPS or breaker that matches
an installed platform without
redesigning the whole powertrain. Other
buyers come from hospitals, factories,
telecom facilities, universities, and
commercial buildings. All of them use
generators, UPS systems, transfer
switches, and electrical distribution
equipment. Lead time can matter, too.
Large new electrical equipment can
involve long manufacturing and project
schedules. A properly tested used system
may solve a requirement much sooner if
the capacity, voltage, and configuration
match. That word match is crucial. A 750
kW generator is not automatically useful
because someone needs a generator.
voltage, frequency, emissions
requirements, controls, and transfer
equipment all need to fit. A transformer
must match the electrical system. A UPS
has to match the load and power
architecture. Switch gear has to match
the distribution design. This is why
complete power trains can sometimes be
more attractive than isolated pieces. A
generator sold with its transfer switch
and paralleling gear preserves equipment
that was already designed to work
together, but eventually some assets
fail the Second Life test. Age can make
support difficult. Maintenance history
may be poor. A UPS platform may have
obsolete modules. Twitch gear can be
damaged or configured so specifically
that finding another buyer becomes
unlikely. A transformer may fail
testing. A generator may need an
overhaul expensive enough to erase the
resale value. At that point, equipment
begins moving down the value ladder. A
complete UPS may become a source of
boards, power modules, breakers, or
static switch components used to support
identical systems elsewhere. Switch gear
can provide breakers and control parts.
Generator engines, alternators, and
controllers can have individual value.
Copper, steel, and other metals can
eventually be recovered when keeping the
machine operational no longer makes
sense. Batteries usually follow their
own route earlier. Lead acid batteries
contain recoverable lead and sulfuric
acid and require specialized handling.
While large lithium battery systems also
need dedicated management rather than
ordinary disposal. So, a closing data
center does not create one waste stream.
It creates a hierarchy of assets. At the
top are complete systems valuable enough
to be removed, tested, and installed
somewhere else. Below them are machines
worth refurbishing. Below those are
donor units valuable because their
components keep other equipment alive.
Only at the bottom are materials worth
more as copper, steel, lead, and
electronics than as functional
infrastructure. That is why a dark empty
data center can still contain a
surprisingly active business. The
servers may already be gone. The
customers may have migrated, the racks
can be empty, and the raised floor
exposed. But behind the doors of the
power room are machines often built for
a longer physical life than the
computing hardware they protected. A
generator that spent years waiting for
outages may still have another facility
to protect. A UPS can receive new
batteries and return to critical
service. Switch gear can be tested and
installed in another electrical room. A
transformer can move to another
commercial site. So, what happens to a
data center's power equipment when the
data center closes? Specialist buyers
walk the site before demolition crews
do. They photograph name plates, check
ratings, review service records, and
calculate what can be removed without
destroying its value. Electricians shut
the systems down. Riggers pull tons of
equipment out of rooms built around
them. Batteries separate toward
recycling. The best generators, UPS
systems, switch gear, and transformers
move toward testing, refurbishment, and
resale. The data center itself may
disappear, but much of the
infrastructure that kept it alive can
continue protecting another building
from the exact same problem. What
happens when the power goes out?

metadata.author: Vision Matrix Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
⚡ Get a quick overview of Module 3A – Electrical Equipment (Part 1) from the Vision Matrix Institute – Data Center Electrical Design Specialist Program.

This video provides a concise summary of the essential electrical equipment that forms the backbone of modern data center power infrastructure. It introduces the key concepts covered in the complete module and is ideal for engineers who want a high-level understanding before diving into detailed study. The module covers the utility interface, MV switchgear, transformers, DG plants, equipment selection, sizing methodologies, protection concepts, and engineering best practices for reliable data center power systems.

📌 In this summary, you'll learn:

✔ Utility Interface & Point of Common Coupling (PCC)

✔ Ring Main Unit (RMU)

✔ Medium Voltage (MV) Switchgear

✔ AIS vs GIS Switchgear

✔ Distribution Transformers

✔ Oil-Filled vs Cast Resin Transformers

✔ Transformer Selection & Cooling Methods

✔ Diesel Generator (DG) Plant

✔ DG Sizing Fundamentals

✔ Protection Relays & Electrical Protection

✔ Vendor Selection Considerations

✔ Real-World Data Center Design Concepts

🎯 Who Should Watch?
Electrical Design Engineers
MEP Engineers
Data Center Engineers
Consulting Engineers
Facility Engineers
EPC Professionals
Engineering Students
Professionals preparing for Data Center projects

If you're building a career in Data Center Electrical Design, this summary is the perfect starting point before studying the complete module.

👍 If you found this video helpful, don't forget to Like, Subscribe, and Share for more professional engineering content from Vision Matrix Institute.

Welcome to Episode 2 of Broma Engineering’s Data Centre Equipment Series.

In this episode, Brendan breaks down Transformers (Tx) — a fundamental component in any data centre power system, responsible for stepping voltage up or down to keep your entire electrical infrastructure running safely and efficiently.

Whether you're a graduate, junior engineer, or new to the data centre industry, this episode will give you a clear, practical introduction to a key piece of infrastructure you’ll encounter on real projects.

This series is designed to guide you through the core equipment used in data centres — from design through to installation, commissioning, and handover.

📸 Instagram: @broma.engineering
💼 LinkedIn: linkedin.com/company/broma-engineering

metadata.title: Data Center Electrical Load Calculations Explained | UPS, Transformer & Generator Sizing
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
How do engineers calculate the electrical capacity required for a modern data center?

Data center electrical load calculations go far beyond adding server nameplate ratings. Engineers must account for actual IT demand, peak cooling requirements, electrical losses, redundancy topology, future growth, UPS capacity, transformer sizing, generator performance, power quality, and utility requirements.

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains how to build a reliable electrical load calculation for modern data centers, including AI and high-density computing facilities.

What You'll Learn

• IT load and rack power calculations
• Peak design-day electrical demand
• Why annual-average PUE is not enough for equipment sizing
• Cooling and mechanical load calculations
• UPS and transformer sizing
• Generator capacity and transient performance
• N+1 and 2N redundancy considerations
• Future growth allowances
• AI rack power and rapid load changes
• Liquid cooling and CDU electrical loads
• Harmonic considerations for VFDs
• NEC continuous-load requirements
• Generator load-step and power-factor issues
• Large data center utility interconnection
• Grid-level dynamic and power-quality considerations

Why Data Center Load Calculations Matter

Undersizing can result in equipment trips, insufficient capacity and unreliable operation during peak conditions. Oversizing can tie up capital, increase losses and create permanently underutilized infrastructure. The correct design load therefore needs to reflect the actual operating and environmental conditions of the facility.

A major engineering mistake is using annual-average PUE to determine peak electrical capacity. The video demonstrates how a 500 kW IT load can produce approximately 725 kW under an annual-average condition, 775 kW on the design-day peak, and approximately 930 kW after future growth is considered.

assume the facility load.
But the generators cannot necessarily
accept 100% of the mechanical load
instantaneously.
Mechanical loads must often be
introduced in controlled steps.
The slide illustrates staggered load
pickup with loads being brought online
sequentially.
Diesel generators may tolerate larger
load steps, while natural gas generators
can have more restrictive step loading
characteristics.
This difference has a direct impact on
generator sizing and controls.
There is another issue, leading power
factor.
Modern UPS systems and IT filtering
equipment can operate with highly
capacitive characteristics at light
load. In island mode, generators may
have a limited ability to absorb
excessive reactive power.
This can create leading KVAR conditions
and cause generator voltage regulation
and excitation systems to become
unstable.
Therefore, generator design cannot be
based only on kilowatts. Engineers must
evaluate real power, reactive power,
power factor, transient response, load
step behavior, generator controls, and
the actual sequence in which loads are
restored. For modern data centers,
generator dynamics are a system-level
engineering problem. At very large data
center campuses, the electrical design
extends beyond the facility boundary.
For utility-scale data centers with
demands of 60 MW or more, the
interconnection itself becomes a major
engineering project.
The physical system can extend from
high-voltage transmission lines through
transformers and substations into campus
distribution systems, and finally to the
data center buildings.
The utility interconnection process can
also require long planning horizons.
Utilities increasingly require precise
information about the customer's
expected demand and load ramp schedule
before approving an interconnection.
The slide indicates that transmission
scale schedules can extend beyond 24
months.
Dynamic modeling is another important
requirement.
Large facilities can affect voltage and
frequency behavior on the grid,
particularly during transmission faults
or major load changes.
Therefore, NERC-related dynamic modeling
and ride-through requirements can become
part of the interconnection process.
Finally, power quality must be
considered.
Large data centers can introduce
harmonic currents and other disturbances
into the grid.
The facility must therefore evaluate
harmonic distortion and ensure that
power quality at the point of common
coupling remains within applicable
limits. At this scale, the data center
is no longer simply a customer.
It becomes a major grid-connected
electrical system that must be
engineered accordingly. This case study
illustrates the cost of simplifying the
load calculation. The flawed design
sized generators using an average PUE
assumption. The cooling system was also
sized using a simplified load
calculation.
The problem became apparent when the
system was evaluated under the actual
peak day conditions.
The first chiller restart would create a
significant mechanical load step,
pushing the generators toward an
unacceptable operating condition.
At the same time, the cooling
calculation had underestimated the
actual heat that needs to be removed.
The result was a system with some
equipment effectively oversized while
other equipment was undersized.
The engineered fix required a more
rigorous approach. The generator plant
was resized, mechanical restarts were
staggered through the control system,
and the heat load calculation was
corrected. This avoided a potentially
catastrophic summer outage and reduced
the risk of stranded capacity.
The lesson is important. A simplified
calculation may appear less expensive
during design, but an incorrect
assumption can become extremely
expensive once the facility is
constructed.
Rigorous load modeling is therefore not
simply an engineering formality. It is a
way to protect reliability, capital
investment, and operational performance.
The complete engineering workflow can
now be summarized in eight steps.
Step one is to define the IT peak load,
and importantly, ignore server
nameplates when they do not represent
the actual engineering requirement. Step
two is to model the design day
mechanical demand, including the
environmental conditions that produce
the highest cooling requirement. Step
three is to calculate electrical and
transformer losses. Step four is to
apply the appropriate topology
multipliers for the selected redundancy
architecture, such as N+1 or 2N. Step
five is to size the continuous
electrical load while applying the
applicable NEC continuous load
requirements. Step six is to verify
generator dynamics, including step
loading, power factor, UPS recharge, and
other transient conditions. Step seven
is to conduct detailed system studies.
These studies can include fault
analysis, arc flash analysis, protection
and coordination, and other electrical
performance evaluations.
Finally, step eight is to submit the
required utility ride through and ramp
profiles as part of the interconnection
process.
This workflow connects the entire
system.
It begins with the actual IT load and
ends with utility level performance.
The key is that each step builds on the
previous one, creating a consistent
engineering basis from the rack all the
way to the grid.
The final message is simple.
Modern data center electrical design
requires grid to rack engineering.
Keentel Engineering describes its role
as bridging the gap between utility
physics and IT infrastructure.
That means understanding the complete
electrical chain from high voltage
utility interconnection and generation
through substations, transformers,
distribution systems, UPS
infrastructure, cooling systems, and
finally to high density AI racks.
The experience required for this work
spans utilities, generators, regulators,
and consulting engineering.
The goal is not simply to calculate a
number.
The goal is to understand what that
number means for the physical equipment,
operating conditions, reliability,
protection, grid interaction, and
long-term capacity of the facility.
Keentel Engineering provides services
including power system studies,
substation design, and interconnection
support.
For organizations planning large-scale
data centers, AI infrastructure, or
major electrical loads, rigorous load
calculation is the foundation for making
the right engineering decisions.
From the grid to the rack, every
decision is connected. This is grid to
rack engineering by Keentel Engineering.

videos.full_text: Welcome to Keentel Engineering's engineering guide to data center electrical load calculations. As data centers evolve to support artificial intelligence, high-density computing, and increasingly sophisticated cooling systems, electrical load calculation has become much more than simply adding up server nameplates. Every major component, from the utility interconnection and substation to transformers, generators, UPS systems, distribution equipment, cooling infrastructure, and rack-level power distribution, is ultimately influenced by the calculated electrical load. The challenge is finding the correct design load. If the load is underestimated, the facility may experience equipment trips, insufficient capacity, unstable operation, or even failure on the hottest design day. If the load is significantly overestimated, the result can be stranded capital, oversized equipment, poor efficiency, and permanently higher operating costs. In this presentation, we will walk through the engineering principles needed to calculate and size data center electrical infrastructure reliably, particularly for modern AI-driven facilities. The objective is simple. Design from the real electrical and mechanical demands of the facility, rather than relying on assumptions that may no longer apply. The consequences of incorrect sizing can be divided into two very different failure modes. The first is the visible failure, undersizing. If peak load demand exceeds the rated capacity of the electrical infrastructure, protective devices can trip, and critical equipment can be disconnected. This situation may occur during the first design day event, particularly on a hot day when the facility reaches maximum electrical and mechanical demand. >> [sighs] >> The second failure is much quieter. Oversizing. An oversized transformer or other electrical infrastructure may never trip, but it can create significant economic and efficiency penalties. Equipment operates at a lower utilization level, no load losses continue, capital is tied up in unused capacity, and the resulting efficiency penalty can affect the facility's power usage effectiveness or PUE. This is why load calculation is such a critical engineering activity. Every piece of infrastructure, from the 138 kilovolt substation down to the rack PDU, is ultimately influenced by the load number. Get that number wrong and the facility can either fail because it lacks capacity or waste enormous amounts of capital because it has too much. There are several common simplifications that can create serious problems in data center electrical design. The first is sizing equipment using annual average PUE. Annual averages are useful for evaluating overall energy performance, but they are not an appropriate basis for determining peak electrical infrastructure capacity. Equipment must be sized for the peak design day condition, including mechanical demand during hot weather. The second trap is treating cooling power as simply facility power minus IT power. Cooling must account for the actual heat generated by IT equipment, as well as electrical losses and other spatial or infrastructure related heat sources. The third trap is using a simple generator calculation such as facility kilowatts divided by a fixed power factor. Generator sizing must consider factors such as motor starting, UPS recharge, harmonics, transient behavior, and equipment derating. The fourth trap is applying heavy diversity factors to AI loads. Modern AI training clusters can experience highly simultaneous power demand. Critical capacity therefore needs to be evaluated with very limited diversity, and in some situations, the critical design case may approach 100% simultaneous loading. Finally, engineers must recognize that US 480 volt systems have different design requirements from many 400 volt international systems. NEC continuous load requirements must be incorporated into the design. The lesson is that convenient rules of thumb can become dangerous when applied without understanding the actual operating conditions. The foundation of the entire calculation is the IT load. One of the most important principles is to avoid relying exclusively on server nameplate ratings. Modern server power supplies can be significantly oversized relative to the actual power consumed by the equipment. Instead, sizing should be based on vendor measured peak demand or the rack design power that represents the actual engineering requirement. This becomes especially important with AI infrastructure. AI liquid cooled racks can reach extremely high power levels with the presentation illustrating rack loads from approximately 40 kilowatts to more than 130 kilowatts. But the challenge is not only the magnitude of the load. It is also the speed at which the load changes. Traditional cloud workloads can have relatively stable power demand while AI training workloads can produce significant power swings as thousands of GPUs change operating conditions during training steps. These rapid changes can occur on millisecond time scales. Such transient behavior can affect UPS tracking, generator governors, island mode operation, and even the stability of the grid interconnection. Both the magnitude of the IT load and its dynamic behavior. This slide highlights one of the most important concepts in data center load calculation. Annual average PUE is not the same thing as peak design capacity. PUE, or power usage effectiveness, is primarily an energy performance metric. It tells us how efficiently the facility uses energy over time, but it does not automatically tell us how large the electrical infrastructure must be. Consider the example shown here. The annual average condition produces a total facility load of approximately 725 kW based on 500 kW of IT load, 150 kW of mechanical load, and 75 kW of losses and other loads. But on the design day peak, the mechanical requirement increases. The facility load rises to approximately 775 kW. And when future growth is considered, the illustrated peak case reaches approximately 930 kW. This difference is extremely important. If we size critical infrastructure using the annual average, we risk undersizing the facility. The correct approach is to identify the critical design condition, the combination of IT demand, mechanical demand, electrical losses, environmental conditions, and planned growth that defines the infrastructure requirement. Average energy performance and peak capacity planning are two different engineering questions. >> Cooling is another critical part of the electrical load calculation. The fundamental relationship shown here is that cooling capacity, expressed in tons of refrigeration, is related to the total heat rejected by the facility. The conversion shown on the slide uses approximately 3.517 kW per ton of refrigeration. But an important engineering distinction must be made. Cooling capacity is not simply the same thing as facility electrical overhead. The cooling system must physically remove the heat generated by IT equipment and other sources. This creates a complete thermal and electrical loop. Electrical power enters the facility through the grid and electrical distribution system. Some of that energy is consumed by IT equipment. Electrical distribution equipment, UPS systems, and transformers also create losses, and those losses become additional heat. The mechanical cooling plant must then remove this total heat. UPS rooms also require dedicated cooling because UPS conversion losses and transformer losses generate heat. Therefore, the mechanical load calculation must include not only the heat generated by the IT equipment, but also the heat generated by the electrical infrastructure itself. Ignoring these hidden thermal loads can result in an undersized cooling plant and an incorrect overall facility load calculation. Redundancy changes the way electrical capacity must be calculated. The first apology shown is N + 1. In an N + 1 configuration, the system has one additional unit beyond the required operating capacity. >> [snorts] >> This can be cost-effective, but it still retains a single point failure risk within parts of the distribution system. The second apology is 2N or an A and B path architecture. Here, two independent electrical paths serve the critical load. Each path normally carries approximately 50% of the load. However, there is an important sizing principle. If one path fails, the remaining path must be capable of supporting the critical load. That means each path must be sized for the full critical requirement, rather than simply 50%. The third example is distributed redundancy. Multiple blocks share the load, and the system is designed so that the remaining blocks can absorb additional demand when another block fails. This approach can provide resilience while distributing capacity across the system. The key engineering point is that redundancy is not simply a reliability label. It directly changes equipment sizing, capacity requirements, operating points, and capital cost. Therefore, topology multipliers must be incorporated into the electrical load calculation from the beginning. Let's apply these principles to a practical example. Assume the data center starts with a 500 kW base IT load. That 500 kW is only the beginning. The design must then account for approximately 200 kW of peak mechanical and cooling demand. Next, we add approximately 50 kW for electrical losses associated with UPS systems and transformers. Another 25 kW is included for support systems and lighting. Finally, the design incorporates a 20% future growth allowance. Following the sizing waterfall produces an illustrated continuous facility load of approximately 930 kW. This example demonstrates why simply saying the data center has a 500 kW IT load is not sufficient for infrastructure sizing. The electrical system must support the complete facility requirement. The slide also provides a hardware reality check. To reliably support the illustrated 930 kW continuous load, the example specifies two 1,250 kW generators in an N+1 topology with consideration for a motor inrush, UPS recharge, and high ambient derating. This is the difference between calculating an IT load and engineering an actual facility. AI workloads are also changing the electrical design because of the rapid adoption of liquid cooling. In a direct-to-chip liquid-cooled rack, coolant is circulated directly through cold plates associated with high-power processors. A coolant distribution unit or CDU provides pumps and controls that maintain the required coolant flow. This introduces a new electrical load into the data center. The CDU pumps, controls, and associated equipment become critical loads and may require A and B UPS power. This is particularly important because liquid cooled systems have very limited thermal buffering. If coolant flow stops, processors can reach thermal limits very quickly. AI processing may throttle or shut down almost immediately. As a result, cooling is no longer simply an auxiliary mechanical service. For high-density AI facilities, cooling becomes part of the critical electrical architecture. There is also a power quality consideration. Large CDU pumps commonly use variable frequency drives or VFDs. These drives can introduce harmonic currents into the electrical system. Therefore, the electrical design must evaluate harmonic distortion and ensure compliance with applicable power quality requirements, including IEEE 519 considerations. Liquid cooling therefore changes both the thermal model and the electrical model of the data center. Data center electrical design in the United States must also account for the requirements of the National Electrical Code. One important difference is the use of 480-V systems, commonly configured as 480/277-V. Compared with 400-V systems commonly used in other regions, the higher US distribution voltage can reduce conductor size for an equivalent power transfer. But voltage selection does not eliminate the need for careful code-based sizing. The slide illustrates the NEC 125% continuous load rule. For example, a calculated load of 1,178 A multiplied by 1.25 produces approximately 1,472 A, leading to the illustrated selection of a 1,600-A breaker. The principle is that continuous loads require appropriate conductor and overcurrent protection sizing. Arc flash safety is another critical consideration. For larger equipment, applicable NEC requirements can require arc energy reduction techniques, including technologies such as zone selective interlocking. The result is that load calculation, equipment sizing, protection, and worker safety are closely interconnected. A correct load calculation must ultimately translate into a compliant and safe electrical system. Generator sizing becomes particularly challenging when a data center must operate in island mode. Consider the sequence shown here. First, the utility supply is lost. The UPS batteries immediately support the critical load. The generators then start and must assume the facility load. But the generators cannot necessarily accept 100% of the mechanical load instantaneously. Mechanical loads must often be introduced in controlled steps. The slide illustrates staggered load pickup with loads being brought online sequentially. Diesel generators may tolerate larger load steps, while natural gas generators can have more restrictive step loading characteristics. This difference has a direct impact on generator sizing and controls. There is another issue, leading power factor. Modern UPS systems and IT filtering equipment can operate with highly capacitive characteristics at light load. In island mode, generators may have a limited ability to absorb excessive reactive power. This can create leading KVAR conditions and cause generator voltage regulation and excitation systems to become unstable. Therefore, generator design cannot be based only on kilowatts. Engineers must evaluate real power, reactive power, power factor, transient response, load step behavior, generator controls, and the actual sequence in which loads are restored. For modern data centers, generator dynamics are a system-level engineering problem. At very large data center campuses, the electrical design extends beyond the facility boundary. For utility-scale data centers with demands of 60 MW or more, the interconnection itself becomes a major engineering project. The physical system can extend from high-voltage transmission lines through transformers and substations into campus distribution systems, and finally to the data center buildings. The utility interconnection process can also require long planning horizons. Utilities increasingly require precise information about the customer's expected demand and load ramp schedule before approving an interconnection. The slide indicates that transmission scale schedules can extend beyond 24 months. Dynamic modeling is another important requirement. Large facilities can affect voltage and frequency behavior on the grid, particularly during transmission faults or major load changes. Therefore, NERC-related dynamic modeling and ride-through requirements can become part of the interconnection process. Finally, power quality must be considered. Large data centers can introduce harmonic currents and other disturbances into the grid. The facility must therefore evaluate harmonic distortion and ensure that power quality at the point of common coupling remains within applicable limits. At this scale, the data center is no longer simply a customer. It becomes a major grid-connected electrical system that must be engineered accordingly. This case study illustrates the cost of simplifying the load calculation. The flawed design sized generators using an average PUE assumption. The cooling system was also sized using a simplified load calculation. The problem became apparent when the system was evaluated under the actual peak day conditions. The first chiller restart would create a significant mechanical load step, pushing the generators toward an unacceptable operating condition. At the same time, the cooling calculation had underestimated the actual heat that needs to be removed. The result was a system with some equipment effectively oversized while other equipment was undersized. The engineered fix required a more rigorous approach. The generator plant was resized, mechanical restarts were staggered through the control system, and the heat load calculation was corrected. This avoided a potentially catastrophic summer outage and reduced the risk of stranded capacity. The lesson is important. A simplified calculation may appear less expensive during design, but an incorrect assumption can become extremely expensive once the facility is constructed. Rigorous load modeling is therefore not simply an engineering formality. It is a way to protect reliability, capital investment, and operational performance. The complete engineering workflow can now be summarized in eight steps. metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
How does a data center maintain continuous power from the utility connection to the server rack?

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains the complete data center electrical design chain, including medium-voltage utility service, switchgear, transformers, UPS systems, backup generators and rack-level power distribution.

Learn how double-conversion UPS systems provide zero-transfer-time backup, how generators support extended outages, and how N+1, 2N and A/B distribution architectures reduce single points of failure.

The video also covers:

• Medium-voltage and 480 V distribution
• UPS batteries and backup generators
• VRLA versus lithium-ion batteries
• N+1, N+2 and 2N redundancy
• A/B power distribution to server racks
• Tier III and Tier IV reliability principles
• Load-flow and short-circuit studies
• Protection coordination and arc-flash analysis
• Utility and large-load grid interconnection

Read the complete data center electrical design guide:
https://keentelengineering.com/data-center-electrical-design

Discuss your data center power or interconnection project:
https://keentelengineering.com/contac

Subscribe for practical guidance on data center power systems, critical infrastructure, grid interconnection and power-system engineering.

#DataCenterElectricalDesign #DataCenterPower #UPSSystems #CriticalPower #DataCenterEngineering

segments.text: Welcome to keintel engineering. Today we
are covering data center electrical
design. Engineering continuous power
from the utility feed to the server
rack. Availability is fundamentally an
electrical promise. A layered system
where no single failure ever reaches the
IT load. That means 480 volt building
distribution n plus1 redundancy as the
standard baseline and a 59's target.
Roughly 5 minutes of downtime per year.
This guide covers five areas. the power
chain from utility to rack, UPS
conditioning and bridging, backup
generators, redundancy architecture, and
the studies that make the system
trustworthy. A few seconds without power
can reboot tens of thousands of servers,
corrupt in-flight data, and take
services offline. Unlike an office
building, a data center cannot tolerate
even a momentary interruption. The
entire electrical system is engineered
around that single constraint. The
approach here is to treat the utility
interconnection, the protection and
coordination studies and the internal
distribution design as one continuous
problem, not three separate ones. A gap
in any of those areas creates an
exposure that redundant equipment alone
cannot fix. The guide's path follows
five topics. The power chain from
utility service to the server rack. How
the UPS conditions and bridges power
backup generators and the handoff
sequence. Redundancy architecture from N
to 2N. and the power system studies that
validate the design. Power moves from
the utility to the server rack through a
series of controlled voltage
transformations. Each step bringing it
closer to the electronics in the racks.
The chain starts at the service entrance
where utility medium voltage 13.8 to
34.5 kovts is metered and terminated.
Next is switch gear. The control and
protection hub that isolates circuits
and clears faults selectively. Step down
transformers reduce that voltage to 480
volts three-phase for building
distribution. Power distribution units
or PDS transform again to 28 or 120
volts for IT equipment. And at the rack,
branch circuits and rack PDS deliver
power directly to the dual power
supplies in each server. Every stage
adds its own protection and fault
isolation so a problem at any point can
be contained without propagating to the
load. The UPS is the critical
conditioning and bridging layer between
incoming utility power and the servers.
In a double conversion design, power
flows through a rectifier that converts
incoming AC to DC, continuously charges
a battery system from the DC bus, and
then passes through an inverter that
converts DC back to clean regulated AC
to supply the load. The key insight, the
load is always supplied by the inverter,
never directly by the utility. If
utility power fails, the rectifier stops
receiving input and the batteries keep
feeding the same inverter. No switch
over, no transfer time, no flicker. Line
interactive UPS units regulate voltage
and switch to battery when needed with a
brief transfer gap, suited for small or
edge deployments. Mission critical data
centers use double conversion because
the transfer time is zero and even a
single cycle of interruption is
unacceptable. The UPS battery system
carries the full facility load through
the bridge period, typically a few
minutes up to around 15, just long
enough for generators to start and
stabilize. Two technologies dominate.
VRLA or valve regulated lead acid has
lower upfront cost and a long track
record, but a shorter service life of 3
to 5 years, larger footprint and greater
temperature sensitivity requiring
tighter cooling. Maintenance is more
manual. Lithium ion has higher upfront
cost, but a service life of 10 or more
years, smaller and lighter form factor,
and an integrated battery management
system monitoring cell level health
automatically. It tolerates higher
ambient temperatures, reducing the
cooling burden on the battery room. The
choice maps to project priorities. VRLA
for cost-driven or legacy installs.
Lithium ion for space constrained or
long life cycle builds. Batteries bridge
seconds and minutes. Generators carry
the facility through hours and days. The
handoff follows seven steps. Utility
power is lost. The UPS instantly carries
the full load from batteries. No
transfer time. The transfer scheme
signals generators to start. Generators
reach stable output and accept load,
typically in 10 to 60 seconds. The
transfer switch moves the load to
generator power. The UPS recharges while
continuing to condition power. When
utility returns, the system transfers
back and generators cool down. The
result from the server's perspective is
a power source that never went away.
Most large data centers use diesel
generators rated at several megawatts
each, paralleled for redundancy. On-site
fuel storage provides hours to a few
days of autonomy, extended by contracted
fuel deliveries during extended outages.
Redundancy means spare capacity and
duplicate paths. So a failure or
maintenance event never affects the
load. N is exactly the capacity required
with no spare. Any single failure can
reach the load. N +1 adds one spare unit
absorbing a single component failure or
maintenance event without impact. This
is the most common level in practice. N
plus2 allows a failure even while one
unit is already offline. 2N duplicates
the entire infrastructure. Two fully
independent systems, each sized to carry
100% of the load. And 2N plus one adds a
spare unit on top of full duplication,
tolerating a failure within one path
while its twin is being serviced. 2N
redundancy is only as good as how it is
wired to the load. That is where A/B
distribution comes in. Side A and side B
are independent power paths, each with
its own source, UPS and PDU, running in
parallel to the rack. Servers with dual
power supplies are corded to both. If
side A fails entirely, side B carries
the load uninterrupted. For single input
equipment, a static transfer switch
connects the two paths and transfers in
milliseconds. This architecture enables
concurrent maintainability. The defining
characteristic of tier 3. With true A/B
distribution, an entire power path can
be taken out of service for maintenance
while the IT load runs on the other
side, never seeing an interruption. The
redundancy levels map directly onto the
industry tier framework. Tier 1 provides
basic capacity with a single
non-redundant path. Tier 2 adds
redundant capacity components on a
single path. Tier 3 is concurrently
maintainable, any path taken out of
service for maintenance without downtime
using N plus1 with multiple paths when
active. Tier four is fault tolerant
absorbing a single worst case failure
with no impact requiring two n or two n
plus1 with multiple simultaneously
active paths. At the top sits 59's
availability 99.999%
roughly 5 minutes of downtime per year
not achieved by any single device. It is
the product of layered distribution,
instantaneous battery backup,
disciplined redundancy at every level,
and protection that responds correctly
every time. Redundant equipment only
delivers reliability if the system
connecting it is engineered correctly.
Established through studies, not assumed
from equipment specifications. Load flow
analysis confirms voltages and equipment
loadings stay within rated limits
including under the more constrained
conditions of running on generator power
where impedances and voltage profiles
differ from utility operation.
Shortcircuit analysis establishes fault
currents at every node. Equipment must
be rated to interrupt those currents
safely or a fault that should clear in
milliseconds becomes a cascading event.
Protective device coordination tunes
relays and breakers so the device
closest to a fault clears it first,
isolating the smallest section. Without
coordination, a single fault can trip
upstream devices and take down far more
than necessary. Arc flash analysis
quantifies incident energy at every
switch gear and panel board location,
driving labeling and PPE requirements
for maintenance personnel. Done well,
these four studies are the difference
between a system that is redundant on
paper and one that actually rides
through faults and maintenance without
dropping the load. Common questions on
data center electrical design. What is a
UPS and why is it necessary? It sits
between incoming power in the servers
conditioning electricity and providing
instantaneous battery backup. Data
centers cannot tolerate even a momentary
interruption. The UPS ensures the
servers never see one. What is N +1
redundancy? One spare unit beyond what
is required. If four UPS modules are
needed, five are installed. The most
common level, balancing reliability and
cost. What is 2N redundancy? Full
duplication. Two independent systems
each capable of carrying the full load
by itself. Two feeds, two switch gear
lineups, two UPS systems, two
distribution paths. What is concurrent
maintainability? Any component or
distribution path can be taken out of
service for maintenance without
affecting the IT load. The defining
characteristic of tier 3 requires true
A/B distribution. What is the difference
between tier 3 and tier 4? Tier 3 is
concurrently maintainable. Planned
maintenance never drops the load. Tier 4
is fault tolerant. It absorbs an
unplanned worst case failure with no
impact requiring two N or 2N plus one
with multiple simultaneously active
paths. Why does interconnection matter
for new data centers? Loads reaching
hundreds of megawatts push into the
utility interconnection process. Q
positions, system impact studies, and
protection obligations. Securing
capacity on a workable timeline
increasingly determines site viability.
Let's close out on why data center power
design is engineered so precisely.
Availability is fundamentally an
electrical promise. A few seconds
without power can reboot thousands of
servers and corrupt data worldwide. So
the whole system is layered so no single
failure ever reaches the IT load. The
double conversion UPS is the heart of
that design. The load is always fed by
the inverter, never the utility
directly. So when power fails, the

videos.full_text: Welcome to keintel engineering. Today we are covering data center electrical design. Engineering continuous power from the utility feed to the server rack. Availability is fundamentally an electrical promise. A layered system where no single failure ever reaches the IT load. That means 480 volt building distribution n plus1 redundancy as the standard baseline and a 59's target. Roughly 5 minutes of downtime per year. This guide covers five areas. the power chain from utility to rack, UPS conditioning and bridging, backup generators, redundancy architecture, and the studies that make the system trustworthy. A few seconds without power can reboot tens of thousands of servers, corrupt in-flight data, and take services offline. Unlike an office building, a data center cannot tolerate even a momentary interruption. The entire electrical system is engineered around that single constraint. The approach here is to treat the utility interconnection, the protection and coordination studies and the internal distribution design as one continuous problem, not three separate ones. A gap in any of those areas creates an exposure that redundant equipment alone cannot fix. The guide's path follows five topics. The power chain from utility service to the server rack. How the UPS conditions and bridges power backup generators and the handoff sequence. Redundancy architecture from N to 2N. and the power system studies that validate the design. Power moves from the utility to the server rack through a series of controlled voltage transformations. Each step bringing it closer to the electronics in the racks. The chain starts at the service entrance where utility medium voltage 13.8 to 34.5 kovts is metered and terminated. Next is switch gear. The control and protection hub that isolates circuits and clears faults selectively. Step down transformers reduce that voltage to 480 volts three-phase for building distribution. Power distribution units or PDS transform again to 28 or 120 volts for IT equipment. And at the rack, branch circuits and rack PDS deliver power directly to the dual power supplies in each server. Every stage adds its own protection and fault isolation so a problem at any point can be contained without propagating to the load. The UPS is the critical conditioning and bridging layer between incoming utility power and the servers. In a double conversion design, power flows through a rectifier that converts incoming AC to DC, continuously charges a battery system from the DC bus, and then passes through an inverter that converts DC back to clean regulated AC to supply the load. The key insight, the load is always supplied by the inverter, never directly by the utility. If utility power fails, the rectifier stops receiving input and the batteries keep feeding the same inverter. No switch over, no transfer time, no flicker. Line interactive UPS units regulate voltage and switch to battery when needed with a brief transfer gap, suited for small or edge deployments. Mission critical data centers use double conversion because the transfer time is zero and even a single cycle of interruption is unacceptable. The UPS battery system carries the full facility load through the bridge period, typically a few minutes up to around 15, just long enough for generators to start and stabilize. Two technologies dominate. VRLA or valve regulated lead acid has lower upfront cost and a long track record, but a shorter service life of 3 to 5 years, larger footprint and greater temperature sensitivity requiring tighter cooling. Maintenance is more manual. Lithium ion has higher upfront cost, but a service life of 10 or more years, smaller and lighter form factor, and an integrated battery management system monitoring cell level health automatically. It tolerates higher ambient temperatures, reducing the cooling burden on the battery room. The choice maps to project priorities. VRLA for cost-driven or legacy installs. Lithium ion for space constrained or long life cycle builds. Batteries bridge seconds and minutes. Generators carry the facility through hours and days. The handoff follows seven steps. Utility power is lost. The UPS instantly carries the full load from batteries. No transfer time. The transfer scheme signals generators to start. Generators reach stable output and accept load, typically in 10 to 60 seconds. The transfer switch moves the load to generator power. The UPS recharges while continuing to condition power. When utility returns, the system transfers back and generators cool down. The result from the server's perspective is a power source that never went away. Most large data centers use diesel generators rated at several megawatts each, paralleled for redundancy. On-site fuel storage provides hours to a few days of autonomy, extended by contracted fuel deliveries during extended outages. Redundancy means spare capacity and duplicate paths. So a failure or maintenance event never affects the load. N is exactly the capacity required with no spare. Any single failure can reach the load. N +1 adds one spare unit absorbing a single component failure or maintenance event without impact. This is the most common level in practice. N plus2 allows a failure even while one unit is already offline. 2N duplicates the entire infrastructure. Two fully independent systems, each sized to carry 100% of the load. And 2N plus one adds a spare unit on top of full duplication, tolerating a failure within one path while its twin is being serviced. 2N redundancy is only as good as how it is wired to the load. That is where A/B distribution comes in. Side A and side B are independent power paths, each with its own source, UPS and PDU, running in parallel to the rack. Servers with dual power supplies are corded to both. If side A fails entirely, side B carries the load uninterrupted. For single input equipment, a static transfer switch connects the two paths and transfers in milliseconds. This architecture enables concurrent maintainability. The defining characteristic of tier 3. With true A/B distribution, an entire power path can be taken out of service for maintenance while the IT load runs on the other side, never seeing an interruption. The redundancy levels map directly onto the industry tier framework. Tier 1 provides basic capacity with a single non-redundant path. Tier 2 adds redundant capacity components on a single path. Tier 3 is concurrently maintainable, any path taken out of service for maintenance without downtime using N plus1 with multiple paths when active. Tier four is fault tolerant absorbing a single worst case failure with no impact requiring two n or two n plus1 with multiple simultaneously active paths. At the top sits 59's availability 99.999% roughly 5 minutes of downtime per year not achieved by any single device. It is the product of layered distribution, instantaneous battery backup, disciplined redundancy at every level, and protection that responds correctly every time. Redundant equipment only delivers reliability if the system connecting it is engineered correctly. Established through studies, not assumed from equipment specifications. metadata.title: Executive Desk With Wireless Charging and Hidden Drawer
metadata.author: The Wood Whisperer
metadata.shortDescription:
Take a woodworking class with me in the Guild: https://thewoodwhispererguild.com/marc/

When I moved to Colorado, I was lucky to buy a home that featured a very nice office space. It's one of those offices where there's actually no space for a desk against a wall and the only logical place to put one is in the middle of the floor. Fortunately, I also have a power outlet in the floor as well as an ethernet cable. I had a makeshift desk in place that had absolutely no storage so my desk was always a mess. This Executive Desk project features not only storage, but a few technology upgrades and creature comforts like in-drawer power, wireless charging, built-in outlets, and a ventilation fan. If you're interested in a full video series and a complete set of plans, check this project out in the Wood Whisperer Guild.

At the back of the top drawer, I'll cut a hole for a power outlet. This one features USB, as well as standard receptacles. The door requires a glass pane, so I'll cut it to size, and use my fancy glass cutting mittens to break it. To hold the glass in place, I'll construct a little rabbited frame, that'll be screwed to the back of the door. For the finish, I'll make my own oil, wax blend. My mix is three cups of polymerized Linseed oil, one tablespoon of beeswax, two tablespoons of carnauba wax, and a bucket load of spag love. You can add more or less wax, depending on the results you're after, but the more wax you add, the harder it's gonna be to apply the material to the surface. The mixture is slowly heated, and then added to a squeeze bottle for easy application. I'll apply the finish using a buffing pad, on my random orbit sander. I'll use the buffing pad anywhere I can, and then go manual for the tight spots. But on the plus side, there are no harmful fumes, it's incredibly easy to apply, and spot repairs can be done in the future. metadata.author: Living in Fort Myers
metadata.shortDescription:
This is the BEST video with in-depth detail about wire transfer fraud and how to protect yourself!

Wire transfer scams can be called different things - wire fraud, wire scams, ACH scams, wire transfer fraud or just about anything else that implies wiring, and then losing, your money. The premise is that an unsuspecting customer wires a sum of money to someone pretending to be from a title company, a bank, a lawyer’s office, or a real estate office but the problem is that the recipient is not employed by any of those people, they are likely overseas, and the vast majority of time, as soon as you wire the money, it’s gone for good. With real estate wire fraud people are often wiring tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of dollars and the worst part is that this is often peoples life savings or retirement next egg. And it can be gone in the blink of an eye!

So how can you protect yourself from becoming a victim of wire fraud? Watch the video to learn more!
