Javier, hello Mario, how are you? Thank you very much as always for being here with us in your home. Mario, Sobre orugas has always been a very important support for us in our advertising. Thank you. You are always welcome. Thank you very much, Mario. This is a company that was founded in 1958 in Queloa, Canada, by the Richi brothers. One of the founders is Mr. Dave, who, thank God, is still alive today. This man is a great guy who had the vision to form this company with solid, well-defined principles, codes of ethics, and codes of transparency, which are the pillars of our company today, and we continue to do so. I would also like to take this opportunity to tell you that previously the company was basically managed with the typical Richy Brothers platform, that is, live auctions. Among others, we have Iron Planet, whose system we were managing and continue to work with now is based on online auctions. A contract is signed and then the sale to the public takes place on Thursdays. This has brought us many advantages, since we have expanded our horizons and our consignor platforms. Previously, they had to wait, here in Mexico, for 3 months, since as you know, Mario, we held them in March, June, September, and December. Now, through the Iron Planet platform, they check online, check the availability, check the inventory, and go directly online to bid on the equipment. If they are winners, then that's it, under the same auction system. As consignors enter the equipment, they are uploaded to the page after certain protocols, document review, and inspection that we also do on the equipment. Hey, Mario, how about you come with me? We'll take a tour of the facilities here and I'll tell you a little bit about what we do and what we work on. Excellent. For people who have never participated in an auction and want to participate as a buyer, what are the requirements or what is the process for doing so? Well, first of all, we welcome our proud 60-year-old, thank you. Obviously , we basically have two main actors: buyers and consignors. Go ahead, please . What we're seeing here is the registration area, the reception area. This is where our customers arrive, our staff will kindly assist them, welcome them, and register them. They'll be given a catalog. In order to buy, it's essential that you register. A deposit of $ 10,000 or the equivalent in Mexican pesos is required to participate. If you don't buy, that money is returned in full. There's no cost to participate. They register with the catalog that will be given to them, so now they have the right to participate. If they buy, well, that's their decision. There are some clients who, for whatever reason, financial or political in their company, some tell us, "You know what? Keep this money for me and then you're going to give it to me in full and I'll pay you the equivalent of what I bought." That's their decision. Once they've registered , well, they can participate directly in the auction. Once they register here, engineer, they already have their catalog, their buyer number is there, then they go to the theater where the auctions are held. Let's go to the auction theater, please . Well, this is our auction theater with a capacity for 566 people comfortably seated. Fortunately, we've exceeded the capacity in all the auctions, Mario. The thing is, there are a lot of people standing on that side. That's right. For those who haven't been with us at the auction, well, let me tell you, there are basically three ways to participate. The most common is live, where people come and sit here comfortably, watching the equipment that goes by on the ramp or those that don't, are sold by photograph. There is another one, which is online, where the client, as an essential requirement to participate, is to be registered, they must have that number. With that in mind, if for some reason the client cannot physically attend the facilities, they can do so from the comfort of their office or home, directly online. They will be able to see in real time the equipment that is being sold. They are interested in any of them. The auctioneer will say a number, a value, they are interested, they click on it, and at that moment our Bitcatcher that we have there at the central offices in Vancouver takes it. Immediately, that offer is taken here and the auctioneer will jump to the next amount. The other way to participate is also an absentee auction. There are times, Mario, when we have the audience live right here, but for some reason they no longer have time to wait for the sale of the equipment and decide to leave. So, we have a format where they register their number, register the lot or lots they are interested in, and also register the maximum value they would be willing to bid for the equipment. Well, those are basically the three classic ways to buy, I repeat, live, online, and absentee. On the consignors 'side, one condition is that the equipment has to be here in the yard. If they are not allowed to have it in their yards, they have to come here. The equipment is physically here where the potential buyer is at their disposal. In fact, what we recommend is that they come. We invite them to come. We want them to come so that they can inspect it, check it, do the physical tests, review the documents, and do their calculations so that when they are bidding they already know what they are going to get. The auction is held in dollars. If the buyer does not have an account, well, they can do it through a brokerage firm or through us. We do that conversion and solve it at the value of the equipment. Well, as you know, it is by law, except for agricultural equipment. Everything else must be charged 16%VAT. And we also have something that we call an administrative fee, 3.85%commission, for equipment that is sold between $ 5,000 and $ 33,500. The minimum CFI rate is $ 500 and it is also capped at $ 1,290 for equipment of any value. That is per lot. Apart from equipment that goes through a ramp, such as heavy equipment that cannot go through the ramp, that is sold by photography. And we have another method that we call synchronized auction. Inside the catalog, you will find some lots that are not sold in the traditional way up here through an auctioneer. Instead, you can use that little machine where you arrive with the pin they gave you, go in there, and you are interested in, what can I say? Some small compressors, some concrete cutters, some rollers, bulldozers, things like that. Each lot will close at a specific time. Every minute or so, we close the reception of buyers. So, there is lot X that will close at 12 noon. So you have to be on the lookout and tell them, "Well, I'll bid up to $ 5,000 for this equipment, and you can see if they've already surpassed you. You can go and bid a little more, $ 200, $ 500, whatever you want." We've been there. The screens show the time when the lots close and they're gone. You can see once it closes how much that lot went for and, as the engineer rightly says, if you're interested in something, you can see if it's at the price you set or if it's already been exceeded, and you have time to bid more , or two, or as many as necessary. The option, I think, would be to buy by default, saying, well, I'll put this lot up to this amount. And the system will automatically win the bid as long as it doesn't exceed the amount you set , right? That's right. That's right. You've already been awarded the equipment that you bought. Well, it's been awarded to you, and you pay for it. There are no partial releases. Yes, partial payments are received, but we can't release equipment until it's 100%paid for. You have that week, those 5 business days, to pay for it. After that period, unfortunately we have to charge interest. It's a very low rate, but at the end of the day, well, it's an interest rate and once the equipment is paid for at that time, let's go and do what you bought it for, to put it to work. That's the idea. The buyer takes their equipment, takes their documentation and that would practically close the purchase cycle. Let's go to the patio so I can tell you a little bit about the participation as consignors or people who bring equipment here to sell. Sounds great to me. Now we're outside. This is the ramp. On auction day, all this equipment goes down this ramp, parades through this part and ends up right in front of the entire audience that's sitting in the theater. Here you can see the equipment parading, you can see it go down this ramp and catch the bets in the theater. Very good, engineer. Well, he already explained how we can participate as a buyer, but what about those people, companies that decide to sell their equipment, that want to sell equipment? What is the process to be able to bring equipment to sell to Richy Bros? Okay. Look, Mario, we already have, uh, consignors, as we call them, who are the original owners of the equipment. We act as consignees. But the owners of the equipment are spread out throughout the country. There, we have, uh, through marketing, uh, we are making ourselves known by word of mouth, social media, in short, we have what we call territory managers or TMs spread out throughout the country. We have around 9 or 10 throughout the country. We have that territory manager in one area and he controls or is under his responsibility for several states. For example, here in Guadalajara we have a territory manager located there and he is responsible for practically the states of Jalisco, Aguascalientes, Colima, and Nayarit. So, he is in charge of taking care of that entire area and if there are consignors interested in working with us, well, they can contact him directly. He gets in touch, sees the equipment, checks it , and makes our recommendations. The question that a consignor or equipment owner will always ask you is, "How much can this equipment sell for?" Well, unfortunately, we don't have a crystal ball because under the public auction system and without reserves, we don't know how much this equipment can sell for. What we do give you is based on our statistics, which you can also check in the company's history or in the magazine about Caterpillars. Or in the magazine about Caterpillars. Very good. He can check the statistics there, depending on the model, brand, equipment, and the hours of work it has , he checks there and we can give you an estimate. Here in our facilities, Mario, we have an area, a reconditioning workshop where we can recondition it. Hey, we give you a quote, look, we suggest changing the transits, we suggest repairing here, there, we suggest changing the seat, we suggest painting. There are pieces of equipment, well, what can I tell you, Mario, from $ 50, $ 100, $ 200,000, that for a small investment the cost benefit can go up; but, in the end, the decision is made by the consignor. They take care, at their own expense, of bringing the equipment here to the auction and, once it's here, we take care of everything. In fact, for them, for the cook as such, he doesn't have to do any marketing. We take care of everything completely. That's our job. We know the know-how. Hey, the equipment comes, if we need any repairs , we take care of that. He doesn't have to come and check, "Hey, uh, like in a workshop, uh, hey, how are you? How are you? What are you missing?" Nothing, he sends the equipment and we take care of getting it ready so that it's in perfect condition on the day of the auction with the idea that it wins higher bids. If you want to buy, sell or renew equipment, imagine, you could do both at the same time. I'm selling my machine, whether I want to renew it for something newer or I want to exchange it for another type of equipment to do another type of work and you can do it in a single day. Engineer, thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mario. Thank you very much, Augas, for being with us and of course, the invitation is open to participate in the weekly auctions every Thursday on the Iron Planet platform, buying equipment online. Thank you very much. You know, friends, until next time.

metadata.title: Performing Undercarriage Inspection and Measurements
metadata.author: Jim Mack
metadata.shortDescription: Demonstration of some of the common measurements used to evaluate the condition of track undercarriages.

segments.text: So when it comes to inspecting undercarriage there's a few things we want to measure or
check. We're hopefully going to be able to demonstrate them here for you today.
The first thing we're going to demonstrate is how to check our grouser height or grouser wear.
Those grousers are what provide the traction; over time they will wear down. So to measure them,
what you'll need is a straight edge and a ruler we're using CAT part number 5P3277 ruler
which measures in both standard and decimal measurements. So we would take our straight
edge put it across two tracks this way and then we will measure down to the base of the track shoe
or track pad and there we can see our measurement. So we're at 1.6 and I have
four lines after that and on this tape measure here that would be 1.68 inches would be our
grouser height. You can measure it in a few locations and then take an average reading.
Our next thing that we want to measure is our track link height as this track wears
these links will wear on the surface of the rollers and the idler and you want to check
the height to make sure it's not worn down too far. Once again we'll use our straight edge
and put that across our link and we'll measure with the tape measure up to the base
of the track shoe which is equal to the top of the link
and measure down to our straight edge the straight edge makes it much easier than trying to find a
rounded edge it gives us a crisp line to go to; and here we are measuring 3.5 and i see two lines
after the five, so 3.54" on this tape measure. If you're measuring it metric this one here,
looks like it would measure 91 millimeters.
You can also measure the track bushing external wear. Remember that track bushing,
as it goes around this is what contacts the sprocket in the back. Over time there will
be wear that occurs. Here you can see on this bushing, I have removed from another track, that
you can clearly see a worn area from it contacting the sprocket. This is also one way you can tell if
tracks have already been turned; if the bushings have been turned and you reach in there and feel
you will feel this worn spot or flat edge up at the top, which I do not feel on this so these
track links or bushings have never been turned on this track. To measure that you're going to want
to use a tool like this, a caliper, and you can go in there and adjust it to the thickness of the
bushing. By itself the caliper will not give you a measurement but once you have it set to
the same dimension you would simply hold that up to the tape measure and there you can obtain
your reading to get your bushing wear, the external bushing wear. In a different video
we'll show you how to check for internal pin and bushing wear by measuring track pitch.
You can also use a caliper, probably a larger size than this, to check the wear on the
rollers. Up top here we have our carrier roller; you would want to check the width of it.
On our track rollers down below you would do the same thing, you want to check the surface
where the track links are riding, where they're rubbing. The idler flange; identify
the specifications for that, a lot of times what they'll have you do is measure across the raised
surface and then measure down to determine how much wear has occurred on your idler flange.
You want to do a visual inspection of some other things; you want to check for any outside pin
wear on these links. Ideally they should look like this which are relatively unworn, they shouldn't
be contacting any of the guards that can be a sign of looseness or something being misaligned.
You can check for idler flange side wear; you shouldn't see too much wear on the side of
here, it could be a sign of misalignment, maybe it's working sideways on slopes which is not
really a good practice, that can also cause that side wear and same with roller flange side wear.
The drive sprocket, some machines or particularly older machines will provide a profile gauge,
anymore that's not normally provided. When you change track links or put new bushings in there,
you would need to change the sprocket with it to match that new bushing surface.
So in most cases the sprocket is going to be changed when you turn pins and bushings
or replace the track chain. But what you want to look at is make sure it's not excessively sharp;
as these wear they become sharper, pointier and they would begin to look like a bicycle sprocket.
As you get more experienced and see more sprockets you'll be able to recognize a
severely worn one from a relatively new one. Underneath this guard here, we don't have it
removed, but there is a large recoil spring; you want to check that to make sure that recoil spring
is not cracked or damaged in any way. You would remove the guard, make sure you reinstall it.
Check the track frame; that's the part that's going to be holding all the components
and thereby supporting the weight of the machine. You want to look for any cracks or broken welds,
obviously any missing fasteners whether they're in track rollers, you know, or an idler,
that would be a problem. And on the track shoes, make sure all the bolts are there.
That's going to require moving the machine forward because right now we can only see half the track;
we cannot see what is down against the ground. Lastly you're going to want to check the guards;
this has a guard in the front and the guard midway back here. Same thing, make sure all the fastening
parts are there make sure they're not mangled, rubbing anything. They can take a lot of abuse;
sometimes they need to be straightened, re-welded; sometimes they may need to be replaced.
So that's how we do a visual inspection of our tracks and some of the measurements
to help determine the amount of life and what service needs to be done on that undercarriage.

metadata.shortDescription:
Unlock the secrets of interpreting oil sample reports with our informative video, featuring a real-world scenario involving a lifeboat engine. Designed for maintenance professionals, marine engineers, and anyone interested in the practical aspects of oil analysis, this video serves as a guide to understanding and utilising oil sample reports effectively.

In this engaging session, we present a detailed case study of a lifeboat engine exhibiting signs of both fuel dilution and dirt ingress. The video begins with an introduction to the essential components of an oil sample report, explaining key terms and metrics. We focus on how to read and interpret these reports to make informed maintenance decisions.

The core of the video is a step-by-step walkthrough of the lifeboat engine's oil sample report. We analyse the data, paying special attention to indicators of fuel dilution, such as decreased viscosity and increased levels of fuel-related contaminants, and signs of dirt ingress, like heightened silicon levels. The report also includes other crucial information, such as wear metal concentrations and additive levels.

Our expert presenter guides viewers through the process of deducing which issue – fuel dilution or dirt ingress – occurred first in the lifeboat engine. This involves a careful analysis of the oil report data, considering the operational context of the lifeboat engine and understanding the typical progression of these conditions.

Throughout the video, we emphasize the importance of regular oil analysis as a preventive maintenance tool. By learning to read oil sample reports accurately, maintenance teams can diagnose issues early, make informed decisions, and prevent catastrophic failures.

This video is not just a tutorial; it's an interactive learning experience. Viewers are encouraged to think critically about the presented data and draw their own conclusions before the final reveal. Whether you're a seasoned engineer or new to the field of oil analysis, this video offers valuable insights into the art of reading oil sample reports, using an intriguing real-life example.

Join us to unravel the mystery of the lifeboat engine and become proficient in interpreting oil sample reports, an essential skill in the realm of machinery maintenance and reliability.

Visit https://learnoilanalysis.com & https://oilanalysislab.com to find out more.

metadata.title: Why Oil Analysis Should Be Part of Your Preventative Maintenance Program
metadata.author: EquipmentWorld
metadata.shortDescription:
Regular engine oil testing can serve as an affordable insurance policy for your construction equipment, helping to backup manufacturer warranty claims and make more informed equipment maintenance and disposition decisions.
 
In this episode of The Dirt, we hear from Shelly Eckert, business consultant for Chevron Lubricants, who explains how to properly collect an engine oil sample and interpret the results.
 
Beyond oil health, lab results can detect contaminants and identify abnormal wear on engine components. Over time, those trends can help optimize service intervals and extend the life of your machine. Eckert says, in most cases, contractors can start an oil analysis program for less than $20 per sample.
 
To learn more about the importance of engine oil testing and how it can prevent breakdowns and save on maintenance costs, check out the latest episode of The Dirt.
 
Equipment World serves up weekly videos on the latest in construction equipment, work trucks and pickup trucks – everything contractors need to get their work done. Subscribe and visit us at equipmentworld.com!

Newsletter Signup: https://randallreilly.dragonforms.com/loading.do?omedasite=eqw_subscriptions
 
In This Episode:
00:00 - Engine Oil Testing
00:39 - Why Test Your Engine Oil?
02:42 - What Does Engine Oil Analysis Test For?
03:56 - Why You Need to Test Your Oil Regularly
04:52 - What Is the Turnaround Time on an Oil Test?
05:50 - Can You Access Historical Oil Analysis Data From the Labs?
06:40 - How Much Does an Oil Test Cost?
07:36 - How Do You Take an Oil Sample for a Test?
11:47 - How Does a Contractor Interpret Oil Analysis Results?
13:56 - How Do You View Oil Analysis Results?
14:30 - How Do You Get Started With Oil Analysis?
17:47 - Final Thoughts

videos.full_text: - This Equipment World video is brought to you by Chevron Delo 600 ADF ultra low ash diesel engine oil. It's time to kick some ash. Today we're here to talk about oil testing. I think fluid testing is one of those things that there's still a lot of unknowns in the industry and we tend to shy away from it because it kind of feels like it's this add-on service that no one really needs. In reality, there's a lot of benefits to fluid testing and it can materially impact your business. Without going into more detail we're gonna talk to Shelly Eckert with Chevron who's gonna break down fluid testing and why it is so important for your business. (upbeat music) Why is fluid testing a bigger deal than just learning when it's time to change your oil? - Well, if you think about it, and a lot of us out here will refer to the engine oil as the bloodline of the engine. So if you wanna go to the doctor and see what your cholesterol level is, you have to go and give blood. Well, if you wanna know what the health is of the engine, you gotta draw the oil sample and send it into the lab. The way I look at it, it's a cheap insurance policy to start with. Can use the oil analysis results to back up any warranty claims, show that you're doing maintenance and taking care of the equipment. - [Bryan] Because none of us have ever gotten in a dispute with a dealership over whether it was my fault or the dealership's fault that the engine may have crapped out on me in the middle of my job. - [Shelly] No, that never happens. - Never happens, never. (laughs) Other than we have a record of me doing regular maintenance, what else can fluid testing kind of do to show me what's going on inside the engine? - Last thing you wanna do is be reactive and have a piece of equipment go down unexpectedly. You don't have the parts ready, you don't have a place to fix it quite yet. You have to haul it back to the shop because you're not doing oil analysis and not being able to do proactive and preventative maintenance. That's the goal to get around that. - For a lot of contractors, I don't know that they really understand the analysis that's going on beyond just like what condition your oil is in. If I understand it correctly, you can get into some real diagnostic stuff just from the results of an oil analysis. Is that correct? - That is correct. I'll give you an example. And this is on highway versus off highway example. We were doing a drainable study one time and he was supposed to be setting samples in every 5,000 miles. And instead, what happened was that all five samples came in at the same time and as they were going through the laboratory, the condition of the sample was getting worse. And so I picked up the phone and called the vice president of maintenance, said, it looks like you're gonna blow a rod through this engine. And he said, "Yep, I just did yesterday." - Oh wow. - So that's one reason to do oil analysis. - And so what are you able to detect in oil analysis that I in the shop I'm not able to pick up on just doing regular oil changes. - [Shelly] You can see wear patterns, making sure that the oil is being kept clean, free of (indistinct), free of a fuel dilution. Make sure that the engine's not running hot, and oxidizing that oil. Increasing the viscosity, reducing the fuel economy of benefit. And of course then there's all the engine parts are made by different metallurgy. So we're looking at the wear metals to determine what we are gonna recommend to review at the shop level. - [Bryan] So if I've got a rod or a bearing that's starting to go, through oil analysis, we can figure out, oh, there's a little bit of metal shavings in here and it looks like that's coming from one of your bearings. You've got a bearing going out. - Yeah, that's correct. That's exactly what I'm getting at. However, to get to that point and looking at reports, you have to create a good solid oil analysis program. And that starts with getting the equipment list, outlining the components that are gonna be sampled. Get that list to the laboratory so that they are aware because from one engine to another engine there's gonna be different limits which are typically driven by the OEMs or sometimes it's statistically driven by how much data the labs have been accumulating by make and model. - But expound on how are we creating a library? What is that doing for me by actually having a history of the machine rather than just, oh, I think something's going wrong. Here's an oil sample. - There are times in which somebody grabs a sample because the engine has failed and they wanted to go into the lab to find out why. And we call that an autopsy. - Yeah, it's pretty accurate. - Right, you can't really figure it out once everything's gone wrong, right? - Sure. - These guys have gotten a lot better. It used to be that you would do a report and you would mail it and then it turned into emailing the reports and then online websites so that you can run your own reports or the lab will work with you and create reports so that you're looking at the entire fleet. Therefore you can make buying decisions, which engine is outperforming another engine? For longevity, for performance, what's costing the most to repair? And you can use all that from oil analysis. - Now let me ask you this. What kind of turn around time is it on getting an oil sample back and the reason I ask is could I potentially use this as a tool when I'm going to purchase a new piece of equipment? Is the turnaround time quick enough that within a couple of days I can get those results back before I go spend 60 grand on a used piece of equipment? - [Shelly] It takes typically 24 to 48 hours. - [Bryan] So a couple days. So this could be a tool beyond just my regular fleet. This could be a tool that I use to know what I'm getting into on a used piece of equipment before I go make an investment. - That's a very good question. The answer to that is yes. So let's say that the seller of the equipment changed out the oil and then the sample was taken, the lab can tell you that this looks like a brand new sample. - [Bryan] Interesting. - [Shelly] You know, it's about being able to arm yourself with warranty information. It's also arms yourself with when should I trade a piece of equipment? 'Cause you can look at the whole fleet and say, "Hey this engine's failing at 10,000 hours or whatever." And figure out how long it is before you need to trade. - If I understand correctly, the labs are also creating and have been creating for some time this giant library of all the different kinds of equipment that are coming in and being tested. And so even if you don't necessarily have historical data on your piece of equipment or the piece you're buying, you can tap into their library to get a decent feel for what's going on. - I've done that hundreds of times. - So this is a very powerful tool that the industry right now is largely blind on. - That's right. So the labs can go in and they can pull all of the data, they scrub all the customer information, and then you can run statistics on that data or even provide it to the OEM without any customer information so that they can scrub that data and find out if they've got a design problem. So there's a lot of power to it. - And how much on average would you say it is to run an oil sample? You know, are we talking 15 bucks? Are we talking 50 bucks? - [Shelly] Some of that is gonna be determined based on what level of testing you are doing. If you go straight to the lab, it's gonna be more expensive than if you were to go through like Chevron LubeWatch program, which is a branded program. And because we have so many samples that go through the lab, we have- - Volume discounts? - [Shelly] Volume discount, yep. So in general, engine oil sample, less than 10 bucks. - Oh, so I can go out and get real time information on a piece of equipment. Call it on the ridiculously high side, I can get that done for less than 20 bucks. - Yep, less than 20 bucks, typically. - Okay. - Typically, that's gonna vary from lab to lab, Bryan, just so you're aware. - Oh yeah, absolutely. And for the viewers, absolutely, this is not a 100% of the time it's gonna be under $20 but this is a huge tool that you have at your disposal and it's affordable. So we've taken the cost issue kind of out of the equation in my mind. - Yep. - The next big hurdle as I think through this as a contractor is now I'm envisioning myself lying on my back under my machine while I'm trying to do an oil change and I got rags and grease everywhere and now I'm trying to take this little bottle and I'm trying to get oil, dump it, get oil, dump it, get oil, dump it, and then get oil without contaminating, like this sounds like a giant pain in the you know what. In reality, how long does it take and how difficult is it to take a real oil sample? But before we get into that, I want to take a second to tell you about the sponsor of this video, Chevron Lubricants. Protecting your diesel engine and its exhaust after treatment system has traditionally been seen as an either/or proposition when it comes to choosing the engine oil that's going to protect your system. And that's exactly why Chevron spent more than a decade of R&D work developing a no compromise formulation. Now I don't have to tell you why a clogged DPF is bad news, but here's the real kick in the pants. 90% of that ash clogging up your DPF and then upping your fuel and maintenance costs, it comes from your engine oil. You might be thinking, why don't they make an engine oil with less ash in it then? You'll be happy to learn that Chevron agrees with you. They've developed a new ultra low ash diesel engine oil that is specifically designed to combat DPF ash clogging, Delo 600 ADF with OMNIMAX technology cuts sulfate ash by 60%, radically reducing the rate of DPF clogging and extending the DPF service life by two and a half times. Before you had to choose between protecting your engine or your after treatment system, now you don't. Delo 600 ADF with OMNIMAX technology, it's time to kick some ash. How long does it take and how difficult is it to take a real oil sample? - So again, it goes back to setting up a good solid oil analysis program before you even start it. There are sampling tools. My preference, which is industry standard, is to use sampling valves. They're on the engine block or whatever you're taking. I've got a few examples 'cause I like my little- - You have a sample sampling valve. - Sampling sampling valves. And I got multiple. So there's a variety of different- - Perfect. - Different (indistinct). So that's the first priority is using a sampling valve. 'Cause it's consistent and you're taking a sample from the exact same place every time. The second way is using a vampire pump. - That sounds intimidating and looks intimidating. - I'm old school, it's a sampling pump, but a lot of us grew as a vampire pump. So you usually just take, which I happen to have a Chevron LubeWatch kit also in my office. - Nice. Excellent. So is this what you would get from Chevron? Is this little kit? - Yeah, I'm gonna put it back together kind of. Give a better look at it. - Yep, so it's just a little black container with I'm assuming a sampling bottle inside. - Yep. Black container, mailing container, sample bottle. And I know that you don't see it, but there is actually on the bottle it says this is the fill line. So to fill it up to here. - You gotta dummy proof it for us in the field. We're a little dense. - No, it's okay. It comes sealed because it's a clean bottle. And I'm not gonna open it 'cause I'm gonna probably take it as a sample for myself eventually. - [Bryan] Sure. - So basically you just take the cap off and you would screw it in here and then you would take tubing and you stick it down the top of this into the bottle about halfway. And then you take the other end of it and put it into the engine from the dipstick. Read it through the machinery right to the sump and then you just suck it out. Hence the reason why it's called a vampire pump. - And that's it. - That's it. It's not that difficult. And then you fill out the paperwork or you can use an app to log a sample or you can use labels. Then you just stick this in here, put the cap on, and off it goes to the lab. - So in my mind now we've taken care of price, we've taken care of difficulty of pulling samples. My third big hurdle for a guy in the field is okay, now two days later I get this packet of paper with a bunch of fancy scientific stuff on it and graphs and charts and I'm not a graphs and charts person. I dig in the dirt for a living. - [Shelly] Right. - How in the world am I gonna interpret these things to know that this amount of tungsten and this amount of copper mean that I have a bearing out? Well like how does that work? Who's gonna help me interpret this stuff? - When you're reading a report, the first thing that you start with is you look at what the diagnostician put on the report. The guy that's reviewing the data. - [Bryan] So he's gonna put his like own notes in there of hey, this is what this means? - That's correct. - Perfect. So I don't have to interpret any of this. It's all dummy proof for me. - It's done for you. Right. But then you also look at what's being flagged and over time you'll learn. But I'm not a big fan of just looking at one report at a time. 'Cause that's just looking at one sample in time. - [Bryan] There's no trend, it's a snapshot. - It's a snapshot, right. You know, when you diagnose samples you are looking at the trend analysis. And another big, big, big piece of oil analysis is having the right hours on the engine and the right hours on the equipment because number of hours changes the perspective of a diagnostician. - If you think about that that makes sense because if we're talking a brand spanking new machine, you're probably gonna see a lot more wear in the beginning as the machine's getting broken in. - [Shelly] That's correct. - [Bryan] And then it's gonna taper down and then you actually start getting into real world wear. - [Shelly] That's correct. - [Bryan] And again, that's also gonna let them reference that big library that they have internally at the correct hour mark rather than this is an 1,800 hour machine and we're comparing it to a 2,500 hour machine. - [Shelly] That's right. If it's like a piece of equipment that's supposed to be going out to 3,000 hours and it's sampled at 1,000 hours, the amount of wear that's tolerated at 3,000 hours versus 1,000 hours is completely different. So the time on the equipment is extremely important. And then it then empowers just the overall fleet reports 'cause you are graphing and looking at wear patterns based on the time on their oil. - I 100% agree. I think trending is the more powerful tool over time rather than just getting a quick snapshot of your equipment. Is it based per lab or how is it that I can go maybe online and see all of my results? Or is it something where I have to save all of these packets of paper? - [Shelly] And so yes, it advanced to a website that has online reporting tools. We use multiple third party companies to provide the Chevron LubeWatch program. Two of them. And then we pull all that data together so that we can have it all together. But we do that because we wanna have access to the labs all across the country. So it's easier to get samples into the lab too. - So we've addressed kind of all of my big major hurdles. My final hurdle is where do I even get started on this? - [Shelly] That's when you have to have a solid oil rep in the field. What we do is it's part of it, again, setting up the oil analysis program from the beginning. Getting your equipment, getting the sampling established, giving them sampling procedures. 'Cause there could be multiple ways that they have to take the samples based on if some of the equipment does have the bad valves and some of it does not. And then setting you up with the laboratory to order the kits. 'Cause these do not come from us, they come from the labs. - And so if I'm starting today, Shelly, this afternoon, after we get off of this call, what is a resource I can go to? - [Shelly] First of all, you have to be a Chevron customer really to get a Chevron kit. - I'm not a Chevron customer, I go to O'Reilly's and I pull that jug off the shelf and I do it like Grand Pappy did. So how do I get started even with Chevron, like what is step one for me to get into this world? - You could either contact your local Chevron marketer who can set you up. Now if you're a national account, then you can contact your Chevron rep, and they'll set you up. It's that simple. - Okay. Now not to take Chevron out of the picture, but if I'm not a Chevron customer, are there just independent labs that I can go find and pursue? Or is that's kind of the protocol is just find an oil testing lab somewhere? - Yes, I mean I typically stay with the two most common, which one is ALS Tribology, and the other is POLARIS Laboratories. The two of them are the ones that support the Chevron LubeWatch program and they're the monsters for oil analysis in the field. There's also The Caterpillar Labs, they know their equipment. You can go get to the Caterpillar dealer and get kits from them as well. You can even get a sample kit at NAPA if you really were in dire need. - So you know if you're going with those, you're gonna get quality samples, you're gonna get quality reports. They've got the online tools. - Yes. - And I'm assuming this isn't necessarily a subscription service, I can just go order a kit from them, pay for the testing, get those results. And if I wanna call it good there, I can call it good there. - Yeah, these are typically sold in packs of 10. I think Polaris might be 12. Don't hold me to that. - So you may have some extra bottles, if you decide to can this thing after the first report, you may have some extra bottles, but I'm not on the hook for $100 a month service for the next two years. - No, no. - Okay. - There's also two ways to do the program. You can either prepay for the kit and the testing upfront or you can pay for the kit material and then as you send samples in, you can pay for the testing. It's more cost effective if you do prepay. - And just, I already know the answer, but to reiterate to the audience. I don't have to be a 50 plus equipment fleet. This is literally a very powerful tool that is very easy to access and it is not costing much money at all. - That's right. I've been around oil analysis for 29 years. It needs to get empowered out in the field. - It does. Agreed, now, especially after this conversation, I am in 100% agreement, this needs to be a regular thing for everybody, even if you just have a backhoe on the farm, this is huge. - That's right, that's right. - Well, as always, thank you to Shelly and Chevron for coming on the show to give us some more wisdom and some more insight as to how fluid testing can really impact your business in a very positive way and save you money in the long run. metadata.shortDescription:
This clip shows the procedure on how to take and undercarriage inspection using the Komatsu ultrasonic measuring tool.

Komatsu is a leading distributor of Undercarriage solutions for various makes and models of earthmoving machinery. 

Our Undercarriage solutions cater for a wide range of market segments including: Mining, Construction, Quarry, Utility, Agriculture, Land Fill, Demolition, Fixed Plant and Government.

We also offer a free ultrasonic Undercarriage inspection to all Komatsu customers.

For more information call Komatsu on 1300 566 287 or visit komatsu.com.au

Don’t pay out of pocket for costly equipment or machinery for your business if you don’t have to. In this video, Karrin, a small-business expert at NerdWallet, explains how equipment financing works, how to qualify, and where to get the best equipment loan in 2025.

 ✅ What equipment financing is and how it works
 ✅ Why equipment loans are different from other types of business loans
 ✅ How much you can finance (and what “soft costs” are)
 ✅ Pros and cons of online lenders, banks, credit unions, and SBA lenders
 ✅ Tips to find the best rates and terms for your small business

segments.text: If you run a small business that relies on costly equipment or machinery to operate,
then you may be interested in exploring equipment financing as an affordable
way to make such a big purchase.
I'm Karrin, a small business expert in NerdWallet.
And today I am going to explain how equipment financing works and where
you can go to get an equipment loan.
First, the basics.
Equipment financing is a loan, typically a term loan used specifically
to purchase equipment, machinery, or hardware for your business.
You repay the loan with interest over an agreed upon repayment period,
typically somewhere between two and seven years, depending on the lender.
And once you pay off the loan, you own the equipment.
One thing that sets an equipment loan apart from other term loans
is the fact that the equipment or machinery you're purchasing
serves as collateral on the loan.
That means you often don't need to put up physical collateral of your own,
though you may still be required to sign a personal guarantee and or agree to the
lender filing a lien on your business.
These are measures the lender takes to ensure they get paid in full,
even if you default on your loan.
Lenders may finance up to a hundred percent of the
total cost of the equipment.
Though some offer up to 125%.
The additional 25% can be used to cover what are considered soft costs.
So those are things that are necessary to set up and begin using the equipment like
the cost of delivery and installation.
Now, where can you go to get an equipment loan?
Well, generally you have a few options each with its own benefits
and drawbacks, which I'll cover.
Online lenders typically have the most flexible qualifications of
your three main lender options.
Some online lenders accept borrowers with bad credit and startup business
owners, and many of these lenders have simple online forms that allow
for faster application reviews, loan processing, and funding.
The downside to online lenders is that their interest rates tend to
be higher and their repayment terms shorter than those offered by banks,
credit unions, and SBA lenders.
Banks and credit unions are likely to offer you the most favorable
rates and terms on an equipment loan.
In fact, a bank or credit union that you already have an account
with is a great place to start your equipment financing search.
However, it's important to note that these more traditional lenders also tend to have
the strictest qualification requirements.
You'll likely need a high personal credit score, at least a few years in business
and really strong financials to qualify.
Finally, if you strike out with an equipment loan from a bank, but you
have a personal credit score of 650 or higher, at least two years of business
history and strong annual revenue, consider turning to an SBA lender.
SBA lenders can offer up to 10 year terms with reasonable
interest rates on equipment loans.
Just be prepared for a rigorous application process
involving a lot of paperwork.
For more information on equipment loans, or to apply for one through our loan
marketplace, visit NerdWallet.com.
And if you found this video helpful, hit like and subscribe.

metadata.title: How to Track Material, Equipment & Subcontractor Costs by Job
metadata.author: The Profitable Contractor
metadata.shortDescription:
Keep material, equipment, and subcontractor costs tied to the right job—so you can catch missing paperwork, unexpected charges, and budget issues sooner. A simple, consistent review can help you see where job costs stand while there’s still time to follow up.

#ContractorTips #ConstructionBusiness #JobCosting #ConstructionManagement #TheProfitableContractor

segments.text: Your labor hours can be tracked
perfectly, and your job can still lose
money. [music] Materials, equipment
rentals, and subcontractors often make
up most of a job's direct cost.
One uncoded delivery or one unreturned
rental can hide an overrun until it's
too late.
So where do these costs go missing?
A fire protection purchase order for
pipe and fittings carries the job
number, quantities, and agreed prices.
It records the intended commitment.
The foreman checks what arrives, noting
quantities and condition on the delivery
ticket or receipt.
The vendor invoice states what the
supplier charged.
Accounts payable matches all three
records before approving the charge.
That comparison can catch a quantity
mismatch, an incorrect price, or a job
number that points somewhere else.
A charge posted to the office leaves the
receiving job's costs understated. A
charge posted to another project
distorts both jobs. The project manager
guides the job assignment. The foreman
confirms receipt, and accounts payable
checks that the invoice follows the
material to the correct job.
Pipe cutoffs and damaged fittings stay
charged to the job that generated the
waste.
The project [music] manager uses field
reports to separate the waste allowed in
the estimate from excess waste, making
the overrun visible without charging for
the same material twice.
Returned material needs an adjustment,
too. [music] Accounts payable posts the
supplier credit to the job that carried
the original charge, keeping the return
receipt and credit memo as support. Any
restocking fee stays with that job. A
changed supplier price belongs against
the relevant purchase with the revised
price documented.
When material serves several jobs, the
project manager uses crew usage logs to
actual quantities wherever possible. If
exact counts are unavailable, a
consistent documented allocation basis
supports the split. Spare budget on
another project is never a reason to
move the material cost there.
A lift's rental record carries the job
number, rental start date, and return
date. The agreement controls minimum
rental periods, weekend charges, and the
event that stops billing. [music]
The crew's last day using the lift may
come before that event. [music]
Equipment sitting idle on site can still
accrue charges.
Off rent means the agreed or confirmed
billing stop, which may require a return
or a notice acknowledged by the vendor
depending on the [music] terms.
The project manager records that
confirmation separately from the last
day of use, then compares the invoice
period with the recorded dates and
[music] agreement.
A vendor acknowledgement, off rent
confirmation number, or return receipt
stays with the rental record as evidence
of close out and support for resolving
any billing [music] mismatch.
A machine serving several jobs needs a
cost split supported by the field log.
For a daily rate rental, the project
manager divides the charge according to
each job's recorded equipment days.
For an hourly rental, the split follows
recorded equipment hours.
Each project receives the same
proportion of the shared charge as its
share of documented use.
The log connects those days or hours to
job numbers, giving the office support
for each allocation.
The project manager applies the chosen
basis consistently, and accounts payable
posts each share to its own project.
Charging the entire bill to one job
distorts every project involved.
Assigned subcontract records an expected
obligation against its job.
That commitment stays separate from
invoices recorded as actual costs.
The project manager compares the agreed
amount and invoices received with the
subcontract budget, checking that build
work matches the signed scope.
Cumulative billing above the commitment
or a charge for work outside that scope
needs investigation before approval.
The remaining amount still to be
invoiced stays visible.
When accounts payable records a bill, it
reduces that pending balance by the
corresponding amount, so the same cost
does not appear as both pending and
billed.
The record distinguishes committed,
invoiced, paid, and credited amounts.
The project manager monitors scope and
budget. Accounts payable updates
invoices, [music] payments, and credits,
keeping the subcontract's remaining
exposure visible even before the next
bill arrives.
Each week, the project manager reviews
every active [music] job by cost
category against its budget.
A simple table keeps the job number,
cost category, budget, committed amount,
invoices and credits, [music] and
missing paperwork in separate columns.
Pending material deliveries, rental
time, and subcontract commitments stay
on the review even when bills have not
arrived.
That keeps expected costs visible
alongside posted charges.
The team flags missing documents,
charges assigned to the wrong job, and
unresolved questions.
Each flagged item gets a named owner and
a follow-up date. The project manager
coordinates follow-up.
Accounts payable identifies gaps in
office records while field staff confirm
what arrived or was used. At the next
review, the team checks corrections,
clears resolved items, and carries open
questions forward with an updated action
and deadline.
A fictional calculation illustrates the
impact. It represents neither contractor
results nor an industry benchmark. This
is general education, not individualized
accounting advice. [music]
The budget allows $8,000 for materials,
$1,000 for rental, and $3,000 for
subcontracting. $12,000 across these
categories.
At an illustrative $200 daily, five
rental days use the $1,000 allowance. 10
days costs $2,000, $1,000 over
allowance.
If waste or a price increase brings
materials to [music] $8,400,
actual costs become $8,400
+ $2,000 + the unchanged $3,000
subcontract, $13,400.
[music]
That's $1,400
over budget.
With revenue and other costs unchanged,
job gross profit falls $1,400.
That doesn't determine company-wide net
profit or cash flow.
Cash flow concerns when money comes in
and goes out. [music] An invoice's
payment date alone doesn't establish job
profitability. Tracking costs cannot
[music] guarantee profit.
For the next job, require its job number
on every purchase order and all
delivery, rental, and subcontractor
paperwork before the weekly review.
When scope grows, change orders need to
capture the added work and its costs.
A useful cost record supports decisions,
[music] not just explanations.
On your next job, put that information
to [music] work. The value lies in what
you can still change.

segments.text: The costs of not implementing a solid
fleet management system. How about
project delays, accidents, lawsuits,
broken machinery, just to name a few.
What do you know about fleet management?
Whether it's a truck, crane, excavator,
or any other equipment on the job site
or equipment yard, fleet management is
crucial for every company. The right
fleet management system should reduce
costs, improve efficiency, ensure
safety, and most importantly, keep you
out of hot water with the government. We
know you want to get the best bang for
your buck. So, before you sign any
checks, be sure to go over these
questions with your team. Considering
your general scope of work, what
specific equipment is needed and why?
Where will you purchase the equipment?
Will it be new or used? When is the best
time of your fiscal year to complete
these transactions? What maintenance
plan do you have arranged for the fleet?
How will the fuel be handled? What
system should be followed for inspection
and tracking? Have you considered all of
the laws and regulations in your state?
How will operators be supervised? With a
goal in mind to maximize the
availability of the fleet, regular
inspections and servicing can greatly
increase the lifespan of equipment.
Neglecting this routine maintenance will
only cost you in the end, leading to
expensive repairs and even the
possibility of replacing equipment.
Believe me, you don't want your key
crane dying when you're halfway through
the job. A schedule should be created
based on mileage, time, engine hours,
and fuel consumed, and should include
the following duties.
A checklist of maintenance tasks based
on specific requirements of each piece
of equipment. A timeline to when these
tasks should be performed. A convenient
system for operators to record
inspection details and possible
complaints about the equipment.
Scheduled periodic staff meetings to
discuss the status of the fleet.
In-house or outsourced trained mechanics
to complete repairs and maintenance.
Preventative maintenance tasks should
include testing the equipment,
inspection, lubrication, cleaning,
repair, replacing worn parts. Remember
that equipment models differ in various
ways, so it's important to consider
manufacturer recommendations before
swapping those tires or using the wrong
oil on the hydraulic system. Specific
maintenance tasks may include changes to
engine oil and filters, belts and hoses,
cooling system, brake system, exhaust
system, transmission fluid, suspension
system. For a complete maintenance
checklist, visit
equipmentandcontracting.com.
Software programs are an invaluable tool
to develop, implement, and maintain a
fleet maintenance program. These
telematics systems gather data relating
to the various aspects of the fleet,
including fuel usage, mileage, operator
time, tire logs,
claims and accidents, inventory
management, stock reports. Integrating a
new operator should emphasize initial
training that focuses on mapping routes,
economical driving, the use of
telematics systems, and job safety. Once
an operator has been integrated into the
fleet, there are three crucial elements
to keep an eye on: speed, fuel, and
safety. Speed is an obvious risk to both
the operator behind the wheel as well as
other members on the job site. But, poor
speed management can also result in a
decrease in fuel and emission
efficiency. This is where telematics
pays off. Utilizing the right software
can allow a fleet manager to easily
generate reports to uncover poor driving
habits before they become a bigger
issue. Fuel management is another
crucial key to managing operators. How
much time does your equipment spend
idling? Are your routes optimized for
fuel efficiency
and safety? Needless to say, nobody
wants an accident, particularly an
equipment-related accident, which is
considered to be one of the most deadly
and expensive injury claims. To ensure
safety, both new and veteran operators
should continue to be educated with the
latest training and fleet safety rules
and policies. What makes a good fleet
manager?
A good fleet manager should understand
all aspects of equipment care, equipment
tracking, and equipment safety.
Furthermore, they should have at least a
basic understanding of telematics
software. A good fleet manager is a
visionary. Consider the ramifications of
a fleet leader without a vision.
Accidents, lawsuits, wasted investments,
broken machinery, project delays.
The margin for error is slim, but with
modern technology, managers can execute
their vision with data-driven assurance.
And last, but not least, consistency is
key for any skilled fleet manager.
There's no better way to improve or
maintain fleet performance than to
remain consistent with equipment
repairs, regulating operators, and
perfecting schedules.
Well, that's all we got for now.
If you think we left anything out, be
sure to post in the comments section
below.
And don't forget to visit
freeconstructionmagazine.com
to receive your free subscription to
Equipment and Contracting Magazine.

A good fleet manager is a visionary. Consider the ramifications of a fleet leader without a vision. Accidents, lawsuits, wasted investments, broken machinery, project delays. The margin for error is slim, but with modern technology, managers can execute their vision with data-driven assurance. And last, but not least, consistency is key for any skilled fleet manager. There's no better way to improve or maintain fleet performance than to remain consistent with equipment repairs, regulating operators, and perfecting schedules. Well, that's all we got for now. If you think we left anything out, be sure to post in the comments section below. And don't forget to visit freeconstructionmagazine.com to receive your free subscription to Equipment and Contracting Magazine.

metadata.title: Contracts L45 Part 2: Warranties: express, merchantability and fitness | Lewis v. Mobil Oil
metadata.author: First Year Law - CONTRACTS
metadata.shortDescription:
A seller's affirmation of fact, promise, description or sample that becomes part of the basis of the bargain is an express warranty, presumed part of the bargain without proof of reliance; mere opinion, commendation or value is not (UCC § 2-313). A merchant impliedly warrants that goods are merchantable, fit for their ordinary purposes as buyers of such goods reasonably expect (§ 2-314). A seller who has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and reliance on the seller's skill or judgment impliedly warrants fitness for that purpose (§ 2-315). Leading cases: Keith v. Buchanan (Cal. Ct. App. 1985), Lewis v. Mobil Oil Corp. (8th Cir. 1971), Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (Mass. 1964).

Study kit, quiz and cases: https://firstyearlaw.com/contracts/L45.html

First Year Law: Contracts, Lecture 45, Part 2 of 2, with Bob DesLauriers. Module: Module 15 - Sales under the UCC.

Key points of the lecture:
- Casebooks teach: Article 2 gives three warranties. Express is made by what the seller says (§ 2-313). Merchantability is made by what the seller is (§ 2-314). Fitness for a particular purpose is made by what the buyer relies on (§ 2-315).
- Statute (§ 2-313): an affirmation of fact, promise, description, sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain is an express warranty. No formal words or intent are needed, but value, opinion or commendation is not a warranty.
- Held (Keith v. Buchanan, Cal. Ct. App. 1985): brochure statements that the boat was 'very seaworthy' were specific, unequivocal affirmations of fact. Reliance need not be proved, and the seller did not overcome the presumption. Express warranty established; breach to be tried on remand.
- Held (Keith): an inspection on land that could not reveal seaworthiness did not waive the warranty. There was no fitness warranty, because the buyer relied on his own experience and experts.

Cases in this part:
- Lewis v. Mobil Oil Corp., 438 F.2d 500 (8th Cir. 1971)
- Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room, Inc., 347 Mass. 421 (1964)

Full course playlist: "Contracts - First Year Law" on this channel. Watch in order: Part 1, then Part 2.

General information, not legal advice. Not a law school course for credit; no degree or certificate. Case quotations are checked against the published opinions.

segments.text: Now a buyer who did rely.
Cove, Arkansas.
A man has run a sawmill since nineteen
fifty six.
In nineteen sixty three he converts to
hydraulic equipment, and in November nineteen
sixty four he installs it.
He asks Frank Rowe, the local Mobil dealer
he has bought from for years,
for the proper hydraulic fluid to operate
his machinery.
Rowe said he didn't know what the proper
lubricant for Lewis' machinery was,
but would find out.
The only information given was that the
pump was a gear type pump.
Rowe asked nothing more.
Rowe checked with Mobil and sold him Ambrex
eight ten, a straight mineral oil with
no chemical additives.
Within days, the oil changed color,
foamed over, and got hot.
Six months later the whole system failed
and was replaced.
Over the next two years six new pumps broke
down.
The mill owner kept asking Rowe to be sure
he was supplying the right oil.
Ambrex kept coming.
In May nineteen sixty seven a Mobil engineer
finally visits the mill.
The system is flushed, and on his recommendation
a new oil with additives goes in,
principally a defoamant.
Following these changes, plaintiff's system
worked satisfactorily up until the time
of trial, some two and one half years later.
The jury gave the mill owner eighty nine
thousand two hundred and fifty dollars.
The Eighth Circuit, in Lewis against Mobil
Oil, nineteen seventy one,
Judge Gibson, affirmed the warranty.
Under this provision of the Code,
there are two requirements for an implied
warranty of fitness.
That the seller have reason to know of
the use for which the goods are purchased,
and that the buyer relies on the seller's
expertise in supplying the proper product.
Both of these requirements are amply met
by the proof in this case.
Mobil argued that the buyer never said
he needed additives and never gave enough
information to work it out.
The court answered with the statute's own
comment.
The buyer need not bring home to the seller
actual knowledge of the particular purpose
for which the goods are intended or of
his reliance on the seller's skill and
judgment, if the circumstances are such
that the seller has reason to realize the
purpose intended or that the reliance exists.
And then the sentence that decides these
cases.
Here Lewis made it clear that the oil was
purchased for his system, that he didn't
know what oil should be used,
and that he was relying on Mobil to supply
the proper product.
If any further information was needed,
it was incumbent upon Mobil to get it before
making its recommendation.
The seller who undertakes to choose must
ask the questions.
The buyer who says I do not know has done
his part.
Mobil tried one more argument,
that the mill's system was abnormal,
with poor filtration and too much air.
The court called that a causation question,
not a warranty question, and added this.
The whole point of an implied warranty
of fitness is that a product be suitable
for a specific purpose, and that a seller
should not supply a product which is not
so suited.
Now merchantability, and a bowl of chowder.
Boston, Saturday, the twenty fifth of April,
nineteen fifty nine, about one in the afternoon.
A woman born and brought up in New England
takes her sister and her aunt to lunch
at the Blue Ship Tea Room,
on the third floor of an old building on
T Wharf which overlooks the ocean.
She orders clam chowder.
There is none.
She orders a cup of fish chowder.
A small bowl arrives, hot,
milky, haddock and potatoes in chunks.
She stirs it in an up and under motion,
for an even distribution of fish and potatoes.
She eats three or four spoonfuls and stops.
Something is lodged in her throat.
Two esophagoscopies at the Massachusetts
General Hospital later, a fish bone is
found and removed.
She sues the restaurant for breach of the
implied warranty of merchantability.
The jury finds for her.
The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts,
in Webster against Blue Ship Tea Room,
nineteen sixty four, Justice Reardon,
reversed, and did it with a whole cookbook.
We must decide whether a fish bone lurking
in a fish chowder, about the ingredients
of which there is no other complaint,
constitutes a breach of implied warranty
under applicable provisions of the Uniform
Commercial Code.
The court traced chowder from the cauldrons
of Brittany through Newfoundland to New
England, quoted a recipe from Daniel Webster
in which the removal of fish bones is not
mentioned at all, and quoted Fannie Farmer,
who boils the head, tail and backbone and
adds the liquor to the pot.
In the construction of chowders in these
parts in other years, worries about fish
bones played no role whatsoever.
Then the holding.
It is not too much to say that a person
sitting down in New England to consume
a good New England fish chowder embarks
on a gustatory adventure which may entail
the removal of some fish bones from his
bowl as he proceeds.
We should be prepared to cope with the
hazards of fish bones, the occasional presence
of which in chowders is, it seems to us,
to be anticipated, and which,
in the light of a hallowed tradition,
do not impair their fitness or merchantability.
Notice what the court did and did not decide.
It drew a line.
We sense a strong distinction between them
and those relative to unwholesomeness of
the food itself, and it named tainted mackerel
on the other side.
Stones in beans, trichinae in pork,
a foreign substance, those breach the warranty.
A bone that belongs to the fish in a fish
dish does not.
The court borrowed an Ohio case on oyster
shell.
The possible presence of a piece of oyster
shell in or attached to an oyster is so
well known to anyone who eats oysters that
we can say as a matter of law that one
who eats oysters can reasonably anticipate
and guard against eating such a piece of
shell.
The test is what the ordinary buyer of
these goods reasonably expects.
Fit for the ordinary purposes for which
such goods are used, and the ordinary purpose
of chowder includes fishing for bones.
Put the three side by side.
Keith, a specific factual statement in
a brochure, an express warranty,
and reliance is presumed.
Lewis, a buyer who said I do not know and
a seller who said I will find out,
a fitness warranty, and the seller had
to ask the questions.
Webster, a restaurant that is a merchant
in chowder, a merchantability warranty,
and no breach because the hazard was one
the ordinary eater anticipates.
One question runs through all three.
What did the seller undertake,
by his words, by his trade,
or by his choice?
Now let's change one fact.
The brochure had said only that the Island
Trader is the finest cruising yacht on
the market today.
Choose an answer before I go on.
Then there is no express warranty.
That is an affirmation merely of the value
of the goods, a statement of opinion or
commendation.
It lacks specificity, it asserts no fact
about the boat that can be true or false,
and no reasonable buyer treats it as anything
but sales talk.
The Keith court found a warranty because
seaworthy is a condition of the vessel,
specific and unequivocal.
Finest on the market is a chisel that cuts
nothing.
Change one fact again.
The mill owner had walked into the dealer's
office and asked for Ambrex eight ten by
name, because a magazine had recommended
it.
Choose.
Now the fitness warranty fails,
for the reason the boat buyer's failed.
The buyer selected the product himself.
The seller had no reason to know that he
was being relied upon, and the buyer did
not in fact rely on the seller's skill
or judgment.
The merchantability warranty may remain,
if the oil is unfit for the ordinary purposes
of a hydraulic oil, but fitness for this
mill's particular system was never undertaken
by Mobil.
Reliance is the hinge of section two dash
three fifteen.
Change one fact a third time.
What lodged in her throat was not a fish
bone but a fragment of glass from a broken
bowl.
Choose.
Then the warranty is breached.
The Webster court was explicit that it
was deciding about a bone that belongs
in a fish dish, and that there is a strong
distinction between such cases and those
of foreign substances and unwholesome food.
Glass is not a hazard the ordinary eater
of chowder anticipates, and no hallowed
tradition puts it there.
The goods were not fit for the ordinary
purposes for which such goods are used.
The chowder was unmerchantable.
Here is what people get wrong here,
and why it is tempting.
The first mistake is to demand proof of
reliance for an express warranty.
The old law did.
The Code does not, and Keith says the concept
has been purposefully abandoned.
The seller must prove the bargain did not
rest on the statement at all.
The second mistake is to confuse the two
implied warranties.
Merchantability asks whether the goods
do what such goods ordinarily do.
Fitness asks whether they do what this
buyer needed, and it arises only where
the seller knew the need and the buyer
relied.
The third mistake is to think that any
inspection by the buyer wipes out the seller's
express words.
It does not, unless the defect was actually
discovered and waived, and an inspection
that could not have revealed the defect
waives nothing.
Here is the rule, in one breath.
A seller's affirmation of fact,
promise, description or sample that becomes
part of the basis of the bargain is an
express warranty, presumed part of the
bargain without proof of reliance,
but mere opinion, commendation or value
is not.
A merchant in goods of the kind impliedly
warrants that they are merchantable,
fit for their ordinary purposes as buyers
of such goods reasonably expect.
And any seller who has reason to know the
buyer's particular purpose and that the
buyer is relying on the seller's skill
or judgment to select suitable goods impliedly
warrants that they are fit for that purpose.
Now, five questions in the study kit.

metadata.shortDescription:
Can outsourcing really destroy a successful company?

In this video, we break down the سقوط of Kelsey-Hayes Windsor, once a leading wheel manufacturer in Canada, and how poor outsourcing decisions led to its downfall.

You’ll learn:
- The hidden risks of outsourcing
- How companies lose control of their supply chain
- Real business lessons you can apply today

If you're interested in:
business failures, outsourcing risks, case studies, supply chain mistakes

→ This video is for you.

Subscribe for more real-world business breakdowns.

segments.text: November 2nd, 1990. Howard Avenue,
Windsor, Ontario. The last shift walked
out. No ceremony, no speeches. Just 450
men and women pulling on their coats in
the gray November cold, [music] stepping
through a gate that would never open for
them again. The machinery they left
behind, presses, [music]
dyes, stamping lines built over decades,
was already tagged for removal. [music]
Destination: Romulus, Michigan. Price:
$8.5 [music]
million.
77 years.
Sold for
>> [music]
>> $8.5 million.
This was the factory that Henry Ford
personally requested. The factory where
in December 1936, [music] a young union
organizer pulled the main power switch
and ignited a labor movement that gave
every Canadian [music] worker the rights
they still hold today. the factory that
put steel wheels on virtually every car
rolling off a Canadian assembly [music]
line for half a century. And it was
gone. Not after a slow decline, not
after years of warning, but 11 months
after a new owner signed the check. How
does a factory that helped build [music]
a nation get erased in under a year? The
answer isn't foreign [music]
competition. It isn't automation. It's
something far more calculated and far
more Canadian [music] than either of
those.
In 1910, Henry Ford had a problem. He
was building cars faster than anyone in
history, and he was running out of
wheels to put on them.
He needed a supplier he could trust,
someone close enough to Detroit to keep
pace with the Rouge, but operating under
Canadian tariff rules that made crossber
importing expensive.
He turned to a Detroit wheelmaker named
John Kelsey and made him a simple
proposition.
Set up on the Canadian side of the river
and Ford would be his first customer.
Kelsey didn't hesitate. In November
1913, the Kelsey Wheel Company opened
its doors on Howard Avenue in Windsor,
Ontario, a short drive from the
Ambassador Bridge, directly across the
river from the city that was becoming
the automotive capital of the world. The
location was not accidental. Windsor
was, in every practical sense, Detroit's
Canadian shadow. The same industry, the
same labor pool, the same steel and
stamping culture, separated by a river
narrow enough to see across on a clear
morning. The early years were
straightforward and relentless. Kelsey's
plant turned out wooden hickory spoke
wheels for Ford, Chalmer's, Studebaker,
and Hutmobile. When the First World War
came, the factory pivoted without
missing a beat. military wagons, gun
carriages, ordinance wheels for the
British and Canadian war effort. By
1919, the plant had doubled in size. The
work was hard, the hours were long, and
there was always more of it. But wood
was already dying. Through the early
1920s, wire wheels were taking over the
market. Lighter, transferable between
axles, cheaper to produce at scale.
Kelsey's Windsor plant made the
transition along with the rest of the
industry. Then in 1927 came the merger
that would define the next six decades.
Kelsey Wheel combined with its main
American rival, the Hayes Wheel Company
to form the Kelsey Hayes Wheel Company.
Two Wheel Dynasties now won. The Windsor
plant became the Canadian arm of a
growing continental operation, and the
best was still ahead. In 1934, Kelsey
Hayes engineers in the United States
developed something that would quietly
change every road on the planet. The
drop center steel wheel. A singlepiece
stamp steel rim, stronger and cheaper
than anything before it, perfectly
suited for the pneumatic tires that were
becoming standard on every new vehicle.
It replaced the wooden spoke wheel
almost overnight and became the industry
standard within a few years. every car,
every truck, every bus, steel wheels,
and for decades, a significant share of
them came from Windsor. By the time the
Second World War arrived, the Howard
Avenue plant was no longer a startup
finding its footing. It was an
established humming piece of Canadian
industrial infrastructure, one that once
again shifted to war production when
called upon and shifted back afterward
without losing a step. Windsor had built
something real on Howard Avenue,
something that employed families,
anchored a neighborhood, and connected a
midsize Canadian border city to the
economic engine of the continent. What
no one could have predicted in those
early years, least of all Henry Ford,
who simply needed wheels, was that this
factory was about to become the site of
something far more consequential than
anything it ever manufactured. By the
1950s, Kelsey Hayes Windsor had settled
into a rhythm that felt, to everyone who
worked there, like it could last
forever. The post-war boom was real, and
it was enormous. Canadian families were
buying cars at a rate the country had
never seen. Ford, GM, and Chrysler were
running their Canadian assembly plants
at full capacity. Windsor, Ashawa, St.
Thomas, Oakville. And every one of those
cars needed wheels, steel wheels,
stamped, finished, and shipped from
places exactly like Howard Avenue.
Kelsey Hayes Windsor was at the center
of that supply chain. The plant ran
multiple shifts. The parking lot filled
before dawn and emptied well after dark.

corporate consolidation,

overcapacity, aging infrastructure, a

When a corporation has been saved by a
