It's something far more calculated and far more Canadian [music] than either of those. In 1910, Henry Ford had a problem. He was building cars faster than anyone in history, and he was running out of wheels to put on them. He needed a supplier he could trust, someone close enough to Detroit to keep pace with the Rouge, but operating under Canadian tariff rules that made crossber importing expensive. He turned to a Detroit wheelmaker named John Kelsey and made him a simple proposition. Set up on the Canadian side of the river and Ford would be his first customer. Kelsey didn't hesitate. In November 1913, the Kelsey Wheel Company opened its doors on Howard Avenue in Windsor, Ontario, a short drive from the Ambassador Bridge, directly across the river from the city that was becoming the automotive capital of the world. The location was not accidental. Windsor was, in every practical sense, Detroit's Canadian shadow. The same industry, the same labor pool, the same steel and stamping culture, separated by a river narrow enough to see across on a clear morning. The early years were straightforward and relentless. Kelsey's plant turned out wooden hickory spoke wheels for Ford, Chalmer's, Studebaker, and Hutmobile. When the First World War came, the factory pivoted without missing a beat. military wagons, gun carriages, ordinance wheels for the British and Canadian war effort. By 1919, the plant had doubled in size. The work was hard, the hours were long, and there was always more of it. But wood was already dying. Through the early 1920s, wire wheels were taking over the market. Lighter, transferable between axles, cheaper to produce at scale. Kelsey's Windsor plant made the transition along with the rest of the industry. Then in 1927 came the merger that would define the next six decades. Kelsey Wheel combined with its main American rival, the Hayes Wheel Company to form the Kelsey Hayes Wheel Company. Two Wheel Dynasties now won. The Windsor plant became the Canadian arm of a growing continental operation, and the best was still ahead. In 1934, Kelsey Hayes engineers in the United States developed something that would quietly change every road on the planet. The drop center steel wheel. A singlepiece stamp steel rim, stronger and cheaper than anything before it, perfectly suited for the pneumatic tires that were becoming standard on every new vehicle. It replaced the wooden spoke wheel almost overnight and became the industry standard within a few years. every car, every truck, every bus, steel wheels, and for decades, a significant share of them came from Windsor. By the time the Second World War arrived, the Howard Avenue plant was no longer a startup finding its footing. It was an established humming piece of Canadian industrial infrastructure, one that once again shifted to war production when called upon and shifted back afterward without losing a step. Windsor had built something real on Howard Avenue, something that employed families, anchored a neighborhood, and connected a midsize Canadian border city to the economic engine of the continent. What no one could have predicted in those early years, least of all Henry Ford, who simply needed wheels, was that this factory was about to become the site of something far more consequential than anything it ever manufactured. By the 1950s, Kelsey Hayes Windsor had settled into a rhythm that felt, to everyone who worked there, like it could last forever. The post-war boom was real, and it was enormous. Canadian families were buying cars at a rate the country had never seen. Ford, GM, and Chrysler were running their Canadian assembly plants at full capacity. Windsor, Ashawa, St. Thomas, Oakville. And every one of those cars needed wheels, steel wheels, stamped, finished, and shipped from places exactly like Howard Avenue. Kelsey Hayes Windsor was at the center of that supply chain. The plant ran multiple shifts. The parking lot filled before dawn and emptied well after dark. On Howard Avenue, the end of a shift sounded like a small city releasing its breath. Hundreds of men and women streaming through the gate, the smell of pressed steel and machine oil still on their clothes, heading home to houses in the same neighborhoods where they'd grown up. For many Windsor families, Kelsey Hayes wasn't just a job. It was the job. The one your father had. the one that paid for the house, the car in the driveway, the week at the cottage in August. A man could start on the floor straight out of high school and retire 30 years later with a pension, benefits, and enough left over to help his kids get started. That wasn't a fantasy in Windsor in the 1950s and 1960s. That was Tuesday. The plant itself kept growing to meet demand. In 1964, Kelsey Hayes acquired additional land on both sides of the original Howard Avenue site. Parcels purchased from Matthews Lumber to the east and Windsor Ice and Coal to the south and expanded the facility significantly. New buildings went up, new lines were added. The operation that John Kelsey had started on a single plot in 1913 now occupied an entire industrial block. On the broader corporate level, Kelsey Hayes was becoming one of the most technically sophisticated automotive suppliers in North America. Through the 1960s, the company pioneered disc brake systems that became standard equipment on Lincoln Continentals and Ford Thunderbirds. By the early 1970s, 85% of Americanmade cars carried Kelsey Hayes braking components. The company had displaced Bendix as Ford's number one brake supplier, a position that represented not just revenue, but institutional trust built over decades. In Windsor, the product was steel wheels, and the plant was very good at making them. The Howard Avenue operation supplied wheels to all three of the major North American automakers operating in Canada. Ford across the river, GM in Ashawa, Chrysler down the road. The plant had the contracts, the equipment, the workforce, and the knowledge base that takes generations to accumulate. There is a particular kind of institutional confidence that settles into a factory that has been doing the same thing well for 50 years. The millites know every machine. The supervisors know every process. ers know every rhythm of the line, when it runs clean, when it needs attention, what a good shift sounds like versus a bad one. That knowledge doesn't appear on a balance sheet. It doesn't show up in a quarterly report, but it is real. And it takes decades to build and moments to destroy. In the mid 1960s, standing on the floor of the Kelsey Hayes plant on Howard Avenue, none of that felt fragile. Windsor was industrial Canada in full stride. The plant was expanding. The contracts were solid. Three generations of families were building their lives around the sound of that end of shift buzzer. But 1973 was coming. And with it, the first owner who didn't see a factory, only a line item. Before we follow the money that eventually destroyed this factory, we need to go back to the moment that made it matter. December 1936. Windsor is in the grip of winter, in the grip of something else, a tension that had been building on factory floors across North America for years. The Great Depression had hollowed out the middle class. Workers in the auto industry were earning poverty wages, working at speeds that cost them fingers, hands, and occasionally their lives with no union, no seniority, no recourse. If a foreman didn't like your face, you were out by noon. If the line sped up and you couldn't keep pace, that was your problem. At the Kelsey Hayes plant in Detroit, the American sister operation to Windsor, conditions had reached a breaking point. The assembly line in Department 49 ran so fast that workers were losing limbs trying to keep up. Complaints went nowhere. Grievances disappeared. Management held every card. Into this situation stepped two brothers from a workingclass family in Wheeling, West Virginia. Walter Ruther was 29 years old, recently fired from Ford for his union activities, and newly elected president of UAW Local 174 on Detroit's west side. His brother, Victor, worked inside the Kelsey Hayes plant. Together, they identified Kelsey Hayes as their first major target. Not because it was the biggest, but because it was exactly the right size, large enough to matter, small enough to organize, and critically, its brake drums and wheels supplied directly to the Ford Rouge complex, which meant a shutdown at Kelsey Hayes would Ford within days. The Ruthers were precise, patient, and methodical. They spent months building a network of trusted workers inside the plant, signing up members quietly, identifying the foremen who were watched, and the corners where conversations could happen without being reported to management. Company spies were everywhere, so every detail of the plan was kept to a small circle. Even the date was a secret until the last possible moment. The signal they chose was deceptively simple. A young woman on the line would pretend to faint. That was it. When she went down, Victor Ruther would move. December 10th, 1936. 20 minutes before the end of the first shift, she fell. Victor Ruther stepped away from his station, crossed the floor, and pulled the main power switch. The line stopped. into the sudden silence. He climbed on top of a crate and shouted words that would echo for decades. Strike! We've had enough of this speed up. For a moment, nothing happened. Then everything happened at once. Workers who had been waiting for exactly this signal began moving through the departments, pulling others away from their stations. Company officials attempted to enter the plant to remove machinery. Thousands of supporters blocked every doorway. Kelsey Hayes management held out for 10 days. On Christmas Eve 1936, they settled. By the standards of what unions would eventually win for workers, it was a starting point, not a destination. But what happened next was anything but modest. Factory after factory across Detroit's west side was calling in. workers who had been waiting for proof that it could be done, that a union could actually win against an automotive supplier, that management would actually sit down and sign something. One day before the Detroit strike began, the two actions fed each other across the river. The organizing energy moving in both directions simultaneously. When the UAW eventually won recognition from Ford in Windsor in the 1940s, when Canadian workers secured pensions in 1950 and a guaranteed annual wage in 1955, when the rights that define Canadian industrial employment to this day were codified into contracts, the chain of causation runs directly back to the floor of the Kelsey Hayes plant on Howard Avenue. The workers who stood at those stamping presses every day were not just making wheels. They were, without quite knowing it, building the architecture of the Canadian middle class. That is what made what happened in 1990 something more than a plant closure. A corporation can close a factory. It happens every year in every industrial country on Earth. Lines move. Markets shift, capacity gets consolidated. That is the arithmetic of manufacturing. But there is a different quality to losing a place that carried this kind of weight. The Kelsey Hayes plant on Howard Avenue was not simply a building where steel was pressed into circles. There is a fundamental difference between a company that makes things and a conglomerate that owns companies that make things. The first kind of organization measures its success by the quality of what comes off the line, the reliability of its contracts, the depth of its workforce knowledge. The second kind measures success by return on capital. And when a division stops delivering adequate returns, the response is not to invest and improve. The acquisition was a business decision made in a period when conglomerate expansion was standard corporate strategy across North America. Buy established companies, consolidate operations, extract efficiencies. It was the dominant management philosophy of the era taught in business schools from Toronto to Chicago. And Fuhof was simply doing what every large corporation was doing in 1973. But good intentions and good outcomes are not the same thing. For the workers on the floor in Windsor, none of this was directly visible. The line kept running, the shifts kept turning, the wheels kept shipping. But at the corporate level, Kelsey Hayes had become a problem to be solved rather than a business to be built. By the mid1 1980s, Fuhof itself was in serious financial difficulty, battered by the same forces reshaping American heavy industry. Import competition, volatile fuel prices, the deep recession of the early 1980s that hammered the trucking and automotive sectors simultaneously. The company that had acquired Kelsey Hayes as a stable, profitable asset, was now struggling to manage its own survival. And Kelsey Hayes, stranded in the middle of someone else's crisis, began accumulating the financial burden that would eventually make it vulnerable to exactly the kind of buyer it least needed. In 1987, after years of antitrust litigation and corporate restructuring, Kelsey Hayes was finally separated from Fuhof and reemerged as an independent entity, the KH Corporation. Some analysts believed KH could make a genuine go of it as a standalone operation. That is not a number a midsize automotive supplier can simply absorb and continue operating normally. Every dollar of revenue that should have been reinvested in equipment, research, and workforce development was instead being redirected toward interest payments. The company was solvent, but it was running in place, spending its energy servicing a debt load that made long-term investment nearly impossible. Capital improvements that had been discussed for years remained on the planning list, perpetually deferred. The plant was still productive. A plant built around steel wheel production in a building expanded in 1964 to meet the peak demand of a different era was carrying more capacity than the shifting market required. Founded in the mid 19th century, the company had grown into a global manufacturer of farm equipment, tractors, combines, harvesters with operations on every inhabited continent and a brand name that Canadian farmers had trusted for generations. At its peak, Massie Ferguson was one of the largest agricultural equipment manufacturers in the world. A source of genuine national pride in a country that had always understood itself at some level as a nation built on the land. By the late 1970s, that pride had curdled into crisis. A combination of factors, collapsing commodity prices, rising interest rates, catastrophic losses in key markets, and a management structure that had failed to adapt to a rapidly changing global industry drove Massie Ferguson to the edge of insolveny. The losses were staggering. The debt was existential. In 1980, the company's largest shareholder, the Argus Corporation, donated its shares to the employee pension plans and walked away. A move that said more clearly than any press release that the people closest to the company no longer believed it could survive. What followed was one of the most significant corporate bailouts in Canadian history. The government of Canada and the government of Ontario stepped in with a combined rescue package of $250 million funded by Canadian taxpayers structured to keep Massie Ferguson alive, operating, and headquartered in Canada. The conditions attached to that support were explicit. The company would maintain its Canadian operations, honor its obligations to Canadian workers, and remain a Canadian enterprise. Ottawa and Queens Park were not simply writing a check. They were making a statement about what kind of country Canada was one that stood behind its industrial institutions when they were in trouble. The workers in Windsor knew about the bailout. The workers in Brford knew. The retirees drawing pensions from Massie Ferguson plants across Ontario knew. This was their money. money collected from their paychecks, from their neighbors paychecks, from the taxes paid by every working family in the country, being deployed to save a company that employed people like them. In 1986, Massie Ferguson was restructured and renamed Varity Corporation. The name was new. The obligations were supposed to remain. They did not. Almost immediately after the renaming, Varity's new leadership under chief executive Victor Rice began repositioning the company away from agricultural equipment and toward automotive components. The farm machinery divisions were sold off or shuttered. The corporate identity that had been built over a century was dismantled with remarkable speed. And then came the move that angered Canadian politicians and workers in equal measure. Varity packed up its head office and relocated to Buffalo, New York, directly violating the terms of the agreement under which Canadian governments had provided the $250 million rescue. The reaction in Canada was immediate and furious. Politicians in Ottawa and at Queens Park condemned the move publicly. The word used most often in legislative debates and in newspaper editorials from Windsor to Vancouver was betrayal. A company that had been saved by Canadian public money, had taken that money, restructured itself on Canadian terms, and then relocated to the United States the moment it was financially stable enough to do so. The $250 million that Canadian taxpayers had contributed to keep Massie Ferguson alive had effectively subsidized the creation of an American headquartered corporation. No one was prosecuted. No money was recovered. The agreement, it turned out, had enforcement mechanisms that were either inadequate or never seriously pursued. Victor Rice and Varity Corporation moved to Buffalo, changed their stationary and continued operating from Buffalo. Rice executed the strategy he had been building toward all along. Varity would reinvent itself as an automotive components manufacturer. In 1986, the company acquired Dayton Walther, an American wheel and brake components producer. Then in November 1989 came the defining transaction. Varity purchased the KH Corporation Kelsey Hayes for $577 million in cash and securities. It was by any measure a significant acquisition. Kelsey Hayes at the time of purchase had 21 manufacturing facilities, 12 in the United States, four in Canada, and five in Europe. annual revenues of approximately $1 billion, a workforce of more than 7,400 employees, a reputation as the leading North American producer of electronically controlled anti-lock brake systems, technology that was becoming mandatory equipment on new vehicles, and represented the clearest growth opportunity in the entire automotive supply sector. The four Canadian plants included the Windsor operation on Howard Avenue, still producing steel wheels, still employing several hundred workers, still running on equipment and infrastructure that stretched back decades. From Varity's perspective in Buffalo, the acquisition of Kelsey Hayes was a transformation. The company was no longer a struggling former farm equipment manufacturer trying to find its footing. It was now a serious automotive supplier with a billiondoll revenue base and genuine technological leadership in anti-lock braking. Kelsey Hayes's revenues alone accounted for nearly $13 of Varity's total income in fiscal year 1990. But a billion dollar revenue base built on $577 million in acquisition costs layered on top of the existing debt that KH had been carrying since the Fuhoff years created a financial structure under enormous pressure. The interest obligations alone were staggering. Every plant in the Kelsey Hayes network needed to justify its existence not just as a productive facility but as a sufficiently profitable one. Profitable enough to service the debt that now sat above it. Windsor made steel wheels. Steel wheels were a mature low margin overcapacity product in 1989. The plant was old. The equipment needed investment. The market was contracting at the premium end toward aluminium. The arithmetic was not complicated. 11 months after Varity signed the purchase agreement for Kelsey Hayes, the Howard Avenue plant was gone. The company that Canadian taxpayers had rescued in 1980 on the explicit condition that it would remain Canadian and protect Canadian workers had used those nine years of stability to position itself to make exactly this kind of decision. efficiently, legally, and without a moment's hesitation. The workers on Howard Avenue never had a chance. They were never part of the calculation. November 1989, the ink on the Varity purchase agreement was barely dry. For the workers at the Howard Avenue plant, the change of ownership registered as background noise, the kind of corporate reshuffleling that happened regularly in the automotive supply industry and rarely changed anything on the floor. A new name on the letterhead, a new set of executives in the head office. This time in Buffalo instead of wherever they had been before. The line still ran. The orders were still coming in. The end of shift buzzer still sounded at the same time every day. What the workers could not see was what was happening in the spreadsheets. Varity had paid $577 million for Kelsey Hayes. That purchase price combined with a debt load KH had been carrying since the Fuhoff years meant the new parent company was operating under an obligation structure that left almost no room for tolerance. Every facility in the network was being evaluated not on its history, not on its workforce, not on the institutional knowledge accumulated over decades, but on a single question. Is this plant generating sufficient return to justify its continued existence? For Windsor, the answer was becoming harder to defend with each passing month. The global steel wheel market in 1989 and 1990 was experiencing exactly the kind of structural overcapacity that makes accountants reach for red pens. Too many plants across North America and Europe were chasing a market that was not growing. The major automakers were under intense pressure to reduce costs throughout their supply chains. And when a customer with the purchasing power of Ford or GM asks its suppliers to cut prices, the suppliers with the oldest equipment and the highest cost structures are the first to feel the squeeze. Howard Avenue had been built in 1913, expanded in 1964. The infrastructure was aging. The equipment repeatedly deferred through the debt laden fruhoff years and the financially constrained KH independence period had fallen behind what a competitive lowcost steel wheel operation required. Retooling the Windsor plant to the standard needed to compete long-term would require capital investment that Varity carrying its enormous debt load was in no position to provide. Through the winter and spring of 1990, the internal reviews continued. The numbers kept pointing in the same direction. Windsor was not the only Kelsey Hayes facility under scrutiny, but it was among the most vulnerable. A single product operation in an aging building in a highcost Canadian labor market, making a commodity product in a saturated global market. By midsummer 1990, the decision had effectively been made. What remained was the process of formalizing it, preparing the legal documentation, arranging the sale of the equipment, and determining the precise timing of the announcement. The workers on Howard Avenue went to work every morning through the summer and into the fall, unaware that the building they walked into each day had already been written off. That is perhaps the detail that stays with you longest, not the closure itself. Plant closures happen and always have, but the gap between the moment a decision like this is made in a boardroom and the moment the people it affects are told. Months in this case, months during which 450 people planned their lives, paid their mortgages, enrolled their children in school, made the 10,000 small decisions of ordinary existence. While somewhere in Buffalo, the paperwork was being prepared to end it. October 18th, 1990, a Thursday, Kelsey Hayes Canada issued a press release at some point during the business day. It was three paragraphs long. It stated that the Windsor steel wheel manufacturing plant would be closed by November 2nd, 15 days away, citing grave operational problems and mounting losses due to significant overcapacity in the steel wheels manufacturing industry. It confirmed that all production machinery and equipment would be sold to the Kelsey Hayes company in Romulus, Michigan for $8.5 million. It noted that Kelsey Hayes Canada would continue operating its break component divisions in Woodstock and St. Cathine's. That was it. Three paragraphs, 15 days, 77 years. Many of the 450 workers did not hear the news from their employer. They heard it the way people heard important news in 1990 on the radio, driving home from the shift that, had they known would have felt very different. Some heard it from neighbors. Some heard it from family members who had caught the story on the afternoon news. The plant itself did not hold a meeting. There was no assembly, no address from management, no moment where the people whose working lives were about to end were told directly face to face that it was over. In the days that followed the announcement, the reality of what 15 days actually meant became clear. There was no negotiation. The union local 195, the same local that Victor Ruther's sit-down strike had founded 54 years earlier on this exact site, had no meaningful leverage. The decision had been made at a level far above the plant in a corporate structure that stretched from Windsor to Romulus to Buffalo and ultimately to the financial institutions holding Varity's debt. A local union in a midsized Canadian city had no mechanism to reverse an arithmetic conclusion reached by a billion-doll corporation managing a $600 million debt obligation. What local 195 could do and did was fight for the best possible severance and transition support for its members. That fight mattered to the people it helped, but it did not change the outcome. Meanwhile, the dismantling began. The millites, the skilled trades people who had spent years, in some cases decades, maintaining the machinery on the Howard Avenue floor, were given the task of preparing their own plant for removal. They tagged the equipment. They disconnected the lines. They loaded onto trucks the presses and dyes and stamping machinery that they knew better than anyone else alive. Machinery they had repaired at midnight. and coaxed back to life on a Friday afternoon when a breakdown threatened to kill the shift's production numbers. They did this work with the professionalism that skilled trades people always bring to a job because that is what you do when you have taken pride in your work your entire career. And then they drove home for the last time. The equipment went south to Romulus. The purchase orders, the existing contracts with Canadian automakers went with them. the institutional knowledge, the process expertise, the decades of accumulated understanding of how to run that particular operation that went nowhere. It simply ceased to exist. By November 2nd, [clears throat] 1990, the Howard Avenue plant was empty. the railway spur line that had served Kelsey Hayes for decades. The short branch that had also fed Champion Spark Plug and the other industrial operations that once made that stretch of Windsor hum was torn up shortly after the closure. The tracks that had carried raw steel in and finished wheels out that had connected Howard Avenue to the Continental Rail Network and through it to every assembly plant in Canada were pulled from the ground and hauled away. Windsor had seen plant closures before. It would see more after. But there was something specific about this one. Something in the combination of the history, the speed, the ownership chain, and the particular cruelty of the arithmetic that lodged itself in the city's memory in a way that purely economic events rarely do. a man whose father had spent 38 years on that floor, who had retired from Kelsey Hayes and died at 66 in 1987, just 3 years before the closure, just short of seeing what became of the place that had defined his working life, said it as plainly as it can be said. His father never missed a day. 38 years, not once. That was what the plant got from the people who worked there. What the people who worked there got in the end was 15 days notice and a check for the equipment. The building didn't disappear. That is one of the quiet ironies of industrial closure. The physical structure outlast the institution that gave it meaning. Standing on the same ground under the same roof as a reminder that the site still exists even when everything that made it significant does not. The 254,000q foot facility on Howard Avenue was too large and too solid to simply sit empty for long. By 1992, less than 2 years after the last Kelsey Hayes worker walked out, a new occupant had moved in. Veltry Canada Limited, the Canadian division of a Michigan-based metal fabrication company, took over the building and began producing welded underbody components for the automotive industry. The customers were familiar names. Daimler Chrysler's Windsor minivan plant down the road, the Jeep Liberty plant in Toledo, the Bramly assembly facility outside Toronto, and the Ford Kentucky truck plant across the border. The work was still automotive. The building was still full of metal and machinery and the sounds of industrial production. From the outside on Howard Avenue, not much looked different, but the nature of what was happening inside had changed in ways that mattered. Kelsey Hayes Windsor had been a Canadian operation with a century of institutional history, a company that had grown from a single plot of land, through two world wars, through the birth of the Canadian labor movement into a major continental supplier with deep roots in the community around it. Veltry Canada was a branch plant, a division of a Michigan company established to serve the supply chain needs of American automakers operating in Canada with no particular connection to Windsor beyond the availability of a large vacant industrial building at the right moment. That distinction between an institution and a branch plant, between a company with history and a company with a lease is not visible from the street. The trucks still back up to the loading docks. The workers still arrive for their shifts. The neighborhood still hears the sounds of manufacturing. But the decision-making, the ownership, the strategic direction, none of it lives in Windsor. It never did again. Veltry Canada operated on Howard Avenue through the late 1990s and into the early 2000s, supplying the automotive assembly plants that were themselves under increasing pressure as the industry continued its long structural reorganization. In 2004, Veltry entered bankruptcy. The building and its associated properties were acquired by FlexeningGate, another Michigan-based automotive supplier, one that would grow over the following two decades into one of the largest private companies in the United States. The address on Howard Avenue became once again a facility in someone else's supply chain, useful, productive in its way, but no longer rooted. There is a particular kind of institutional memory that lives in a place when a company has been there long enough. The old-timers who remember how the line ran in 1962. The foreman who knows which press needs an extra 10 minutes to warm up in January. The maintenance crew that has memorized every electrical fault in a building that was wired in three different decades. When Kelsey Hayes closed, that memory left with the people who carried it. What remained was a building, well- constructed, appropriately located, entirely available. Windsor had lost something that cannot be rebuilt by putting a new tenant in an old space. Not because the new tenants did anything wrong, but because what had been lost was not square footage. It was continuity. It was the particular irreplaceable weight of a place that had mattered for a very long time. The railway spur was gone. The Kelsey Hayes name was gone. The local 195 presence on Howard Avenue, the union local that had been born in this building in December 1936, was gone. What remained was a structure that looked from the outside like a factory and was in some diminished sense still functioning as one. But the soul of the place had been loaded onto trucks in October 1990 and driven south across the border for $8.5 million. Kelsey Hayes was not the first factory Windsor lost and it was not the last. That is the context that transforms a single plant closure into something larger. Not just the story of one company on one street, but a chapter in a longer story about what happened to industrial Canada in the final decades of the 20th century and what that meant for the people who had built their lives inside it. Windsor in 1990 was already carrying scars. The Windsor transmission plants had closed before Kelsey Hayes, taking with it another block of skilled manufacturing jobs that had anchored families and neighborhoods for a generation. Other suppliers had consolidated, restructured, or quietly relocated production to lowerc cost jurisdictions. The process was not dramatic in the way that a single large closure is dramatic. It was gradual, plant by plant, shift by shift. a slow erosion of the industrial base that had made Windsor one of the most prosperous workingclass cities in Canada. What Kelsey Hayes represented in that context was not an isolated event. It was a data point in a pattern. And the pattern was becoming impossible to ignore. The men and women who had built their lives around Windsor's manufacturing sector had made a reasonable bet. They had chosen skilled trades over university degrees at a time when skilled trades paid better than most degrees and offered something a degree rarely could. The security of knowing that what you made was real, that it was needed, that it would always be needed. A car without wheels is not a car. A city without the people who make the parts is not an industrial city. The logic seemed sound. For 30 years, it was sound. What shifted was not the logic. What shifted was the ground beneath it. The automotive supply chain that had sustained Windsor was being reorganized by forces that operated at a scale far above the city, the province, or even the country. corporate consolidation, financial engineering, the relentless pressure on publicly traded companies to deliver quarterly earnings growth regardless of the long-term consequences. The emergence of lowerc cost manufacturing jurisdictions that made a plant built in 1913 and expanded in 1964 look on a spreadsheet like a liability rather than an asset. None of these forces asked Windsor for its opinion. None of them factored in the three generations of families who had organized their entire existence around the assumption that the work would continue. None of them assigned any value to the institutional knowledge, the community infrastructure, the union one benefits and pension rights that represented decades of negotiated progress. The human cost settled into Windsor slowly the way these things do. It was not visible in a single statistic or a single moment. It was visible in the trajectories of individual lives. The milright in his mid-50s whose specific skills had no direct equivalent in the jobs that were available after the closure. the woman who had expected to work another decade before retiring and instead found herself in a retraining program that prepared her for work that paid half what she had earned. The young man who had planned to follow his father into the plant and instead left Windsor entirely, joining the quiet outmigration of working age people that hollowed out industrial communities across Ontario through the 1990s. a son of a Kelsey Hayes worker put it in terms that required no economic analysis. He had been raised to believe the world got better for the next generation. That was the promise, not an extravagant promise, not a guarantee of wealth or ease, but the basic assurance that if you worked hard and stayed loyal, your children would have more opportunity than you did. What he saw instead in Windsor in the years after 1990 was that promise quietly being withdrawn. Not announced, not debated, simply no longer available. The tragedy of Kelsey Hayes is not only that it closed. Factories close. The tragedy is what its closure represented. The point at which the compact between a community and its industrial employers, a compact that had been built through struggle and negotiation in genuine mutual commitment over half a century, was revealed to be conditional, contingent, cancellable at 15 days notice by a corporation in Buffalo that had itself been saved by the taxes of the people it was now leaving behind. Windsor recovered in the way that resilient cities do. The automotive sector continued to anchor the local economy. New investments arrived, new facilities opened, the city adapted. But adaptation is not the same as restoration. What Windsor lost in the closures of the late 1980s and early 1990s was not simply employment. It was a particular quality of economic security, a specific kind of workingclass confidence that came from knowing that the plant down the street had been there for 70 years and would be there for 70 more. That confidence once broken does not fully return. The next generation of Windsor workers understood in a way their parents had not been required to that the ground could shift, that loyalty ran in one direction, that a corporation's relationship with a community lasted exactly as long as the numbers supported it. Kelsey Hayes taught Windsor that lesson in 15 days. December 10th, 1936. Victor Ruther pulls the main switch on the floor of the Kelsey Hayes plant in Detroit. The line stops. The silence lasts only a moment before the shouting begins. And in that moment, something shifts permanently in the relationship between workers and the corporations that employ them across North America. November 2nd, 1990. The line stops again. This time there is no shouting, no crowd gathering outside, no negotiation to come, just the sound of the last shift ending and then nothing. 54 years separate those two moments. In between them, the factory on Howard Avenue outlasted two world wars, the Great Depression, the Korean War, the oil crises of the 1970s, the recession of the early 1980s, and three changes of corporate ownership. It survived everything that history threw at it. What it could not survive was 11 months inside a balance sheet managed from Buffalo by a corporation that owed its existence to Canadian taxpayers and chose to forget that debt the moment it became inconvenient. That is the irony that stays with you, not the closure itself. As this documentary has tried to make clear, the economic logic behind the Windsor decision was not mysterious. overcapacity, aging infrastructure, a mature, low margin product in a consolidating market. These are the conditions under which plants close and they were genuinely present on Howard Avenue in 1990. The closure was not an act of malice. It was an act of arithmetic. But arithmetic does not exist in a vacuum. The arithmetic that closed Kelsey Hayes Windsor was performed by a company that had been rescued from insolveny by $250 million in Canadian public funds on the explicit condition that it would remain Canadian and protect Canadian workers. That condition was discarded when it became inconvenient. The arithmetic was performed inside a financial structure built on $577 million in acquisition debt. Debt that made the Windsor plant not just marginal but impossible before a single wheel was stamped in 1990. The arithmetic was performed on a factory whose workers had 54 years earlier done more to protect the rights of working people across this country than any single legislative act in Canadian labor history. None of that registered in the calculation. None of it was designed to. And that is precisely the point. The Kelsey Hayes story is not ultimately a story about wheels. It is not even at its core a story about one factory in one city. It is a story about what happens when the people who make decisions about industrial communities are structurally insulated from the consequences of those decisions. The executives who signed the closure order in October 1990 did not live on Howard Avenue. They did not send their children to the schools that depended on the tax base those 450 jobs supported. They did not use the community services that working families fund. They experienced the closure as a line item moving from the liability column to the resolved column. And then they moved on to the next item on the agenda. The workers experienced it differently. The man whose father spent 38 years on that floor, who never missed a shift, who raised a family on those wages, who retired and died in 1987, believing he had left something solid for the people who came after him. That man's son is still in Windsor, still watching what happens to the city his father helped build, still asking in the way that people who have witnessed this kind of thing always ask, whether the world was supposed to get better for the next generation. He was told it was. He was told that by the same culture, the same industrial compact, the same set of mutual obligations that the workers on Howard Avenue had fought to establish in December 1936. The idea that if you gave your working life to a place, that place had some reciprocal responsibility toward you, that the relationship was not purely transactional, that loyalty had a value that did not appear on a balance sheet, but was real nonetheless. The Kelsey Hayes plant is gone. The UAW local that was born in its walls, Canada's first local 195, no longer meets on Howard Avenue. The railway spur is gone. The stamping lines are gone, long since absorbed into operations in Michigan. The institutional memory carried by the people who worked there is fading, as it always does, one generation at a time. What remains is the building and the question. Not the question of whether the closure was legal. It was not the question of whether the economics were real. They were. But the deeper question, the one that Kelsey Hayes Windsor forces into the open and leaves there without a comfortable answer. When a corporation has been saved by a community's money, employs a community's workers, occupies a community's land, and benefits from a community's infrastructure. What does it owe that community when the numbers stop working in its favor? In Windsor in November 1990, the answer was 15 days notice. The workers who built the UAW on this site believed the answer should be something more than that. They spent their working lives trying to make it so. Whether the next generation of workers in Windsor, in every industrial city in this country, in every place where a factory has stood long enough to become part of what a community is, can hold corporations to a higher answer than 15 days is perhaps the most important unresolved question that Kelsey Hayes Windsor leaves behind. The line is stopped. The building is still there. The question remains

metadata.title: How Do Data Centers Get Power? (Grid to Server, Explained)
metadata.author: BIMandbeam
metadata.shortDescription:
How do data centers get power? Follow electricity from the grid to a single server: high voltage lines and the substation, transformers, switchboards, the UPS and its battery rooms, diesel generators, PDUs, and the A and B power paths feeding every rack.
 
In this video:
- Why many data centers have two separate grid feeds
- How transformers step the voltage down
- What switchboards do
- UPS: how batteries take over the instant the grid fails
- Generators and on-site fuel
- PDUs and dual power cords (A and B)
- Redundancy: N, N+1, 2N
- Why AI racks draw 10x more power than traditional racks
- What it means for architects: transformer yards, electrical and battery rooms, generators, noise
- 3 questions to ask on any data center project
 
Voltage and rack figures are typical orders of magnitude; they vary by country and project.
 
📘 Inside a Data Center, by Souhayl Othman: the full power chain explained in drawings, for architects and engineers.
Free preview → https://bimandbeam.com/book
 
CHAPTERS
0:00 A data center can never lose power
0:11 The grid and the substation
0:23 Transformers
0:33 Switchboards
0:43 UPS and batteries
0:58 Generators
1:10 PDUs and the A/B paths
1:23 Redundancy: N, N+1, 2N
1:36 Why AI changes the scale
1:48 What it means for architects
2:03 3 questions to ask
2:11 Learn more
 


 
#DataCenter #Power #AI
keywords: how do data centers get power

segments.text: A data center can never lose power, not
for a minute, not even for a second.
So, how does electricity travel from the
grid all the way to a single server?
Let's follow it.
It starts on the grid.
High voltage lines bring power to a
substation next to the site.
Many data centers have two separate
feeds, so one can fail without stopping
anything.
That voltage is far too high for a
server.
So, transformers step it down stage by
stage until it reaches a level the
building can use.
Next come the switchboards. Think of
them as the traffic control of the
building.
They send power to each room, and they
can isolate a fault in a fraction of a
second.
Now the key piece, the UPS, the
uninterruptible power supply. It sits
between the grid and the servers with
rooms full of batteries. If the grid
fails, the batteries take over
instantly. The servers never notice.
But batteries only last a few minutes.
That is enough time for the generators
to start.
Big diesel engines with fuel stored on
site can run the whole building for
days.
From the UPS, power flows to the data
hall.
Power distribution units feed each row
of racks.
And every server has two power cords on
two separate paths called A and B.
That is redundancy and is what you need.
N + 1 adds a spare. 2N doubles
everything.
More redundancy means more uptime, but
also more equipment, more space, and
more cost.
And AI is changing the scale.
A traditional rack draws 5 to 10 kW.
An AI rack can draw more than 100.
Same floor space, 10 times the power.
For architects, power shapes the
building. Transformer yards, electrical
rooms, battery rooms, generators with
their fuel tanks, exhaust and noise.
Often these spaces take much room as the
data halls themselves.
So ask early.
How many megawatts?
Which redundancy level? And where do the
generators go?
I explained the full power chain with
drawings in my book Inside a Data
Center, written for architects and
engineers. You can read a free preview.
The link is in the description.

metadata.author: NexLayer Tech
metadata.shortDescription:
How does a data center keep running when the power grid goes down?

In this episode of Data Center Fundamentals, we follow the complete power journey from the utility grid all the way to the server rack.

You'll learn how UPS systems, batteries, backup generators, ATS, PDUs, A/B power feeds, and redundant power supplies work together to keep critical infrastructure online.

We cover:

00:00 What If the Power Goes Out?
00:59 The Data Center Power Chain
02:02 Utility Power
02:48 UPS — The First Line of Defense
03:35 Why Do We Need Generators?
04:25 ATS and Power Transfer
05:09 PDU — Getting Power to the Racks
06:00 A Feed and B Feed
07:05 What Do N and N+1 Mean?
08:14 Power Sources
09:08 What Happens During a Power Failure?
10:09 Power Failure Inside the Rack
11:08 Monitoring Is Just as Important
12:04 Final — The Complete Picture

The goal of data center power isn't simply to provide electricity — it's to provide continuous, reliable power even when something fails.

segments.text: Think about what happens when the electricity goes out at home.
The lights turn off.
Your TV turns off.
Your Wi-Fi disappears.
But imagine the same thing happening inside a data center with thousands
of servers running websites, cloud applications, databases,
and network services.
A data center can’t simply wait for the electricity to come back.
That’s why data centers don’t depend on just one power source.
They use multiple layers of power protection—from the utility grid,
through UPS systems and generators,
all the way down to redundant power supplies inside individual servers.
So in this video, we’re going to follow electricity through a data
center and see how the entire power system actually works.
Let’s start with the big picture.
Power doesn’t come directly from the street into a server.
It travels through several stages.
Electricity normally starts with the utility provider.
From there, transformers and switchgear prepare and control the incoming
electrical power.
Then we have the UPS, or Uninterruptible Power Supply.
Power is distributed toward the data hall through electrical
distribution equipment and eventually reaches
the PDU, or Power Distribution Unit.
Finally, rack PDUs deliver electricity to servers, storage systems,
switches, routers, and other equipment.
But there’s another important part of this design:
the generator.
We’ll see why we need both a UPS and a generator in a moment.
Under normal conditions, most of the data center’s electricity comes
from the utility grid.
But the electricity arriving at a large facility may not be at the
voltage required by the equipment inside.

metadata.title: Why Data Centers Use Smaller Gas Turbines | 624 MW Power Plant Explained | Keentel Engineering
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
Why are modern data center power plants being built with multiple smaller gas turbines instead of a few massive generation units?

We explore the engineering behind data center power plants, using a recent 624 MW Texas project as a case study. The project involves eight approximately 78 MW gas turbines, creating a highly modular generation architecture designed around reliability, redundancy, availability, and delivery flexibility.

The engineering implications of using F-class gas turbines, including the impact of ambient temperature, turbine output, gearbox-based 60 Hz operation, maintenance, load following, and plant redundancy.

For large AI and hyperscale data centers, reliable electricity is becoming one of the most critical infrastructure challenges. Understanding how generation capacity is configured—and how that generation interacts with the electrical grid—is essential for data center developers, utilities, EPC contractors, power engineers, and project owners.

Learn more about data center and power system engineering from Keentel Engineering.

Established OEMs have order books that are essentially full through the back half of this decade, while an alternative proven OEM has an open factory slot sitting right in that gap. The core argument is straightforward. Data center demand has absorbed established supplier capacity years into the future. When lead time becomes the binding constraint, delivery availability starts to matter more than unit price or thermal heat rate. And this isn't a gamble on unproven technology. The diligence shows that the It has over 70 units installed globally and more than 4 million operating hours. It's an established design entering a market that's constrained purely by manufacturing capacity. Why eight turbines instead of two? This is where the engineering logic really starts. Compare two configurations delivering similar total capacity. Two large combined cycle units at 312 megawatts each, lose one and you lose 50% of your capacity instantly. That requires a grid connection or a massive reserve margin just to ride through the outage. And it comes with poor phase delivery. Even though thermal efficiency is high. Now look at eight mid-size simple cycle units at 78 megawatts each. Lose one and you only lose 12.5% of capacity. Easily absorbed by running reserve. You also get excellent phase delivery that matches load growth as the data center ramps up. At the cost of lower efficiency and eight times the auxiliary systems to maintain. The takeaway here matters. A data center is not a merchant power plant. Eight units isn't a compromise. It's a deliberate redundancy architecture built around uptime. Not thermal efficiency. Here's a subtler engineering decision hiding inside this turbine choice, the gearbox. A standard US F-class turbine is direct drive. It spins at 3600 RPM, the synchronous grid speed, with the turbine and generator locked together on one shaft. The AE64.3A takes a different approach. The turbine itself spins at its own optimal aerodynamic speed, and a reduction gearbox steps that down to 3600 RPM for the generator. Why does this matter? Small direct drive machines running at 3600 RPM are actually working against their own aerodynamic scaling. A gear train lets the turbine spin at whatever speed is aerodynamically ideal, which also enables global standardization. The same core machine can serve both 50 hertz and 60 hertz markets just by swapping the gear ratio. But that flexibility isn't free. The engineering reality is that the gearbox adds a highly loaded rotating component that requires its own lubrication, cooling, and vibration monitoring. And the torsional natural frequencies of the entire drivetrain change completely, requiring bespoke dynamic analysis for every installation. Once you have hot exhaust coming off eight gas turbines, you have to decide what to do with it, and there are three paths. Path one, simple cycle. High flexibility, lowest efficiency. The exhaust just vents out through the stack. Path two, combined cycle. High efficiency, high capital cost. The exhaust runs through a heat recovery steam generator to drive a steam turbine, but that introduces a large single point failure risk. Path three is the interesting one for data centers. Cogeneration. The exhaust routes to an absorption chiller, turning waste heat directly into chilling for the server load. It's an elegant efficiency play, but it comes with a real serious engineering consequence. Cogeneration is engineering-intensive, and it permanently ties the thermal power plant and the data center server cooling system into a single architecture with shared failure modes. If the turbine goes down, your cooling might go down with it. How this plant connects to the outside world changes almost everything about its engineering. Behind the meter operation makes islanding a central requirement. The plant must be able to carry its full load independently with no grid to lean on. That means extreme load rejection, block loading, and frequency and voltage control without an infinite bus to stabilize things. It also puts you under active regulatory scrutiny around co-location rules. Grid-connected operation is a different world. Islanding becomes optional. Control dynamics follow standard grid parallel protection coordination, and the regulatory exposure shifts to established generator owner and operator registration under NERC reliability standards. The bottom line, fast start capability is critical for behind-the-meter islanding, and it's a control and protection problem that's substantially harder than standard grid parallel operation. Zoom out to the grid level, and these turbines are doing something the industry desperately needs right now. As renewables, solar, wind, battery storage proliferate across the grid, that grid is losing something it used to take for granted, physical rotating mass. These synchronous machines provide three things inverter-based resources can't easily replicate. Inertia. The physical rotating mass resists frequency change, slowing the rate of change of frequency after a disturbance and buying time for governor response. Short circuit current. Synchronous machines inject massive fault current, raising system strength, while inverter-based resources are current limited and can trigger weak grid instability. And voltage source behavior. The machine provides a genuine physical voltage reference behind an impedance, unlike inverter-based resources that digitally track a measured phase. The headline point? 624 MW isn't just capacity. If connected correctly, it's a critical system strength asset for the grid it serves. Voltage stability requires its own toolkit, and there's a hierarchy of options here, each with different speed and behavior. Mechanically switched capacitors respond in seconds, in discrete steps, and their output is proportional to voltage squared. Great for steady-state voltage profile, but their capability collapses exactly when you need it most, when voltage drops. Static var compensators respond in cycles rather than seconds. Still proportional to voltage squared and work well for continuous control, where deep support isn't the primary driver. STATCOMs step it up further. One to two cycle response, constant current output that's actually proportional to voltage rather than voltage squared, making them best for weak grids and fast disturbance recovery. Though they have their own control dynamics. And then there's the synchronous condenser, governed by the machine's own physical capability, with excitation response in milliseconds and instantaneous inertial response. It's the best option for system strength and short circuit contribution, which circles back to why synchronous machines like these turbines matter so much on a grid full of inverters. Here's the part that doesn't show up on the turbine purchase order at all. Buying eight turbines is just the tip of the iceberg. Underneath it sits an enormous scope of balance of plant engineering. >> [clears throat] >> Electrical balance of plant? Eight step-up transformers, breakers, a collector bus, and a switchyard. Excitation and control? Automatic voltage regulators, power system stabilizers, and coordination logic across all eight units. Protection coordination? Generator, transformer, bus, interconnection, and islanding transition protection. On the other side, studies. Load flow, short circuit, arc flash, motor starting, and transient stability analysis. Auxiliary and station service systems, which are crucial for black start and islanded survival. And fuel supply. Gas pressure, conditioning, pipeline interconnection, and permitting. Every one of these systems has to be engineered and coordinated across all eight units simultaneously. The turbine purchase order is just where this work begins. Here's a risk that's easy to miss until it derails a schedule. Every North American interconnection requires validated dynamic models. For an OEM that's been absent from this market for 30 years, model availability is not guaranteed. Before signing the purchase order, there are critical questions that need answers. Do positive sequence and electromagnetic transient models exist at the fidelity required? Do they accurately represent this specific bespoke gearbox, excitation, and governor train? And does the developer actually have the legal rights to share those models with the transmission planner? If the answer to any of these is no, the consequence isn't a technical dispute. It's a hard schedule stop. Missing or unvalidated models mean the interconnection study simply cannot proceed, no matter how ready the physical equipment is. Beyond the electrical engineering, citing eight gas turbines in Texas creates a permitting footprint across three major fronts. Air and emissions. NOx and CO emissions dictate the post-combustion treatment required. SCR systems, water injection, and operating a highly flexible load following plant requires a permit explicitly written for varied load scenarios, not just a steady base load assumption. Water constraints. Texas water scarcity is a primary design input. Inlet air cooling, which is crucial for hot weather megawatt output, and any potential steam cycle both consume significant water volumes, directly shaping the plant configuration. And acoustics and sighting. Eight large industrial turbines create a massive acoustic source, requiring extensive noise attenuation dictated by the surrounding land use. So, how should a developer actually evaluate an OEM making a 30-year return to this market? There's real opportunity here, but each opportunity needs to be paired with specific diligence. Delivery slots are available precisely because established suppliers are booked out, but confirm the schedule is contractual with meaningful shipping and customs remedies if it slips. Pricing is aggressive for market entry, but evaluate the full life cycle cost. 30 years of spares and auxiliary power burn, not just the sticker price. Service comes with high incentive to succeed on these first projects, but verify actual 2028 North American field service depth and part stocking, not just promises. Standards claim to meet international specs, but verify compliance with the specific American listings, codes, and authority having jurisdiction requirements. And a dedicated generator package may simplify the interface, but vigorously define the engineering boundary between the turbine island and the balance of plant regardless. Step back and you can see this entire plant sitting at the intersection of three independent pressures. Market constraints, factory slots dictate turbine scale and supplier choice. Load requirements, data center criticality demands fractional redundancy, that 12.5% loss versus 50% loss we saw earlier. And grid physics, inverter heavy grids desperately need synchronous inertia and fault current. These three separate pressures happen to align perfectly to produce this exact plant architecture, the eight unit archetype. It's almost an accidental masterpiece of constraint-driven engineering. And here's the thing to remember, this window will eventually close as supply chains normalize. But the plants being built today under these conditions will operate for the next 30 years. Turning this kind of analysis into a built operating plant takes coordinated work across four disciplines. Interconnection and studies, load flow, short circuit, transient stability, EMT studies, and complex islanding and load rejection analysis. Models and compliance, the model deliverable specification, positive sequence and EMT validation, and NERC compliance structuring. Plant electrical design, step-up transformers, switch yards, generator protection, excitation coordination, and black start station service. And owners engineer services, technical diligence, EPC design review, bid normalization, and integrated commissioning oversight. That's the work Kentech Engineering does. Three decades, every side of the table, one standard, accountable engineering.

metadata.title: How To Estimate Equipment Cost In Construction
metadata.author: George Hedley | HardHat BIZCOACH
metadata.shortDescription:
🎁 Download George's FREE Contractor Profit Calculator + tools: https://hardhatbizcoach.com/contractor-profit-calculator/?video=60uc8gnDCiY

Construction estimating lives or dies on the details, and equipment costs are where contractors leak profit. George Hedley shows owners the right way to handle equipment in construction estimating, owned versus rented, so your bids stay competitive and your construction estimating protects every margin.

In this video:
• How construction estimating should treat equipment costs
• Owned versus rented, and what it costs you
• Why equipment is where contractors leak profit
• Keeping bids competitive without eating the margin

📞 Schedule a Complimentary Coaching Session with George: https://hardhatbizcoach.com/coaching/?video=60uc8gnDCiY

In this video, I explain how to estimate equipment cost in construction. I walk through how rental equipment costs are calculated using rental rates and added charges, and how owned equipment costs are calculated by totaling purchase price, return on investment, operating life, and more. Using examples such as a contractor pickup truck and other common construction equipment, I show how these costs are added over the equipment’s lifetime and converted into monthly or job-based rates that can be compared to rental company pricing.

04:04 Ownership cost components and operating expenses

videos.full_text: Hey folks, Machinery Pete here. Joined this morning by Luke Fritshaw, sales director for the Canadian uh prairie uh area up there for Ritchie Bros. And Luke, thanks for joining us this morning. >> Yeah, thanks for having me. Excited to jump on here and talk with you about all things auctions and what's going on in the equipment market. >> Well, I know how busy you are, Luke. Tough to catch. You guys got uh what? I think like 80 total machinery construction farm sales coming up right through the course the busy month of April here. So, you don't have a lot of free time. So, thanks for making time. >> Yeah, absolutely. It's a It's uh It's going to be a quite a run here when we usually start that mid-March right till the end of April. It's usually two to five auctions a day. So, it's an exciting time in the world. >> Yeah, folks, check out uh Ritchie Bros. website rbauction.com. As Luke said, you can you can page through all these upcoming auctions. And uh I love the pictures and videos you guys do, Luke. And uh boy, it looks like you got some just gangbuster farm auctions coming up here the next few weeks. >> Yeah, it's fantastic. There's some There's some beauties out there. Uh some nice ones out in Manitoba all the way across the prairies. There's There's a nice one kind of in every region. And it's It's fun to watch the the quality of the equipment, um the buyer activity right now, the registration activity's better than we've seen in the last couple years. So, uh the used equipment market um as much as there is still some out there and and everywhere you look uh in the auction space, we're see- still being able to uncover buyers and bidders from across North America and and even the globe. >> Yeah, it's really interesting what you touched on there, Luke. I was curious to get your take on it. Our Our auction data started to show in November kind of uh a little uptick uh across the US and Canada. And uh you know, times are obviously challenging uh in ag. But uh interesting mix. I mean, sales of new have been depressed now for for a while. And of course, the price of new is what it is, and uh it just seems to me like folks are really zoning in on on the used market, and in particular, you know, really good quality stuff. Just curious your take the last few months what you've seen. >> Yeah, we're we're seeing that for sure. Like we're we're we track a lot of the used equipment market up here in Canada, and just try and keep our eye on what's going on in the used market, and of course hearing how manufacturers and dealers are pulling back on what's available on the new side, naturally, you know, go back 15 years, it was kind of that same same program. They pull back, and and what's going to happen? Well, if you can't get your hands on a brand new one, you're going to be looking for that 1-year-old trade, that that 1-year-old used, maybe 1 to 3-year-old used to upgrade maybe what you have in the 5-to-10-year-old um vintage. So, we're definitely seeing a lot of action on that. Anything that's low-hour, well-kept, um in that, you know, size and make and model that guys want, we're still seeing a lot of strong action on it. Where where where we're seeing probably the most pressure, like I said, is that kind of 7-to-15-year-old um used equipment. There's, you know, it's it's a fine line. There's still those those um equipment categories that stay strong. The older they get, sometimes the stronger they get. Um but that's where we're seeing the most inventory is kind of in that 5-to-15-year mark. The the lower uh the newer stuff is still it's guys still want it. They still want to upgrade into that. Um and it's obviously that that also includes the newer technology and and a lot of the aspects of equipment that guys are really out there trying to pay for right now. >> Yeah, it's an interesting time. I've been tracking the market every day for 36 and 1/2 years. I don't know that I've ever seen a particular moment like this with uh you know, usually when when used values are starting to, you know, make a move north of a bit, to me and in the past it's always correlated to strong new sales. Uh farmers have money, they're aggressive across the board, but you know, that new side is just continued to be a little depressed now. So, with 1 2 3-year-old stuff, we're kind of seeing a thinning of the of the volume on the dealer lot. I'm just curious what, you know, you guys talk to tons of farmers. Uh and heavy equipment people, just curious what you guys are feeling out there. >> Yeah, there's it's it's tight out there for that advantage and I think there's, you know, there's a lot of those mud program farmers that are flipping every year, but then there's there's the guys that are kind of the next in line. They could they're continuing to do their flips into that 1-year-old stuff and it flows down the line and where we're seeing that bottleneck, like you said, is once you get to that 3 4 5 years old, it's less desirable and it's, you know, I heard heard you and Casey talking about it in the last podcast. It's it's that where it's like, "Do I need to upgrade?" You know, is that really an upgrade? How can I make what I have work versus, you know, jumping into a 5 to 10-year-old unit? Um it's there's less urgency to do that versus the you know, because it's they can have a 10-year-old unit, they want to go to a 5-year-old tractor, there's not a lot of things that are different for them and so it's like, "Do I spend that money now?" Or maybe cash is tight, maybe I just use what I have. And so, you see that softening in that area, but for the guys that are jumping into those newer ones, it is a big upgrade. They are seeing, you know, value in that upgrade, so they're willing to go and spend it. >> Yeah, and even a, you know, 1 2-year-old unit at auction, I mean, it's uh you know, it can be a big number, obviously, but then when you pull back and you're like, "Well, you know, gosh, what's a new a new one is uh quite a bit north of uh what the auction number is." So, I think uh you know, when you drift into warranty availability, you know, folks aren't buying new one thing they got to avoid is downtime. So, are you seeing Sounds like you're seeing maybe a growing interest in that late model stuff. Do you think that's tied to the I mean, farmers got to have reliable equipment to keep keep cranking, right? >> Yeah. Yeah, and I think it's just the it's a matter of I think [snorts] that's the biggest thing in the buying market right now is the buyers are selective, right? And so, it's like does it have warranty? What kind of work orders does it have? Like all those things mean so much. And so, if if you are even looking to sell and you have any vintage of equipment like, you know, we I can tell you right now that having some solid work orders, having history on it, what's been done, how it's been done, all those things just add value and and it's it's a hard value to peg, but it it adds a lot of value to your what you're going to sell. And so, when you think about that as as the buyers, they do look for that and are willing to spend more. And of course, you know, when you look at a 3-year-old unit, what it was new, call it a million-dollar unit, now, you know, you can buy it at auction for, you know, honestly, in the $500,000 range. That's where that's still a big number and it it holds those values, but you're obviously not paying that new price and you can get a unit that, you know, has been on the field, it's worked and, you know, you can if you can trust it with warranty and work orders and things like that, it's a it's a heck of a discount to be able to go get upgrade your fleet. >> Yeah, I I agree, Luke. I've been sort of for the last number of years as I analyze our data over the decades that just the data what it it seems to shout to me on the auction front is in that 3-7 year old range. Now you have the opportunity you know be selective and buy the right things at the right price but the opportunity for you is out there and I think you just have to you know get on the websites and and have a look because it's what you need is out there and you just got to be selective I think everyone's being selective as to how they're buying and what they're willing to spend but also that that comfort of you know what's the history on it where it's coming from. metadata.author: Farm Journal
metadata.shortDescription:
Pete's in North Carolina at the Edwards and Foster Farm retirement auction.  Their line of green machinery includes a 8345 R that proved just how strong the market is.

Hosted by Greg Peterson (aka “Machinery Pete”), the most trusted name in farm equipment, Machinery Pete TV brings to life the fascinating world of machinery – both new and used.  Along with up-to-the-minute industry headlines, “Machinery Pete TV” goes on the road to visit innovative dealerships, plus it gives viewers an inside look at some of the most talked about auctions across farm country.

segments.text: I'm Nick Mitchell. We sell a lot of farm
equipment throughout the country at a
lot of auctions, so we're able to
collect some cool data. The data tells
us how things are selling at the time,
so we share it with you and help you get
more for your equipment that you're
trying to sell online. In the month of
September, US tractors 100 horsepower or
greater saw a decrease in supply, but at
the same time, the prices both at
dealerships and at the auctions that we
go to are going up by at least 0.53%.
So, we think that there's an increase in
demand for these tractors. So, if you're
selling a tractor online 100 horsepower
or greater, maybe a John Deere, Kubota,
New Holland, right now might be a good
time to sell. You might get better
prices than normal just cuz of where the
market's at. Now, for a used medium duty
trucks in the US, we're talking box
trucks with no bed, industrial trucks.
For those, the supply over the last
month is decreasing, and it's also down
about 30% over this last year, but the
asking values both at auctions and at
dealerships over the last month is going
down as well. So, in the short term over
the last month, there just might be less
use of medium duty trucks in the United
States. Right now might not be the best
time to get the highest price for it.
Now, for used heavy duty trucks like
Peterbilts, Internationals, day cabs,
the supply is decreasing both over the
last month and throughout the year. So,
these heavy duty trucks are going fast.
At the same time, because there's less
of them, the prices are going up. So, if
you have a heavy duty truck, right now
might be a good time to sell. There
seems to be a lot of demand. Day cab
trucks saw the biggest drop in supply
last month, so a lot of people are
buying those. Also, sleeper trucks are
seeing the biggest drop in inventory or
supply over the last year. These sleeper
trucks are having a big increase in
selling price and value, so sleeper
trucks high commodity right now.
For used semi-trailers in the US, over
the year there's about a 35% decrease in
the supply of these semi-trailers. so
they're going fast. At the same time,
the demand or the asking prices both at
dealerships and at auctions is going up.
Over the last month, the prices went up
about 1 to 2% but over the year, the
prices are going up 7 to 14%. So, used
semi-trailers, hot commodity right now,
might be a good time to sell those.
For used heavy-duty construction
equipment, we're talking skid steers,
tractors, semi-loaders, excavators, the
supply is going down both over the last
month and over the entire year. Over the
year, it's gone down about 12%. Maybe
just right now, it's not a high-demand
thing and maybe it'll bounce back a
little more next year. Specifically, the
wheel skid loaders saw the biggest drop
in supply. Keep in mind, the prices
aren't going up. Loader backhoes also
are going down a lot in the supply and
the the asking prices aren't going up
that much. Maybe there's not as much
demand for these. Maybe not the best
time to sell those if you're wanting the
best price.
For used medium-duty construction
equipment, the supply is going down over
both the short-term and the long-term.
At the same time, the prices at auction
and at dealerships are also going down.
So, for these, we think that there is a
shrinking market or just not as much of
a need for these medium-duty
construction equipment pieces. And if
you're selling right now, maybe you
don't get the most value. Maybe you want
to hang on to it but still, maybe the
value will increase later.
For used combines in the US, the supply
is going down. Close to a 10% decrease
over the last year. The asking values at
auctions and at dealerships over the
last month are going down as well. So,
maybe just over the last month, there's
not as much of a need for these but over
the long-term or over the last year, the
prices are going up. 3% of an increase.
So, still, it seems that combines are a
hot commodity. They have a lot of value.
People want to buy them but just over
the last month, maybe people didn't need
them as much. That said, we are going
into December, which is a busier time of
the year. You can look for those prices
to increase pretty soon.
For used planners in the United States,
the supply is going up over the last
month about 3%, but over the last year,
the supply is going down about 15%. So,
there's still a lot of demand for these
planners. At the same time, the asking
values at dealerships and auctions are
going down. So, it just seems that over
the last month, maybe there hasn't been
as much of a need for planners, but over
the long term, there's been an increase
in the prices, and they've gone up about
5 to 15% over the last year. So, overall
this year, used planners, a lot of
people are buying them, but over the
last month, not so much action. So,
maybe going into October, this is
something to think about. Once we get to
December, I think people will be buying
a little bit more, so maybe you hold off
on selling a planner for right now, and
just come back a little bit later.
